title: Bad metallicity in the semi-quantum regime of the Hubbard model
comment: main text: 13 pages, 5 figures; SM: 21 pages, 8 figures
summary: Bad metals exhibit approximately $T$-linear dc resistivity beyond the Ioffe--Regel limit. That this behavior occurs in systems with radically different ground states suggests it is a generic manifestation of strong local correlations. We test this hypothesis in the infinite-$U$ Hubbard model with small hole densities using exact diagonalization to compute thermodynamic and transport properties of finite clusters. Upon cooling, we find an intermediate temperature range, an electronic analogue of the ``semi-quantum regime'' of liquid helium, in which quantum effects produce a roughly $T$-independent compressibility, yet the resistivity is $T$-linear and exceeds the Ioffe--Regel limit. Entry into this regime is accompanied by the formation of quasi-local ferromagnetic ``spin cages'' around doped holes, regions that facilitate local quantum motion embedded in a fluctuating spin background, analogous to the transient crystalline cages thought to control incoherent transport in semi-quantum liquid helium. Remarkably, despite the simplicity of the model, the bad metal behavior found here resembles that seen in various material platforms.

AI.tldr: Exact diagonalization of the infinite-U Hubbard model at small hole densities reveals an intermediate "semi-quantum regime" where compressibility is roughly T-independent while resistivity is T-linear and violates the Ioffe-Regel limit, driven by quasi-local ferromagnetic "spin cages" around doped holes.
AI.motivation: Bad metals show approximately T-linear dc resistivity beyond the Ioffe-Regel limit across systems with radically different ground states, suggesting a generic manifestation of strong local correlations. The authors test whether this is a generic feature of strong correlations by studying a minimal model.
AI.method: Exact diagonalization of finite clusters of the infinite-U Hubbard model at small hole densities, computing thermodynamic and transport properties.
AI.result: Upon cooling, an intermediate temperature range appears—an electronic analogue of the "semi-quantum regime" of liquid helium—with roughly T-independent compressibility but T-linear resistivity exceeding the Ioffe-Regel limit. This regime is accompanied by quasi-local ferromagnetic "spin cages" around doped holes that enable local quantum motion in a fluctuating spin background.
AI.conclusion: Despite the simplicity of the model, the bad metal behavior resembles that seen in various material platforms, supporting the hypothesis that bad metallicity is a generic consequence of strong local correlations.

title: Non-Abelian Anyon Condensation: a Path-Integral Monte Carlo Approach
summary: Transitions out of non-Abelian topological order are difficult to describe in microscopic quantum models with numerical methods that remain tractable at large scales. We develop a sign-free path-integral framework for Kitaev quantum doubles $\mathcal D(G)$ by organizing single-link perturbations in terms of non-invertible electric and magnetic 1-form symmetries that proliferate distinct anyon species. For any finite group $G$, an exact $\textit{matterization}$ isometry introduces vertex degrees of freedom and maps the link-only model onto a $G$ gauge--Higgs theory. Furthermore, the 1-form symmetries of the fixed point allow us to define generalized Fredenhagen--Marcu order parameters that become finite when the corresponding anyons condense. For $G = S_3$, quantum Monte Carlo simulations show that proliferating a non-Abelian electric anyon drives a first-order transition in which all nontrivial electric anyons condense. In the purely magnetic limit, the model reduces to a $(2+1)$D pure $G$ gauge theory; for $G=S_3$, it exhibits a first-order confinement transition, diagnosed by the onset of a Wilson-loop area law and the restoration of an emergent magnetic 1-form symmetry. These results provide a unified numerical framework for non-Abelian anyon condensation, confinement, and generalized symmetry breaking.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a sign-free path-integral framework for Kitaev quantum doubles D(G), using a matterization isometry to map the link-only model to a G gauge-Higgs theory, enabling large-scale QMC study of non-Abelian anyon condensation and confinement.
AI.motivation: Transitions out of non-Abelian topological order are hard to study microscopically because numerical methods become intractable at large scales. Existing approaches lack a tractable, sign-free framework to describe anyon condensation and confinement in these systems.
AI.method: The authors organize single-link perturbations in Kitaev quantum doubles D(G) via non-invertible electric and magnetic 1-form symmetries that proliferate distinct anyon species. They introduce an exact matterization isometry adding vertex degrees of freedom, mapping the link-only model onto a G gauge-Higgs theory. Generalized Fredenhagen-Marcu order parameters, built from the fixed point's 1-form symmetries, detect anyon condensation. Quantum Monte Carlo simulations are performed for G = S3.
AI.result: For G = S3, proliferating a non-Abelian electric anyon drives a first-order transition in which all nontrivial electric anyons condense. In the purely magnetic limit, the model reduces to a (2+1)D pure G gauge theory which, for G = S3, exhibits a first-order confinement transition, diagnosed by a Wilson-loop area law and restoration of an emergent magnetic 1-form symmetry.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified, sign-free numerical framework for describing non-Abelian anyon condensation, confinement, and generalized symmetry breaking in Kitaev quantum doubles.

title: Valley-Helical Superconductivity Driven by Repulsion and Quantum Geometry: Applications to Time-Reversal Symmetric Rhombohedral Graphene
summary: Motivated by the recent experimental signatures of chiral superconductivity in valley-polarized graphene- and transition-metal-dichalcogenide-based systems, we investigate the possibility of chiral pairing in the absence of valley polarization or time-reversal symmetry breaking. For systems with opposite Berry curvature in the two valleys, we find that overscreened repulsion (i.e., the Kohn-Luttinger mechanism) can indeed induce pairing of opposite chiralities in each valley, producing a valley-helical state. Moreover, the valley-helical state can outcompete more conventional intervalley paired states at intermediate coupling, despite only the latter having a weak-coupling instability. Using a realistic model of time-reversal-symmetric rhombohedral graphene, we find extended ranges of fillings and displacement fields with dominant valley-helical superconductivity. This occurs for all layer numbers considered here, $4\leq N\leq 8$. We show that the valley-helical states can display topologically projected edge modes, unusual magnetic responses, and intertwined Kekulé-like bond-order; features that can be used to distinguish them from more conventional superconductors.

AI.tldr: Overscreened repulsion can induce valley-helical chiral superconductivity in time-reversal-symmetric systems with opposite Berry curvature in two valleys, dominating at intermediate coupling and realized in rhombohedral graphene.
AI.motivation: Recent experiments show chiral superconductivity in valley-polarized graphene- and TMD-based systems, prompting the question of whether chiral pairing can arise without valley polarization or time-reversal symmetry breaking.
AI.method: The authors study pairing via the Kohn-Luttinger (overscreened repulsion) mechanism in systems with opposite Berry curvature in the two valleys, compare valley-helical versus intervalley paired states, and apply a realistic model of time-reversal-symmetric rhombohedral graphene for layer numbers 4≤N≤8.
AI.result: Overscreened repulsion induces pairing of opposite chiralities in each valley (a valley-helical state), which outcompetes conventional intervalley states at intermediate coupling. In rhombohedral graphene, dominant valley-helical superconductivity appears over extended ranges of fillings and displacement fields for all considered layer numbers. The state exhibits topologically projected edge modes, unusual magnetic responses, and intertwined Kekulé-like bond order.
AI.conclusion: Chiral superconductivity can emerge without valley polarization or time-reversal symmetry breaking, with the valley-helical state being a viable and experimentally distinguishable phase in rhombohedral graphene.

title: Energy partitioning of wave packets in one-dimensional systems
summary: We investigate the non-equilibrium dynamics of wave packets in a one-dimensional critical fermionic system and analyze the resulting partitioning of energy between emergent excitations. Starting from a Gaussian wave packet injected on top of the many-body ground state, we follow its real-time evolution using the time-dependent density-matrix renormalization group. We observe that interactions lead to fractionalization of the initial excitation into counter-propagating left- and right-moving modes, whose energies can be resolved in real space. To interpret these results, we employ Luttinger liquid theory, which allows us to derive analytical predictions for the energy carried by the emergent modes. We find good agreement between field-theoretical predictions and numerical simulations in the low-energy regime. In contrast to charge fractionalization, which is completely determined by the Luttinger liquid parameter, we show that energy partitioning is non-universal and depends on details of the injected wave packet, such as its width. Our results provide a real-space characterization of energy partitioning in one-dimensional systems and establish a quantitative comparison between non-equilibrium numerical simulations and the effective field-theory description.

AI.tldr: A Gaussian wave packet injected into a 1D critical fermionic system fractionalizes into counter-propagating modes; their energy partitioning is non-universal and depends on the packet width, as confirmed by tDMRG and Luttinger liquid theory.
AI.motivation: Charge fractionalization is fully fixed by the Luttinger liquid parameter, but whether the energy carried by emergent excitations is similarly universal remained unclear. The authors aim to characterize energy partitioning in real space and to quantitatively connect non-equilibrium numerics with effective field theory.
AI.method: A Gaussian wave packet is injected on top of the many-body ground state of a 1D critical fermionic system. Its real-time evolution is simulated with time-dependent density-matrix renormalization group (tDMRG). Luttinger liquid theory is used to derive analytical predictions for the energy carried by the left- and right-moving modes.
AI.result: Interactions fractionalize the initial excitation into counter-propagating left- and right-moving modes, whose energies are resolved in real space. Field-theoretical predictions agree well with tDMRG simulations in the low-energy regime. Unlike charge fractionalization, energy partitioning is non-universal and depends on details of the injected packet, such as its width.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a real-space characterization of energy partitioning in 1D systems and establishes a quantitative comparison between non-equilibrium numerical simulations and the effective field-theory description, highlighting the non-universal nature of energy fractionalization.

title: Mollified-sharp decomposition: a probabilistic regularization of parametric POD for shock-bearing flows
summary: This paper introduces the mollified-sharp decomposition, a probabilistic regularization of moving shocks in parametric reduced-order models. Each detected shock location is treated as a random variable with a prescribed probability density. Averaging over this artificial distribution replaces the localized pressure change by a smooth transition whose spatial extent is set by the density width, rather than by direct filtering of the pressure field. Each snapshot is decomposed exactly into a regularized mollified field and a local sharp correction that restores the shock. This probabilistic construction and exact additive split define the general method; the detector, kernel, treatment of multiple shocks, alignment coordinates, and regression are implementation choices. In the present realization, a calibrated indicator detects shocks, a compactly supported Wendland kernel mollifies them, and a peak-normalized and, where necessary, partitioned weight derived from each shock-location probability density defines the centroid, principal axes, and scales of its local alignment domain. Separate POD-GPR models represent the mollified field and aligned corrections, with additional regressions for shock presence and alignment. The method is demonstrated on the transonic airfoil pressure data of Catalani et al. (2023) and compared with a standard POD-GPR model constructed from the same data and POD-energy criterion. The mollified-sharp model reduces the mean test-set relative $L^2$ pressure error by 31.2% and the mean test-set surface-pressure-coefficient error by 33.2%, while also improving the predicted shock locations and pressure changes; the trade-off is a median online evaluation time 2.24 times as long. The construction is applicable in principle to other parameter-dependent fields with moving sharp features, such as moving material interfaces in multiphase flows.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a mollified-sharp decomposition to regularize moving shocks in parametric reduced-order models, treating shock locations as random variables to produce smooth transitions while exactly splitting each snapshot into a mollified field plus a sharp correction. Demonstrated on transonic airfoil pressure data, it reduces relative L2 and surface-pressure-coefficient errors by 31.2% and 33.2% versus standard POD-GPR, at 2.24x median online cost.
AI.motivation: Moving sharp features such as shocks degrade the efficiency and accuracy of parametric reduced-order models, since localized discontinuities are poorly captured by low-dimensional linear subspaces. Standard approaches relying on direct filtering of the pressure field may smear or misalign these features, motivating a regularization that preserves the exact shock while enabling smooth, low-dimensional representation.

title: Unified Transport and Susceptibility Analysis of a Thin BSCCO Film: From Local Pairing to Global Phase Coherence
comment: Main manuscript: 13 pages, 9 figures, and 1 table. Supplementary Material: 4 pages, 2 figures, and 1 table. Submitted to Physical Review B
summary: The superconducting transition in thin high-$T_c$ films can be significantly broadened by disorder, spatial inhomogeneity, and phase fluctuations. Here, we study the transition in a 30-nm-thick sputter-grown Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+δ}$ (BSCCO) film through electrical-transport and ac-susceptibility measurements. The resistive transition is examined using a Gaussian distribution of local $T_c$ values and the Ambegaokar--Halperin model, describing spatial variations in superconductivity and thermally activated phase dynamics, respectively. To relate the transport and magnetic responses, we extend the Choy--Stoneham susceptibility model by introducing the superconducting fraction extracted from transport and a temperature-dependent connectivity factor representing the gradual development of Josephson coupling among superconducting regions. The results identify separate temperature regimes corresponding to the onset of local superconductivity, expansion of the superconducting fraction, development of magnetic screening, and establishment of global phase coherence. The transition therefore proceeds progressively, from locally superconducting regions to a connected, phase-coherent state. This analysis provides a common framework for relating spatial inhomogeneity, dissipative phase dynamics, and magnetic screening in inhomogeneous superconducting films.

AI.tldr: A 30-nm BSCCO film's superconducting transition is analyzed by combining transport (Gaussian Tc distribution, Ambegaokar-Halperin model) and ac-susceptibility (extended Choy-Stoneham model) to link spatial inhomogeneity, phase dynamics, and screening.
AI.motivation: The superconducting transition in thin high-Tc films is significantly broadened by disorder, spatial inhomogeneity, and phase fluctuations, and a unified framework relating spatial inhomogeneity, dissipative phase dynamics, and magnetic screening is lacking.
AI.method: Electrical-transport and ac-susceptibility measurements on a 30-nm sputter-grown Bi2Sr2CaCu2O8+δ film. The resistive transition is modeled with a Gaussian distribution of local Tc values and the Ambegaokar-Halperin model; the Choy-Stoneham susceptibility model is extended by introducing the transport-derived superconducting fraction and a temperature-dependent connectivity factor describing gradual Josephson coupling.
AI.result: Distinct temperature regimes are identified: onset of local superconductivity, expansion of the superconducting fraction, development of magnetic screening, and establishment of global phase coherence, showing the transition proceeds progressively from locally superconducting regions to a connected, phase-coherent state.
AI.conclusion: The analysis provides a common framework relating spatial inhomogeneity, dissipative phase dynamics, and magnetic screening in inhomogeneous superconducting films.

title: Universal Suppression of Dissipation across Conformal Interface in Open Quantum Critical Systems
summary: Conformal interfaces provide an important setting for studying universal transmission phenomena in one-dimensional quantum critical systems. While energy and information transmission across such interfaces are characterized by universal quantities in closed systems, the corresponding role of conformal interfaces in dissipative dynamics is less understood. In this work, we study relaxation in locally dissipative quantum critical chains with a conformal interface and show that a universal characterization emerges at the level of individual relaxation modes. We first show that the relaxation coefficient defined in the recent work [1] from the Liouvillian gap can become non-universal for certain boundary conditions because the mode determining the smallest decay rate can change as the interface transmission is varied. To resolve this ambiguity, we introduce a mode-resolved relaxation coefficient $c_{\rm relax}$ by continuously tracking the same Liouvillian rapidity mode as a function of the interface transmission. Using analytical and numerical calculations for a critical harmonic chain and a critical free-fermion chain, we find that, in the weak-dissipation regime, $c_{\rm relax}$ follows the same universal dependence on the interface transmission in all cases considered, independent of microscopic details such as the boundary conditions, dissipation strength, and location of the local dissipation. For boundary dissipation, this universal behavior persists even at finite dissipation strength. Our results establish a universal mode-resolved characterization of relaxation across conformal interfaces in open quantum critical systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a mode-resolved relaxation coefficient c_relax that universally characterizes relaxation across conformal interfaces in locally dissipative quantum critical chains, resolving non-universalities in the previously defined Liouvillian-gap-based coefficient.
AI.motivation: Conformal interfaces are key to studying universal transmission phenomena in 1D quantum critical systems, and while energy/information transmission in closed systems is well-characterized by universal quantities, the role of conformal interfaces in dissipative (open) dynamics remains poorly understood. The recent relaxation coefficient [1] derived from the Liouvillian gap can become non-universal for certain boundary conditions because the mode determining the smallest decay rate changes with interface transmission, creating ambiguity.
AI.method: The authors introduce a mode-resolved relaxation coefficient c_relax by continuously tracking the same Liouvillian rapidity mode as a function of interface transmission. They perform analytical and numerical calculations for a critical harmonic chain and a critical free-fermion chain, examining dependence on boundary conditions, dissipation strength, and the location of local dissipation.
AI.result: In the weak-dissipation regime, c_relax exhibits the same universal dependence on interface transmission in all considered cases, independent of microscopic details (boundary conditions, dissipation strength, location of local dissipation). For boundary dissipation, this universal behavior persists even at finite dissipation strength.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a universal mode-resolved characterization of relaxation across conformal interfaces in open quantum critical systems, resolving the ambiguity of the gap-based relaxation coefficient and revealing universal dynamics in dissipative critical chains.

title: Observation of multiphoton entanglement in resonance fluoresce
summary: Resonance fluorescence, the process in which a single two-level quantum emitter interacts with a near-resonant coherent light, is a cornerstone of quantum optics as a paradigmatic light-matter interaction. Quantum phenomena in resonance fluorescence have been accounted for in terms of one- and two-photon processes; however, the physical processes arising from the interaction of a single two-level atom with higher photon numbers remain unexplored experimentally. Here we experimentally reveal the multiphoton scattering nature of resonance fluorescence, which intrinsically gives rise to multiphoton entanglement. By accessing quantum fluctuations in the field emitted from a cavity-quantum electrodynamics system, we resolve third- and fourth-order photon scattering events from a single two-level atom. In the three-photon component, the scattered photons are shown to be genuinely energy-time entangled, as verified by a violation of Svetlichny's inequality. As a demonstration of an application, a quantum secret sharing protocol (QSS) is implemented using this entangled photon source. Our study refines the descriptive framework of resonance fluorescence and broadens the scope of its investigation. It also establishes a fundamentally simple route for generating multiphoton entangled states for quantum information processing and quantum metrology.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally reveals the multiphoton scattering nature of resonance fluorescence from a single two-level atom, resolving third- and fourth-order photon scattering events and demonstrating genuine energy-time entanglement in the three-photon component, verified via Svetlichny's inequality violation, and applies this to a quantum secret sharing protocol.
AI.motivation: Resonance fluorescence is a cornerstone of quantum optics, but while one- and two-photon processes are well understood, the physical processes arising from the interaction of a single two-level atom with higher photon numbers remained experimentally unexplored. The authors aim to fill this gap by investigating multiphoton processes in resonance fluorescence.
AI.method: Using a cavity-quantum electrodynamics (cQED) system, the authors access quantum fluctuations in the emitted field and resolve third- and fourth-order photon scattering events from a single two-level atom. Entanglement in the three-photon component is verified by a violation of Svetlichny's inequality, and a quantum secret sharing (QSS) protocol is implemented using the entangled photon source.
AI.result: Third- and fourth-order photon scattering events from a single two-level atom are resolved. The scattered photons in the three-photon component are shown to be genuinely energy-time entangled, confirmed by violation of Svetlichny's inequality. A quantum secret sharing protocol is successfully implemented using this source.
AI.conclusion: The study refines the descriptive framework of resonance fluorescence and broadens the scope of its investigation. It establishes a fundamentally simple route for generating multiphoton entangled states for quantum information processing and quantum metrology.

title: Si- and C-Induced Modifications in Vapor-Solid-Grown InGaAs Nanowires: From Crystal Structure to Carrier Dynamics
summary: Determining the impact of dopants in ternary III-V nanowires (NWs) is crucial for their applications in next-generation optoelectronic and photonic devices; however, the interplay between dopant species, crystal structure, and carrier dynamics in vapor-solid-grown InGaAs NWs remains underexplored. In this study, the influence of silicon (Si) and carbon (C) doping on the structural, morphological, and optical properties of catalyst-free, selective-area grown InGaAs NWs fabricated by molecular beam epitaxy is investigated. Scanning electron microscopy demonstrates that C-doping increases the NW aspect ratio by over 100% compared to undoped NWs, while a concomitant decrease in their planar defect density is observed, indicating enhanced crystal quality with C-doping. Despite their superior crystal quality, the C-doped NWs present a diminished photoluminescence intensity, due to point defects and increased surface recombination velocity. This is further supported by time-resolved photoluminescence spectroscopy, revealing accelerated non-radiative recombination in the C-doped NWs. Lastly, hot-carrier effects in these nanostructures are studied, and their signatures remain observable, albeit with reduced intensity in both Si- and C-doped NWs. This comprehensive study establishes clear correlations between doping parameters and the resulting material characteristics and carrier dynamics, offering valuable insights into the fundamental mechanisms governing the VS-grown InGaAs NWs and their implications in optoelectronic devices.

AI.tldr: Si and C doping in catalyst-free selective-area InGaAs nanowires (MBE-grown) was studied. C-doping more than doubles the aspect ratio and reduces planar defect density (better crystal quality) but lowers PL intensity via point defects and faster surface/non-radiative recombination. Hot-carrier signatures persist but weaken in both doped types.
AI.motivation: Dopants are critical for III-V nanowire optoelectronic/photonic applications, yet the interplay among dopant species, crystal structure, and carrier dynamics in vapor-solid-grown InGaAs NWs remains underexplored.
AI.method: Catalyst-free, selective-area InGaAs NWs grown by molecular beam epitaxy, doped with Si and C. Characterization via scanning electron microscopy (morphology, aspect ratio, planar defect density), photoluminescence (PL), time-resolved PL (carrier dynamics), and hot-carrier effect measurements.
AI.result: C-doping increased NW aspect ratio by >100% versus undoped NWs and decreased planar defect density (enhanced crystal quality). Despite this, C-doped NWs showed diminished PL intensity due to point defects and increased surface recombination velocity; time-resolved PL confirmed accelerated non-radiative recombination. Hot-carrier signatures remained observable but with reduced intensity in both Si- and C-doped NWs.
AI.conclusion: Clear correlations are established between doping parameters and material characteristics/carrier dynamics, offering fundamental insights into VS-grown InGaAs NWs and their implications for optoelectronic devices.

title: Reconfigurable Current Distributions in Percolating Au Films and CrO2 Powder Compacts - Beyond Geometrical Connectivity
summary: Despite fundamental differences in morphology, dimensionality, and microscopic transport, semicontinuous Au films and compacted CrO2 powders converge on a common network-level principle: the electrically relevant network is a condition-dependent subset of the physical contact network. In Au films near the geometrical percolation threshold, increasing bias reversibly shifts the low-temperature response from activated nearest-neighbour hopping with negative magnetoresistance to a weak-localization-like regime with positive magnetoresistance, consistent with broader electronic participation of the fixed island network. In CrO2 powder compacts, magnetic field mainly changes the spin-dependent resistances of existing intergranular junctions and thereby reorders competing current paths; temperature and measuring current can additionally expand or deplete the active network. Cohn's theorem provides a compact sensitivity principle for both cases: local resistance changes influence the measured response in proportion to the current carried by the affected links. The comparison identifies two limiting but interconvertible modes of reconfiguration - link enabling and link reweighting - and shows why geometrical connectivity alone is insufficient for interpreting transport in strongly inhomogeneous conductors.

AI.tldr: Au films near percolation and CrO2 powder compacts both show that the transport-relevant network is a condition-dependent subset of the physical contact network, reconfigurable via link enabling or link reweighting, with Cohn's theorem as the unifying sensitivity principle.
AI.motivation: Despite differences in morphology, dimensionality, and microscopic transport, strongly inhomogeneous conductors may share a network-level organizing principle. The paper asks why geometrical connectivity alone is insufficient for interpreting transport in such systems.
AI.method: Comparative analysis of two systems: semicontinuous Au films near the geometrical percolation threshold, probed by bias-dependent low-temperature transport and magnetoresistance; and compacted CrO2 powder, probed by magnetic field, temperature, and measuring current. Interpretation framed via Cohn's theorem on current-weighted local resistance sensitivity.
AI.result: In Au films, increasing bias reversibly shifts the response from activated nearest-neighbour hopping with negative magnetoresistance to a weak-localization-like regime with positive magnetoresistance. In CrO2 compacts, magnetic field alters spin-dependent junction resistances and reorders competing current paths; temperature and current expand or deplete the active network.
AI.conclusion: Transport is governed by a condition-dependent active subset of the contact network. Two limiting but interconvertible reconfiguration modes are identified - link enabling and link reweighting - and Cohn's theorem explains their sensitivity as proportional to the current carried by affected links.

title: Machine-Learned Dynamical Representations for Accelerated RiteWeight Convergence
summary: The increasing use of generative models has made ensembles of short molecular dynamics trajectories increasingly common, creating a growing need for methods that can recover physically meaningful steady-state populations and kinetics from improperly weighted conformational ensembles. Randomized Iterative Trajectory Reweighting (RiteWeight) addresses this problem through repeated random clustering and iterative reweighting, without requiring the fixed Markovian discretization used in conventional Markov state models (MSM). However, the choice of reduced feature space in which RiteWeight performs random clustering has not been systematically investigated. Here, we compare two machine-learned representations, DeepTICA and SPIB-VAE, with linear TICA for recovering steady-state observables from flawed distributions. DeepTICA learns nonlinear coordinates by targeting slow transfer-operator eigenmodes, whereas SPIB-VAE compresses configurations into a low-dimensional latent space while retaining information predictive of future metastable states. DeepTICA provided a comparatively robust RiteWeight representation under limited hyperparameter exploration, whereas SPIB-VAE benefited more strongly from broader optimization. Moreover, a kinetic score computed from a coarse MSM at a resolution comparable to that used for RiteWeight random clustering provided a useful criterion for efficiently selecting reduced representations and their hyperparameters for RiteWeight.

AI.tldr: This work benchmarks DeepTICA, SPIB-VAE, and linear TICA as reduced feature spaces for the RiteWeight reweighting method, finding DeepTICA most robust and identifying a coarse-MSM kinetic score as an efficient hyperparameter-selection criterion.
AI.motivation: Ensembles of short molecular dynamics trajectories, increasingly produced by generative models, are often improperly weighted, so methods are needed to recover physically meaningful steady-state populations and kinetics. RiteWeight addresses this via random clustering and iterative reweighting without fixed Markovian discretization, but the choice of reduced feature space for its random clustering had not been systematically studied.
AI.method: The authors compare two machine-learned representations, DeepTICA and SPIB-VAE, against linear TICA for recovering steady-state observables from flawed distributions within RiteWeight. DeepTICA learns nonlinear coordinates by targeting slow transfer-operator eigenmodes, while SPIB-VAE compresses configurations into a low-dimensional latent space preserving information predictive of future metastable states. A kinetic score from a coarse MSM at a resolution comparable to RiteWeight random clustering is also proposed as a selection criterion.
AI.result: DeepTICA provided a comparatively robust RiteWeight representation under limited hyperparameter exploration, whereas SPIB-VAE benefited more strongly from broader optimization. The coarse-MSM kinetic score proved useful for efficiently selecting reduced representations and their hyperparameters for RiteWeight.
AI.conclusion: The choice of reduced feature space materially affects RiteWeight performance; DeepTICA offers robustness with minimal tuning, SPIB-VAE requires more extensive optimization, and a coarse-MSM kinetic score enables efficient representation and hyperparameter selection.

title: Machine-Learning Exploration of Defect Topologies and Thermodynamic Stability in Graphene with Atomic Vacancies
summary: Atomic vacancies and vacancy aggregates control the thermodynamic stability and the functional response of graphene, yet the configurational space spanned by many vacancies at variable concentration and separation is too large to be mapped exhaustively by first-principles methods. Here, we map and rationalize this stability landscape by combining semiempirical atomistic thermodynamics, interpretable machine learning, and symbolic regression. Several hundred defective supercells, built from a 72-atom cell by varying the vacancy concentration and the inter-vacancy distance up to the fourth neighbor, were relaxed with the PM7 Hamiltonian in MOPAC, and the heat of formation was adopted as the stability metric. Each structure was encoded with the Dynamic Collision Fingerprint, a translationally and rotationally invariant descriptor that maps the local topology onto transport-like statistics of virtual probe particles. A gradient boosted decision tree model, optimized by Bayesian hyperparameter search, reproduces the heat of formation of an independent test set with a root mean squared error of approximately 23.5~kcal/mol and no evidence of overfitting, and a SHAP analysis identifies the defect concentration and the inter-vacancy distance as the two variables that dominate the stability. Symbolic regression then condenses the learned mapping into a compact closed-form expression that reproduces the heat of formation with a coefficient of determination of $R^{2} = 0.9966$, a mean absolute error of 15.51~kcal/mol, and a root mean squared error of 24.18~kcal/mol. The workflow turns a high-dimensional structure--stability problem into an interpretable analytical law, providing a transferable route to rational defect engineering in two-dimensional materials.

AI.tldr: Combining semiempirical atomistic thermodynamics, interpretable machine learning, and symbolic regression, this work maps the stability landscape of defective graphene and derives a compact closed-form law for its heat of formation as a function of vacancy concentration and separation.
AI.motivation: Atomic vacancies and vacancy aggregates govern the thermodynamic stability and functional response of graphene, but the configurational space of many vacancies at variable concentration and separation is too vast to be exhaustively explored with first-principles methods. A scalable, interpretable route to map this stability landscape is therefore needed.
AI.method: Several hundred defective supercells were built from a 72-atom cell by varying vacancy concentration and inter-vacancy distance up to the fourth neighbor, relaxed with the PM7 Hamiltonian in MOPAC, using heat of formation as the stability metric. Each structure was encoded with the Dynamic Collision Fingerprint, a translationally and rotationally invariant descriptor mapping local topology onto transport-like statistics of virtual probe particles. A gradient boosted decision tree optimized by Bayesian hyperparameter search was trained, followed by SHAP analysis and symbolic regression to condense the mapping into a closed-form expression.
AI.result: The gradient boosted decision tree reproduces the heat of formation of an independent test set with an RMSE of ~23.5 kcal/mol without evidence of overfitting. SHAP analysis identifies defect concentration and inter-vacancy distance as the two dominant stability variables. Symbolic regression yields a compact closed-form expression with R² = 0.9966, MAE = 15.51 kcal/mol, and RMSE = 24.18 kcal/mol.
AI.conclusion: The workflow converts a high-dimensional structure–stability problem into an interpretable analytical law, offering a transferable route to rational defect engineering in two-dimensional materials.

title: Displacement field stabilizes even-denominator and partonic fractional quantum Hall states in the $\mathcal{N}{=}2$ Landau levels of Bernal-stacked bilayer graphene
summary: Bernal-stacked bilayer graphene (BLG), in which a graphene layer is stacked atop another and laterally shifted by a lattice constant, offers remarkable tunability in its single-particle states under applied magnetic and displacement fields. Owing to this tunability, recent transport and scanning tunneling microscopy experiments in the presence of a perpendicular magnetic field and finite interlayer displacement fields have observed even-denominator fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states at half-filling in the first excited, namely, $\mathcal{N}{=}2$, Landau level (LL) of BLG. In contrast, at zero displacement field, a gapless composite fermion Fermi liquid (CFFL) is realized at half-filling of the $\mathcal{N}{=}2$ LL. Motivated by these experiments, we compute the phase diagram as a function of the displacement field in the half-filled $\mathcal{N}{=}2$ LL of BLG by studying the competition between the CFFL and the Moore-Read state---a candidate even-denominator FQH state---by calculating their thermodynamic energies in this setting. We find that the modified effective Coulomb interaction, induced by changes in the single-particle states with increasing displacement field, softens the inter-electronic repulsion at short distances, thereby stabilizing the Moore-Read state over the CFFL in the $\mathcal{N}{=}2$ LL of BLG. We also study the nature of FQH states at fillings $2/5$, $3/7$, $4/9$, and $6/13$ in the $\mathcal{N}{=}2$ LL of BLG. Our results suggest that, with increasing displacement field, the Jain composite-fermion states at $3/7$, $4/9$, and $6/13$ transition into states with distinct topological order that are well-captured by parton wave functions.

AI.tldr: This work computes the displacement-field phase diagram for the half-filled N=2 Landau level of Bernal-stacked bilayer graphene, finding that the softening of short-range Coulomb repulsion stabilizes the Moore-Read state over the composite fermion Fermi liquid, and that higher fillings transition into parton-like states with distinct topological order.
AI.motivation: Recent transport and scanning tunneling microscopy experiments on Bernal-stacked bilayer graphene observed even-denominator fractional quantum Hall states at half-filling of the first excited (N=2) Landau level when a perpendicular magnetic field and finite interlayer displacement field are applied, whereas a gapless composite fermion Fermi liquid appears at zero displacement field. This tunability motivates a theoretical understanding of how the displacement field drives the competition between these phases.
AI.method: The authors compute the phase diagram as a function of interlayer displacement field for the half-filled N=2 Landau level of bilayer graphene. They compare the thermodynamic energies of the composite fermion Fermi liquid and the Moore-Read state, examining how the modified effective Coulomb interaction—arising from displacement-field-induced changes in the single-particle states—affects the inter-electronic repulsion. They additionally analyze fractional quantum Hall states at fillings 2/5, 3/7, 4/9, and 6/13, assessing their topological order via parton wave functions.
AI.result: Increasing displacement field softens the short-range inter-electronic repulsion via the modified effective Coulomb interaction, stabilizing the Moore-Read state over the composite fermion Fermi liquid at half-filling of the N=2 Landau level. At fillings 3/7, 4/9, and 6/13, the Jain composite-fermion states are found to transition with increasing displacement field into states with distinct topological order, well captured by parton wave functions. The 2/5 filling is also examined.
AI.conclusion: The displacement field serves as a key tuning parameter that reshapes the effective interaction in the N=2 Landau level of Bernal-stacked bilayer graphene, driving a transition from a gapless composite fermion Fermi liquid to the Moore-Read state at half-filling and inducing topological-order changes at higher fillings. Parton wave functions provide a suitable description of the resulting states, offering a unified framework for interpreting the experimental observations.

title: Universality of the $1/9$ Magnetization Plateau and Quantum-Disordered States in the Kagome Family $\mathrm{Cs_8AB_3Ti_{12}F_{48}}$ ($A=\mathrm{Rb},\mathrm{Li}$; $B=\mathrm{K},\mathrm{Na}$)
summary: The microscopic origin of the low-field $1/9$ magnetization plateau in spin-$1/2$ kagome antiferromagnets remains unresolved. Here, we show that chemical pressure reshapes the hierarchy of fractional magnetization plateaus in the titanium-based kagome family $\mathrm{Cs_8AB_3Ti_{12}F_{48}}$ ($A=\mathrm{Rb},\mathrm{Li}$; $B=\mathrm{K},\mathrm{Na}$). High-field magnetization measurements up to 60 T reveal a robust $1/9$ plateau-like phase in the expanded $\mathrm{Cs_8RbK_3Ti_{12}F_{48}}$ and $\mathrm{Cs_8LiK_3Ti_{12}F_{48}}$ compounds, despite the absence of the conventionally more robust $1/3$ plateau. In contrast, compressed $\mathrm{Cs_8LiNa_3Ti_{12}F_{48}}$ exhibits neither the $1/9$ plateau-like phase nor a quantum-disordered ground state. Specific-heat measurements and first-principles calculations show that lattice expansion preserves a frustrated, fully connected kagome exchange network and gapless quantum-disordered ground states, whereas compression reorganizes the exchange network into weakly coupled quasi-one-dimensional subsystems and induces successive magnetic transitions. These results demonstrate that the $1/9$ and $1/3$ plateaus need not share a common microscopic origin and suggest that the $1/9$ plateau may represent a more universal feature of frustrated spin-$1/2$ kagome magnetism.

AI.tldr: Chemical pressure tunes the hierarchy of fractional magnetization plateaus in Ti-based kagome antiferromagnets Cs8AB3Ti12F48; lattice expansion stabilizes a robust 1/9 plateau-like phase in gapless quantum-disordered kagome networks, while compression destroys the plateau and drives quasi-1D magnetism.
AI.motivation: The microscopic origin of the low-field 1/9 magnetization plateau in spin-1/2 kagome antiferromagnets is unresolved, and it is unclear whether the 1/9 and 1/3 plateaus share a common microscopic mechanism.
AI.method: High-field magnetization measurements up to 60 T, specific-heat measurements, and first-principles calculations on the titanium-based kagome family Cs8AB3Ti12F48 (A=Rb,Li; B=K,Na), using chemical pressure via A/B substitution to expand or compress the lattice.

Lattice expansion preserves a frustrated, fully connected kagome exchange network and gapless quantum-disordered ground states, whereas compression reorganizes the exchange network into weakly coupled quasi-1D subsystems and induces successive magnetic transitions.
AI.conclusion: The 1/9 and 1/3 plateaus need not share a common microscopic origin, and the 1/9 plateau may be a more universal feature of frustrated spin-1/2 kagome magnetism.

title: Encapsulation epitaxy of air-stable monolayer superconducting films for quantum circuits and qubits
summary: Two-dimensional (2D) superconductors are an emerging platform for strongly correlated physics and quantum information science. Their reduced dimensionality, atomically flat interfaces, and high crystallinity are attractive for realizing compact lumped-element devices in superconducting circuits. However, synthesizing large-area, monolayer 2D superconductors remains challenging because of their susceptibility to oxidation. Here, we report an "encapsulation epitaxy" mechanism that enables the growth of large-area, air-stable, monolayer superconducting NbSe2 films and explore their use in superconducting quantum circuits. A 2D encapsulation layer, such as graphene or hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), pre-deposited on a 3D substrate (e.g., SiO2 or Si3N4), serves both as a template for epitaxial growth of monolayer NbSe2 (1L-NbSe2) underneath it and as a protective cover. This approach produces uniform, large-area (>1-inch) 1L-NbSe2 with greatly enhanced ambient stability, enabling device fabrication in air. The resulting 1L-graphene/NbSe2 heterostructures exhibit robust superconductivity (Tc ~ 1 K) and enhanced charge density wave order (TCDW ~ 177 K), indicative of high material quality. We further integrate 1L-NbSe2 into superconducting circuits using oxidation-free transfer and superconducting edge-contact techniques. The 1L-NbSe2 exhibits a measured kinetic inductance LK ~ 0.7 nH/square, making it suitable for quantum circuits requiring high-kinetic-inductance elements. Encapsulation epitaxy thus provides a route to air-stable 2D superconductors and van der Waals heterostructures, with potential for wafer-scale, monolithic fabrication of superconducting quantum circuitry.

AI.motivation: Two-dimensional superconductors are attractive for strongly correlated physics and quantum information science due to their reduced dimensionality, atomically flat interfaces, and high crystallinity, making them promising for compact lumped-element superconducting devices. However, synthesizing large-area monolayer 2D superconductors is difficult because they are highly susceptible to oxidation.

This layer serves dual roles: a template for epitaxial growth of monolayer NbSe2 (1L-NbSe2) beneath it and a protective cover. Integration into superconducting circuits uses oxidation-free transfer and superconducting edge-contact techniques.

The 1L-graphene/NbSe2 heterostructures show robust superconductivity (Tc ~ 1 K) and enhanced charge density wave order (TCDW ~ 177 K), indicating high material quality. The 1L-NbSe2 exhibits a measured kinetic inductance LK ~ 0.7 nH/square, suitable for high-kinetic-inductance quantum circuit elements.
AI.conclusion: Encapsulation epitaxy provides a route to air-stable 2D superconductors and van der Waals heterostructures, with potential for wafer-scale, monolithic fabrication of superconducting quantum circuitry.

title: Collective Symmetry and Criticality from Single-Component Fluctuations
summary: Symmetry plays a fundamental role in modern physics by guiding the classification of phases and the construction of effective theories of critical systems. Identifying collective symmetry remains challenging because tests based on preselected order parameters can overlook hidden components. A central goal is therefore to extract symmetry and critical information from a single accessible component. We pursue this goal using Lee--Yang zero ratios generated by a single ordering field. Unmeasured components shape the projected fluctuation distribution and hence the relative zero positions. Deep in a phase with spontaneous symmetry breaking, we show analytically that the zero ratios for an isotropic order parameter approach a parameter-free Bessel sequence fixed by the number of collective components. Near quantum criticality, fluctuations deform this distribution. The resulting ratio deviations and their finite-size coupling dependence carry additional critical information. We demonstrate these results with large-scale quantum Monte Carlo simulations of many-body systems with conventional and enlarged continuous symmetries. This approach provides quantitative access to collective symmetry and criticality without measuring every competing order.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that Lee–Yang zero ratios generated by a single ordering field can quantitatively reveal collective symmetry and criticality, using analytic Bessel-sequence predictions and large-scale quantum Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.motivation: Symmetry underpins the classification of phases and effective theories of critical systems, but identifying collective symmetry is difficult because conventional tests rely on preselected order parameters and can miss hidden components. A key goal is to extract symmetry and critical information from only a single accessible component.
AI.method: The authors use Lee–Yang zero ratios generated by a single ordering field. They analyze how unmeasured components shape the projected fluctuation distribution and thus the relative zero positions, deriving analytically the zero-ratio behavior for an isotropic order parameter deep in a spontaneously symmetry-broken phase. They then examine near-critical deformation of this distribution and the finite-size coupling dependence of ratio deviations, validating the approach with large-scale quantum Monte Carlo simulations of many-body systems with conventional and enlarged continuous symmetries.
AI.result: Deep in the symmetry-broken phase, the zero ratios for an isotropic order parameter approach a parameter-free Bessel sequence determined solely by the number of collective components. Near quantum criticality, fluctuations deform this distribution, and the resulting ratio deviations and their finite-size coupling dependence encode additional critical information.
AI.conclusion: Lee–Yang zero ratios from a single ordering field provide quantitative access to collective symmetry and criticality without the need to measure every competing order.

title: Small-Angle Differential Cross Sections for Symmetrical Resonant Charge Exchange in Molecular Hydrogen
summary: We measured state selective scattering angle distributions in non-dissociative-state single electron capture in $\lbrace 5, 7.5, 10\rbrace$ keV/u, $\left[\mathrm{H^+ + H_2}\right]$ and $\left[\mathrm{H_2^+ + H_2}\right]$ collisions, using Cold Target Recoil Ion Momentum Spectroscopy (COLTRIMS). In our measurements, range of the scattering angle was small where diffraction effect is expected to take place, and, the ground state electron capture - symmetrical resonant channel for the $\mathrm{H_2^+}$ projectile and near resonant channel for the $\mathrm{H^+}$ projectile - was fully resolved from other channels. We analyzed the data considering $\mathrm{H_2^+}$ and $\mathrm{H_2}$ possess two independent-identical scattering centers and exhibit multi center interference effect. By comparing these equal-velocity collisions, we investigated the atomic nature of the individual scattering centers. We observed Fraunhofer diffraction from a circular aperture like patterns with equal fringe widths, for both the projectiles, in ground state channel. We applied a simple toy model to reconstruct the circular apertures.

AI.tldr: State-selective scattering angle distributions for single electron capture in equal-velocity H+ + H2 and H2+ + H2 collisions were measured via COLTRIMS and analyzed as multi-center interference from two identical scattering centers, revealing Fraunhofer-like circular-aperture diffraction in the ground-state channel.
AI.motivation: To probe the atomic nature of individual scattering centers in molecular collisions by exploiting equal-velocity H+ + H2 and H2+ + H2 systems, where H2+ and H2 possess two independent-identical scattering centers and exhibit multi-center interference.
AI.method: COLTRIMS was used to measure state-selective scattering angle distributions for non-dissociative single electron capture at 5, 7.5, and 10 keV/u. The ground-state electron capture channel (symmetrical resonant for H2+, near-resonant for H+) was fully resolved from other channels, and the small scattering angle range where diffraction is expected was probed. Data were analyzed within a two-independent-identical-scattering-center interference framework and interpreted with a simple toy model to reconstruct the circular apertures.
AI.result: Fraunhofer diffraction patterns resembling those from a circular aperture, with equal fringe widths, were observed for both projectiles in the ground-state channel at all measured energies.
AI.conclusion: Equal-velocity comparison of H+ and H2+ projectiles on H2 enables investigation of the atomic nature of individual scattering centers, and the observed circular-aperture-like Fraunhofer diffraction in the ground-state capture channel supports a multi-center interference description of the collision.

title: Static-to-dynamic field conversion in a temporally switched Lorentz medium
summary: We investigate static-to-dynamic electromagnetic field conversion in a temporally switched Lorentz medium initially subjected to an electrostatic field. An abrupt change of the oscillator strength drives the material away from its initial equilibrium, while the polarization retains memory of the pre-switch state and acts as the source of the resulting transient. We formulate the resulting initial-value problem in the Laplace domain and derive an analytical representation of the generated field in terms of the poles of the finite Lorentz slab. Material dispersion gives rise to a richer modal structure than in the nondispersive case, including families of slab-mode poles that accumulate toward the singularities associated with the Lorentz polarization dynamics. We further show that material memory governs the earliest stage of the transient, producing a smooth field onset and setting the velocity of the earliest propagating disturbance through the high-frequency permittivity. Because the temporal switch generates broadband spectral content, the transient samples positive-, near-zero-, and negative-permittivity regions of the post-switch material response, leading to qualitatively different spatial field distributions. These results reveal how material dispersion and memory fundamentally shape the generation and evolution of radiation produced from an initially static electromagnetic state.

AI.tldr: Static-to-dynamic electromagnetic field conversion is studied in a temporally switched Lorentz medium; the initial-value problem is solved in the Laplace domain, revealing a pole-based modal structure, dispersion- and memory-governed transient onset, and distinct field distributions sampling positive-, near-zero-, and negative-permittivity regions.
AI.motivation: Temporal switching between static and dynamic regimes probes how radiation can be generated from an initially static electromagnetic state, yet the roles of material dispersion and memory in this conversion process remain insufficiently understood.
AI.method: An abrupt change of oscillator strength is applied to a Lorentz medium initially in an electrostatic equilibrium. The resulting initial-value problem is formulated in the Laplace domain, and the transient field in a finite Lorentz slab is represented analytically through the poles of the system.
AI.result: Material dispersion produces a richer modal structure than the nondispersive case, including families of slab-mode poles accumulating toward singularities tied to the Lorentz polarization dynamics. Material memory controls the earliest transient stage, yielding a smooth field onset and setting the velocity of the earliest disturbance via the high-frequency permittivity. The broadband transient samples positive-, near-zero-, and negative-permittivity regions of the post-switch response, giving qualitatively different spatial field distributions.
AI.conclusion: Material dispersion and memory fundamentally shape the generation and evolution of radiation produced from an initially static electromagnetic state, governing both the onset and spatial structure of the transient field.

title: Disorder-induced modulation of the nonlinear Hall effect in Weyl semimetals
summary: We study the effects of impurity scattering on the nonlinear Hall response of Weyl semimetals within the semiclassical Boltzmann approach. We derive the rectified and second-harmonic conductivity tensors for a general momentum-dependent transport relaxation time and evaluate this quantity microscopically for short-range, Gaussian, screened Coulomb, and magnetic impurities. For scalar disorder, the relaxation time is isotropic and chirality independent. The nonlinear Hall response is then determined by the anomalous velocity associated with the Berry curvature, and a finite net response requires energetically inequivalent Weyl nodes to avoid cancellation between opposite chiralities. Polarized magnetic impurities lead to a qualitatively different behavior. We find that interference between the first- and second-order Born amplitudes generates a helicity-dependent anisotropic correction to the relaxation time. This anisotropy changes the tensor structure of the nonlinear Hall conductivity and gives rise to a finite second-harmonic current for suitable orientations of the electric field relative to the impurity polarization. For representative parameters, however, the anisotropic contribution is several orders of magnitude smaller than the dominant isotropic response. These results establish how the microscopic form of impurity scattering enters the nonlinear Hall response of Weyl semimetals through the transport relaxation time.

AI.tldr: The paper derives rectified and second-harmonic nonlinear Hall conductivity tensors for Weyl semimetals with a general momentum-dependent relaxation time, evaluated for various impurity types. Scalar disorder gives an isotropic, chirality-independent relaxation time and Berry-curvature-driven response requiring inequivalent nodes; polarized magnetic impurities induce helicity-dependent anisotropy via first/second-order Born interference, altering tensor structure, though the anisotropic term is several orders of magnitude smaller than the isotropic contribution.
AI.motivation: Impurity scattering is known to govern transport in Weyl semimetals, but its role in the nonlinear Hall response—particularly how the microscopic form of disorder enters through the transport relaxation time—remains insufficiently characterized. The authors aim to clarify this by treating disorder-dependent relaxation microscopically rather than phenomenologically.
AI.method: Semiclassical Boltzmann approach is employed. The rectified and second-harmonic conductivity tensors are derived for a general momentum-dependent transport relaxation time. The relaxation time is then computed microscopically for short-range, Gaussian, screened Coulomb, and magnetic impurities, including interference between first- and second-order Born amplitudes for polarized magnetic impurities.
AI.result: For scalar disorder the relaxation time is isotropic and chirality-independent, so the nonlinear Hall response is set by the anomalous velocity from Berry curvature and a finite net response requires energetically inequivalent Weyl nodes to avoid cancellation between opposite chiralities. Polarized magnetic impurities produce a helicity-dependent anisotropic correction to the relaxation time from first/second-order Born interference, changing the tensor structure of the nonlinear Hall conductivity and generating a finite second-harmonic current for suitable electric-field orientations relative to the impurity polarization. Quantitatively, the anisotropic contribution is several orders of magnitude smaller than the dominant isotropic response.
AI.conclusion: The microscopic form of impurity scattering controls the nonlinear Hall response of Weyl semimetals through the transport relaxation time. Scalar disorder yields an isotropic Berry-curvature-driven response, whereas polarized magnetic impurities introduce a helicity-dependent anisotropy that reshapes the tensor structure, though it is numerically subdominant.

title: Agentic AI for Density-Functional Development: Revisiting r2SCAN
summary: We demonstrate physics-constrained agentic development of a meta-generalized gradient approximation (meta-GGA) functional using a large language model (LLM) to assist the search and optimization of a band-gap-oriented revision of r2SCAN. No real bonded systems were fitted, preserving r2SCAN's nonempirical philosophy. Across the finalist set, band gaps and several molecular subsets improve relative to r2SCAN; the top finalist, r2SCAN+, reduces the band-gap MAE on a benchmark comprising 24 solids from 1.26 to 0.96 eV and the aggregate MAE on 329 molecular properties from 4.79 to 4.42 kcal/mol. We first curated 78 exchange and 90 correlation candidate correction terms from r2SCAN's dimensionless ingredients, spanning polynomial terms through third degree, exponentials, exponentially damped products, and ratios. Allowing each candidate to combine one to three correction terms from the exchange catalog, the correlation catalog, or both yields about 8 x 10^5 distinct forms, making exhaustive high-throughput screening impractical. We defined the search criteria for the LLM agent using r2SCAN's exact constraints, physical norms, and the targeted iso-orbital derivative response. The agent then combined these criteria with its pretrained knowledge and accumulated search feedback to propose and refine sparse forms, prioritizing terms tied to the iso-orbital response; a second LLM critic screened proposals before deterministic verification. Compared with uniform random search, the workflow learned from prior evaluations, incurred far fewer downstream rejections (0.6% versus 24.6%), and located stronger high-response candidates: 51 agentic candidates exceeded the best random-search response of 1.263, with the overall best reaching 1.331. These results show that agentic search can support density-functional development when flexible hypothesis generation is coupled to automated physical verification.

AI.tldr: An LLM-based agentic workflow searches and optimizes a band-gap-oriented revision of r2SCAN (a nonempirical meta-GGA), yielding r2SCAN+ which improves band gaps and molecular properties without fitting real bonded systems.
AI.motivation: Improving density functionals like r2SCAN typically requires navigating a vast space of candidate correction terms, where exhaustive high-throughput screening is impractical; the paper aims to show that agentic LLM search can guide functional development while preserving r2SCAN's nonempirical philosophy (no fitting to real bonded systems).
AI.method: Curated 78 exchange and 90 correlation candidate correction terms from r2SCAN's dimensionless ingredients (polynomials up to third degree, exponentials, damped products, ratios); allowing 1-3 term combinations yields ~8x10^5 forms. Search criteria were defined via r2SCAN exact constraints, physical norms, and targeted iso-orbital derivative response. An LLM agent proposed and refined sparse forms using pretrained knowledge plus accumulated feedback, with a second LLM critic screening proposals before deterministic verification; compared against uniform random search.
AI.result: Band gaps and several molecular subsets improve over r2SCAN; top finalist r2SCAN+ reduces band-gap MAE on 24 solids from 1.26 to 0.96 eV and aggregate MAE on 329 molecular properties from 4.79 to 4.42 kcal/mol. The workflow incurred fewer downstream rejections (0.6% vs 24.6%) and found stronger high-response candidates: 51 agentic candidates exceeded the best random-search response of 1.263, with the best reaching 1.331.
AI.conclusion: Agentic search can support density-functional development when flexible hypothesis generation is coupled to automated physical verification, outperforming random search in both efficiency and candidate quality.

title: Exergy-Anergy Representation of Turbomachine Performance Characteristics
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables, submitted to the ASME Journal of Turbomachinery
summary: The performance synthesis calculation of aircraft engines relies on tabulated datasets for the simulation of the complex turbomachinery components at acceptable runtimes. Typically, these so-called performance maps express the change of the fluid's energetic state over the component in terms of the total pressure ratio and the isentropic efficiency of the process. However, the definitions of both parameters are different for compressors and turbines and the isentropic efficiency is in both cases not defined for a unity pressure ratio. Moreover, this parameter combination is not directly applicable when modelling the engine at the aircraft level, which is required for modern highly integrated aircraft design. As exergy analysis is an established tool for aircraft design asessment, novel performance maps are proposed that describe the change in exergy and anergy over a given turbomachine component. Both changes are expressed as non-dimensional parameters whose definition is consistent for compressors and turbines, and is compatible with a unity pressure ratio. It is shown that the presented exergy-anergy maps are obtainable on a standard turbomachine test bed or through transformation of existing maps. It is highlighted using examples, that the conversion between existing maps and exergy-anergy maps is completely lossless. The different operating regimes of the turbomachines are clearly distinguishable in the novel map representation, which allows an assessment of the map's physical consistency. It is therefore concluded, that the exergy-anergy maps are an important alternative to the performance map variants established today.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes novel exergy-anergy performance maps for turbomachinery components as an alternative to conventional pressure-ratio/isentropic-efficiency maps, offering definitions consistent for both compressors and turbines and valid at unity pressure ratio, with lossless conversion from existing maps.
AI.motivation: Conventional performance maps express component behavior via total pressure ratio and isentropic efficiency, but these definitions differ between compressors and turbines, are undefined at unity pressure ratio, and are not directly applicable to aircraft-level modelling required for highly integrated aircraft design. Exergy analysis is already established for aircraft design assessment, motivating a map representation aligned with it.
AI.method: The authors propose performance maps describing the change in exergy and anergy across a turbomachine component, expressed as non-dimensional parameters whose definitions are consistent for compressors and turbines and compatible with a unity pressure ratio. They demonstrate that these exergy-anergy maps can be obtained on a standard turbomachine test bed or by transformation of existing maps, and use examples to examine the representation.
AI.result: The conversion between existing maps and exergy-anergy maps is shown to be completely lossless. The different operating regimes of the turbomachines are clearly distinguishable in the novel map representation, enabling assessment of the map's physical consistency.
AI.conclusion: Exergy-anergy maps are concluded to be an important alternative to the performance map variants established today.

title: Comprehensive First-Principles Investigation of the Structural, Mechanical, Electronic, and Optical Properties of Homoelemental Phase T-GaN Monolayer
summary: The exploration of non-hexagonal two-dimensional topologies has opened new possibilities for tailoring the properties of group III-V monolayers beyond those accessible through conventional honeycomb phases. In this context, we have investigated the structural, mechanical, electronic, and optical properties of T-GaN, a two-dimensional tetragonal gallium nitride monolayer composed of alternating four- and eight-membered rings featuring coexisting homoelemental (Ga-Ga, N-N) and heteropolar (Ga-N) bonds, using density functional theory (DFT) within the generalized gradient approximation (GGA/PBE) and the hybrid HSE06 functional. The dynamical stability of T-GaN was confirmed by phonon dispersion calculations, which revealed the absence of imaginary frequencies throughout the Brillouin zone, and was further supported by \textit{ab initio} molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations. The mechanical characterization reveals a pronounced in-plane anisotropy, with critical strains of approximately 16.5\% and 7.0\% along the $x$- and $y$-directions, respectively. The electronic band structure analysis indicates that T-GaN is a nonmagnetic semiconductor with an indirect band gap of 0.35~eV (PBE) and 1.15~eV (HSE06), with the valence band maximum dominated by nitrogen 2\textit{p} orbitals and the conduction band minimum governed by gallium 4\textit{s} and 4\textit{p} states. The optical response was evaluated along three crystallographic directions, exhibiting considerable anisotropy in the absorption coefficient, refractive index, and reflectivity. These findings provide new insights into the physical properties of tetragonal group III-V monolayers and suggest that T-GaN may serve as a promising candidate for anisotropic nanoelectronic and optoelectronic applications.

AI.tldr: A DFT study of the tetragonal T-GaN monolayer reveals a dynamically stable indirect-band-gap semiconductor with strong in-plane mechanical and optical anisotropy.
AI.motivation: Non-hexagonal 2D topologies offer property-tuning opportunities for group III-V monolayers beyond conventional honeycomb phases, motivating investigation of a tetragonal gallium nitride phase.
AI.method: Structural, mechanical, electronic, and optical properties of T-GaN (alternating four- and eight-membered rings with Ga-Ga, N-N, and Ga-N bonds) were computed via DFT using GGA/PBE and HSE06, with phonon dispersion and ab initio molecular dynamics for stability.
AI.result: T-GaN is dynamically stable (no imaginary phonon frequencies; AIMD-supported), mechanically anisotropic (critical strains ~16.5% along x and ~7.0% along y), and a nonmagnetic indirect semiconductor with gaps of 0.35 eV (PBE) and 1.15 eV (HSE06). VBM is dominated by N 2p states; CBM by Ga 4s/4p. Optical response along three crystallographic directions shows strong anisotropy in absorption, refractive index, and reflectivity.
AI.conclusion: T-GaN enriches understanding of tetragonal group III-V monolayers and is a promising candidate for anisotropic nanoelectronic and optoelectronic applications.

title: Multiferroic Quantum Dot in an Artificial van der Waals Heterostructure
summary: Quantum dots (QDs) provide a versatile platform for engineering quantum-confined electronic states with functionalities relevant for optoelectronics, spintronics, and quantum technologies. While substantial progress has been achieved in coupling confined states to spin, valley, topological, or ferroelectric degrees of freedom, the realization of a multiferroic QD in which quantum confinement simultaneously intertwines with magnetism and ferroelectricity remains elusive. Here, we engineer a multiferroic QD in an artificial van der Waals heterostructure grown by molecular beam epitaxy under ultra-high-vacuum conditions. The heterostructure consists of ferroelectric SnTe nanoislands deposited on the layered magnet CrBr$_2$ supported on highly oriented pyrolytic graphite. Combining scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy with ab initio calculations and low-energy tight-binding models, we demonstrate the emergence of spin-polarized discretized electronic states confined within the SnTe islands. Remarkably, the spectroscopic response of the QD strongly depends on the ferroelectric domain configuration of the SnTe nanoislands, demonstrating an interplay between quantum confinement, magnetic exchange, and ferroelectric order at the atomic scale. Our results establish engineered van der Waals heterostructures as a platform for multiferroic quantum confinement and open new routes toward electrically tunable quantum spintronic devices.

AI.tldr: The paper engineers a multiferroic quantum dot in a van der Waals heterostructure (ferroelectric SnTe nanoislands on layered magnet CrBr2/graphite), demonstrating spin-polarized confined states whose spectroscopy depends on ferroelectric domain configuration, thus intertwining quantum confinement, magnetism, and ferroelectricity.
AI.motivation: Quantum dots (QDs) are versatile platforms for quantum-confined electronic states relevant to optoelectronics, spintronics, and quantum technologies, and confined states have been coupled to spin, valley, topological, or ferroelectric degrees of freedom. However, a multiferroic QD in which quantum confinement simultaneously intertwines with magnetism and ferroelectricity had remained elusive.
AI.method: The authors grew an artificial van der Waals heterostructure by molecular beam epitaxy under ultra-high-vacuum conditions, consisting of ferroelectric SnTe nanoislands on a layered magnet CrBr2 supported on highly oriented pyrolytic graphite. They combined scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy with ab initio calculations and low-energy tight-binding models.

The spectroscopic response of the QD strongly depends on the ferroelectric domain configuration of the SnTe nanoislands, revealing an interplay between quantum confinement, magnetic exchange, and ferroelectric order at the atomic scale.
AI.conclusion: Engineered van der Waals heterostructures constitute a platform for multiferroic quantum confinement and open new routes toward electrically tunable quantum spintronic devices.

title: Vestigial chirality from fluctuating loop currents on the kagome lattice
summary: Multicomponent order can melt in stages, leaving a composite order after its primary constituents become short ranged. We study this possibility for commensurate three-$Q$ loop-current order on the kagome lattice. Large-scale cluster and parallel-tempering Monte Carlo simulations reveal direct and two-stage melting regimes in an effective fixed-amplitude sign model. In the latter regime, translation-sector domain walls proliferate before chirality-changing walls, restoring lattice translational symmetry while preserving long-range time-reversal-odd order. The primary $M$-point correlations are short ranged in this intermediate phase. The two-stage regime begins when the lowest-energy chirality-changing wall is only about $12$--$13\%$ more costly than a same-chirality translation wall. Finite-size scaling of a stable amplitude-resolved Ginzburg--Landau theory shows that the phase survives amplitude relaxation. Our results establish a quantitative domain-wall criterion for vestigial loop-current order and a fluctuation route to time-reversal symmetry breaking without long-range loop-current Bragg order. This separation provides a possible thermodynamic framework for time-reversal-odd responses recently reported above the critical temperature for conventional charge-density-wave ordering in kagome metals.

title: Multiple Andreev Reflection Spectroscopy of Spin-Resolved Proximity States

summary: We predict a coherent multiple Andreev reflection regime in superconducting nanoconstrictions with parallel proximity-induced exchange fields in the electrodes. The subharmonic gap structure is controlled by reconstruction of the spin-resolved electrode spectra, rather than by a rigid displacement of BCS gap edges. This produces split and redistributed anomalies governed by the interval between the outer gap edge and a shifted exchange induced density of states singularity. The effect survives channel transparency averaging and provides a direct transport probe of spin-resolved proximity states.

The authors aim to show that proximity-induced parallel exchange fields instead reconstruct the spin-resolved electrode spectra, enabling a distinct multiple Andreev reflection regime and a new transport-based probe of proximity states.
