title: Encounter Propagator for Multiple Targets: A Dirichlet-to-Neumann Spectral Formalism
summary: We develop an encounter-based formulation of restricted diffusion in a bounded domain with multiple targets, resolving separately the boundary local time accumulated on each target. Unlike the single-target problem, the target projection operators do not generally commute with the governing Dirichlet-to-Neumann (DtN) operator, so that its eigenbasis does not diagonalize the local-time dependence. We overcome this difficulty by decomposing the DtN operator into target-restricted blocks. Multi-dimensional Laplace inversion then yields a convergent switching expansion, whose successive terms describe alternating diffusive transfers between the targets. We also derive an equivalent operator-valued renewal equation. For two targets, diagonalizing the target-restricted blocks provides an explicit spectral representation in terms of two DtN block spectra and an inter-target coupling matrix. When the coupling preserves spectral modes, the switching series can be resummed exactly in terms of modified Bessel functions. In general, as the off-diagonal DtN block is smoothing for separated targets, one can resort to low-rank finite-dimensional approximations. We examine an effective two-mode reduction for small, well-separated targets and identify a regime in which repeated inter-target transfers are progressively suppressed. Probabilistic interpretations and implications for diffusion-controlled reactions are discussed.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an encounter-based formulation of restricted diffusion with multiple targets by decomposing the DtN operator into target-restricted blocks, yielding a convergent switching expansion and renewal equation.
AI.motivation: In the single-target encounter-based (local-time) framework, the target projection operator commutes with the Dirichlet-to-Neumann (DtN) operator, so the DtN eigenbasis diagonalizes the local-time dependence. For multiple targets this commutation generally fails, and no such diagonalization is available, leaving a gap in the theory of encounter-based restricted diffusion with several reactive sites.
AI.method: The DtN operator is decomposed into target-restricted diagonal blocks and inter-target off-diagonal coupling blocks. Multi-dimensional Laplace inversion of the resulting equations produces a convergent switching (series) expansion, each term describing successive diffusive transfers between targets. An equivalent operator-valued renewal equation is derived. For two targets, the target-restricted blocks are diagonalized to give an explicit spectral representation in terms of the two DtN block spectra and an inter-target coupling matrix; when the coupling preserves spectral modes, the switching series is resummed exactly using modified Bessel functions. For separated targets the off-diagonal block is smoothing, allowing low-rank finite-dimensional approximations, and an effective two-mode reduction is analyzed.

A regime is identified in which repeated inter-target transfers are progressively suppressed.
AI.conclusion: The non-commutativity obstacle of the multi-target DtN operator can be circumvented by block decomposition, providing a tractable encounter-based description of restricted diffusion with multiple targets. title: Effective Conservation and Bistability of Atomic Alignment under Strong Spin~Exchange
comment: Article: 5 pages, 4 figures. Supplemental Material: 5 psges
summary: We present a phenomenological model of anomalous alignment signals in dense cesium vapor under linearly polarized pumping and fast spin exchange near zero magnetic field. Despite the absence of a conservation law for rank-2 angular momentum, our recent experiments reveal anisotropic narrow resonances, hysteresis, and bistability. We attribute these effects to a stretched state forming a collective mode in which orientation and alignment are bidirectionally coupled. This mode acts as a reservoir, preserving the essential properties of alignment despite rapid spin exchange.

AI.tldr: A phenomenological model explains narrow anisotropic alignment resonances, hysteresis, and bistability in dense cesium vapor via a collective "stretched state" mode that couples orientation and alignment.
AI.motivation: In dense cesium vapor under linearly polarized pumping and fast spin exchange near zero magnetic field, anomalous alignment signals are observed despite the lack of a rank-2 angular momentum conservation law. Experiments show anisotropic narrow resonances, hysteresis, and bistability that existing understanding does not readily account for, motivating a model to explain their origin.
AI.method: A phenomenological model is developed in which a stretched state forms a collective mode. In this mode, orientation (rank-1) and alignment (rank-2) are bidirectionally coupled, enabling the collective mode to act as a reservoir that preserves the essential properties of alignment even when spin exchange is rapid.
AI.result: The model reproduces the experimentally observed anisotropic narrow resonances, hysteresis, and bistability in dense cesium vapor, attributing them to the orientation-alignment-coupled collective stretched-state mode rather than to any rank-2 conservation law.

This mode functions as a reservoir that sustains alignment properties in the presence of fast spin exchange, providing an effective mechanism replacing the absent rank-2 conservation law.

title: Giant Resonant Reflection Gain from Injection-Induced Quenching in a Tunnel Diode
summary: Negative-resistance microwave oscillators can simultaneously sustain autonomous oscillations and coherently scatter electromagnetic waves, enabling active reflection beyond conventional linear amplification. Here we demonstrate giant resonant reflection gain from synchronization-induced phase localization in a self-sustained tunnel diode oscillator operating near 2.96 GHz. Weak resonant RF injection drives a transition from a broadband free running state to a phase localized narrowband reflected carrier. The resulting reflected enhancement reaches 83.1dB relative to the injected signal and is accompanied by greater than order of magnitude linewidth collapse, nonlinear injection pulling, and a synchronization bandwidth of 15.84 kHz. Time resolved spectrograms directly resolve injection locking and frequency entrainment, while noisy Stuart Landau simulations reproduce the observed spectral concentration and detuning dependent gain roll off near the Hopf instability. Artificially increasing phase diffusion with broadband bias noise suppresses the reflected enhancement, confirming synchronization-induced quenching of phase fluctuations as the origin of the giant coherent reflection gain.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a self-sustained tunnel diode oscillator near 2.96 GHz produces giant resonant reflection gain (up to 83.1 dB) via synchronization-induced phase localization when weakly injected with a resonant RF signal, converting a broadband free-running state into a narrowband coherent reflected carrier.
AI.motivation: Negative-resistance microwave oscillators can both sustain autonomous oscillations and coherently scatter waves, enabling active reflection beyond linear amplification; the paper aims to exploit synchronization effects in such a system to achieve giant coherent reflection gain.
AI.method: Weak resonant RF injection into a self-sustained tunnel diode oscillator near 2.96 GHz; time-resolved spectrograms to resolve injection locking and frequency entrainment; noisy Stuart-Landau simulations to model spectral concentration and detuning-dependent gain roll-off near the Hopf instability; broadband bias noise added to artificially increase phase diffusion as a control test.

Simulations reproduce observed spectral concentration and gain roll-off near the Hopf instability. Adding broadband bias noise suppresses the enhancement.
AI.conclusion: Synchronization-induced quenching of phase fluctuations is the origin of the giant coherent reflection gain, demonstrating phase localization as a mechanism for active reflection enhancement.

title: DFT GGA based datasets for H$_2$O potential energy surfaces, permanent moment and polarizability tensors
summary: We present in this article data on the computed potential energy surface, permanent moment surface (from dipole to hexadecapole) and polarizability surface (from dipole-dipole to quadrupole-quadrupole) for the H$_2$O molecule, calculated at the level of the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) in Kohn-Sham density functional theory (KS-DFT) in the grid-based projector augmented wave code GPAW, using the charge perturbation code C-pol. The GGA-based functionals are PBE, RPBE and BLYP. The monomer surfaces are composed of systematic, symmetry-reduced deformations of the H$_2$O monomer and comprise 10,000 configurations per functional, with traceless Cartesian tensor moment values reported as data strings in the xyz file format. In addition, we provide cluster datasets for n-H$_2$O aggregates (n = 2-6), sampled from liquid-like configurations and computed with the same KS-DFT settings, where each extended xyz file encodes the total interaction energy of the cluster in the comment line. Finally, ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) trajectories of periodic liquid water boxes, containing between 25 to 150 H$_2$O molecules at ambient conditions, are included, furnishing time series of atomic configurations and energies that are consistent with the monomer and cluster data and suitable for validating classical and machine-learned water models.

AI.tldr: This data article reports GGA-level KS-DFT (PBE, RPBE, BLYP) reference data for water: monomer potential energy, multipole moment (dipole to hexadecapole) and polarizability (dipole-dipole to quadrupole-quadrupole) surfaces over 10,000 symmetry-reduced configurations per functional, plus cluster interaction energies for n-H2O (n=2-6) and AIMD trajectories of periodic liquid boxes (25-150 molecules).
AI.motivation: To supply consistent, first-principles reference data spanning molecular, cluster, and condensed-phase water, suitable for parameterizing and validating classical and machine-learned water models.
AI.method: KS-DFT with GGA functionals (PBE, RPBE, BLYP) in the GPAW grid-based projector augmented wave code, using the charge perturbation code C-pol to compute multipole moment and polarizability surfaces. Monomer surfaces are built from systematic, symmetry-reduced deformations. Cluster datasets for n=2-6 are sampled from liquid-like configurations with the same settings. AIMD trajectories of periodic liquid water boxes (25-150 molecules) at ambient conditions are also generated.
AI.result: Monomer surfaces comprising 10,000 configurations per functional with traceless Cartesian tensor moments in xyz format; cluster datasets (n=2-6) as extended xyz files encoding total interaction energies; AIMD trajectories providing time series of atomic configurations and energies consistent with monomer and cluster data.
AI.conclusion: A unified GGA-DFT dataset linking monomer, cluster, and bulk liquid water is provided as a resource for developing and validating classical and machine-learned water models.

title: Correlation-Free Transition Path Sampling through Shooting Point Generation Guided by Committor Learning
summary: Studying the dynamical behavior of a system often depends on characterizing how it transitions between long-lived states. Because such transitions are rare, observing them usually requires specialized enhanced sampling techniques. Transition Path Sampling (TPS) is a well-established method for generating reactive trajectories, which is simple to implement and does not require the definition of a preconceived reaction coordinate. However, its efficiency is limited by its sequential nature and the resulting correlations between sampled paths. Previous work addressed this limitation by combining TPS with a sampling scheme based on conditioned Boltzmann Generators, a generative machine learning model capable of sampling a given target probability distribution. This approach produces uncorrelated transition paths but relies on an accurate reaction coordinate, which is rarely known in advance. Building on recent advances in committor learning, specifically on the Artificial Intelligence for Molecular Mechanism Discovery (AIMMD) method, in this work we introduce GenAIMMD, an iterative algorithm that actively and self-consistently learns the ideal reaction coordinate (the committor) and trains a conditioned Boltzmann Generator to sample from arbitrary bias windows along it. GenAIMMD thereby provides a correlation-free and fully parallelizable path sampling scheme that does not require prior knowledge of the system's transition mechanism. We apply GenAIMMD to a two-dimensional toy model and a higher-dimensional polymer system. In both cases, GenAIMMD succeeds in training the Boltzmann Generator and learning the committor. Benchmark results show a substantial increase in performance compared to standard TPS.

AI.tldr: GenAIMMD combines committor learning (AIMMD) with conditioned Boltzmann Generators to deliver a correlation-free, parallelizable transition path sampling method that needs no prior reaction coordinate, and it outperforms standard TPS on a 2D toy model and a polymer system.
AI.motivation: Studying transitions between long-lived states requires enhanced sampling because such rare events are hard to observe. Transition Path Sampling (TPS) is simple and needs no preconceived reaction coordinate, but its efficiency suffers from sequential sampling and correlated paths. A prior fix using conditioned Boltzmann Generators produced uncorrelated paths but required an accurate reaction coordinate, which is rarely known beforehand.
AI.method: Building on committor-learning advances, specifically the Artificial Intelligence for Molecular Mechanism Discovery (AIMMD) method, the authors introduce GenAIMMD, an iterative algorithm that self-consistently learns the ideal reaction coordinate (the committor) while simultaneously training a conditioned Boltzmann Generator to sample from arbitrary bias windows along it.
AI.result: Applied to a two-dimensional toy model and a higher-dimensional polymer system, GenAIMMD successfully trains the Boltzmann Generator and learns the committor in both cases. Benchmark results show a substantial performance increase compared to standard TPS.
AI.conclusion: GenAIMMD provides a correlation-free, fully parallelizable path sampling scheme that requires no prior knowledge of the system's transition mechanism, offering a practical and efficient alternative to standard TPS.

title: Melting of corundum (α-Al2O3) under compression to 8 GPa: A decreasing melting slope
summary: Melting of corundum (α-Al2O3) has been studied under compression up to 8 GPa using in situ electrical resistivity measurements. The melting temperature increases monotonically from T0 = 2317 K at ambient pressure to 3090 K at 7.7 GPa. Fitting the experimental data to the Simon-Glatzel equation yields the empirical parameters a = 5.60 GPa and c = 0.334, providing a closed-form analytical description of the entire melting boundary. Most significantly, the melting slope, dTm/dp, decreases continuously from 138 K/GPa at ambient pressure down to 78 K/GPa at 7.7 GPa, confirming unequivocal negative curvature of the melting curve (d2Tm/dp2 < 0). This phenomenon is consistent with the preferential densification of the liquid phase and the associated reduction in the volume change upon melting as pressure rises. These findings provide a robust empirical standard for the high-pressure melting of corundum, establishing essential constraints for future ab initio simulations, thermodynamic databases, and geophysical models of alumina-rich deep-Earth systems.

AI.method: In situ electrical resistivity measurements were performed on α-Al2O3 under compression up to 8 GPa to locate the melting temperature; the experimental melting data were fitted to the Simon-Glatzel equation.

AI.conclusion: These results provide a robust empirical standard for the high-pressure melting of corundum, offering essential constraints for future ab initio simulations, thermodynamic databases, and geophysical models of alumina-rich deep-Earth systems.

title: Quantum transport across normal-superlattice-normal graphene junctions: Fabry-Pérot interference, Hofstadter butterfly, and supersnake states
summary: Electrostatic modulation of graphene provides a tunable route to engineering miniband structures. We perform quantum transport simulations on a gate-defined graphene superlattice junction, formed by confining a two-dimensional superlattice graphene (SGr) region between two normal graphene (NGr) regions. In the low-field regime at low carrier densities, robust Fabry-Pérot interference fringes emerge even in the unipolar regime due to Fermi-velocity renormalization in the SGr region. At stronger magnetic fields but only up to 3 T, the conductance map clearly reveals the Hofstadter butterfly spectrum. At intermediate fields, our finite-width transport simulations reveal a new type of snake state, the supersnake state, composed of alternating anomalous cyclotron arcs on the SGr side and conventional semicircular arcs on the NGr side, forming a weaving trajectory along the junction. The resulting conductance oscillations agree well with geometrical conditions derived from semiclassical cyclotron orbits. Our results demonstrate that gate-defined NGr-SGr-NGr junctions provide a versatile platform hosting multiple transport regimes within a single device architecture and can be generalized to other types of superlattices not restricted to graphene.

AI.tldr: Quantum transport simulations of a gate-defined NGr-SGr-NGr junction reveal Fabry-Pérot interference at low fields, a Hofstadter butterfly up to 3 T, and a novel "supersnake" state at intermediate fields.
AI.motivation: Electrostatic modulation of graphene offers a tunable route to engineering miniband structures, motivating the study of confined superlattice graphene regions for hosting multiple transport regimes.
AI.method: Quantum transport simulations on a gate-defined graphene superlattice junction formed by confining a 2D superlattice graphene (SGr) region between two normal graphene (NGr) regions, using finite-width simulations.
AI.result: In the low-field low-density regime, robust Fabry-Pérot interference fringes emerge even in the unipolar regime due to Fermi-velocity renormalization in the SGr region. At stronger fields up to 3 T, the conductance map reveals the Hofstadter butterfly spectrum. At intermediate fields, a new supersnake state appears, composed of alternating anomalous cyclotron arcs on the SGr side and conventional semicircular arcs on the NGr side, forming a weaving trajectory; conductance oscillations agree with semiclassical cyclotron-orbit geometrical conditions.
AI.conclusion: Gate-defined NGr-SGr-NGr junctions provide a versatile platform hosting multiple transport regimes within a single device architecture and can be generalized to other superlattice types beyond graphene.

title: Fractional quantum spin Hall crystals from hidden density-wave order
summary: Broken symmetry and topology are distinct descriptions for how matter organizes itself. Here, we propose one gives rise to the other. A mixed singlet-triplet $d$-density wave, which is a particle-hole condensate, has a hidden bond order that breaks translation symmetry and generates a time-reversed pair of Chern bands, without producing conventional charge or spin density order. At fractional fillings with odd denominators, finite size exact diagonalization studies show how repulsive interactions can transform this symmetry-broken topological state into a fractional quantum spin Hall liquid. Its opposite chiralities produce a crossed response in which charge flux transports spin, and spin flux transports charge. The same setting also reveals what borders such a phase. Strong interspin coupling and increasingly dilute fillings favor charge order and make residual band dispersion decisive, while at half filling, the spin-decoupled limit gives a homogeneous correlated liquid with signatures consistent with the physics of a composite Fermi liquid.

At odd-denominator fractional fillings, repulsive interactions can convert this state into a fractional quantum spin Hall liquid with crossed charge-spin responses, while other regimes instead favor charge order or a composite Fermi liquid.
AI.motivation: Broken symmetry and topology are usually treated as distinct ways in which matter organizes itself. This work asks whether one can give rise to the other, proposing that a symmetry-broken condensate can generate topological band structure.
AI.method: The authors study a mixed singlet-triplet d-density wave, a particle-hole condensate possessing hidden bond order. They use finite-size exact diagonalization to examine the effects of repulsive interactions at fractional fillings with odd denominators, and also probe neighboring regimes such as strong interspin coupling, dilute fillings, and the half-filled spin-decoupled limit.

At odd-denominator fractional fillings, repulsive interactions can transform this symmetry-broken topological state into a fractional quantum spin Hall liquid, whose opposite chiralities yield a crossed response where charge flux transports spin and spin flux transports charge. Strong interspin coupling and increasingly dilute fillings favor charge order, with residual band dispersion becoming decisive, whereas at half filling the spin-decoupled limit gives a homogeneous correlated liquid with signatures consistent with a composite Fermi liquid.

title: Surface-condition-mediated supercooling of the A-B transition in confined superfluid helium-3
summary: Chiral $p$-wave superconductors and superfluids are central model systems in the search for topological quantum matter, but in reduced dimensions their properties are inseparable from the boundary conditions imposed by surrounding surfaces. Superfluid $^3$He provides a uniquely clean, well-established spin-triplet $p$-wave condensate in which these boundary conditions can be engineered directly. Here, we use a fourth-sound Helmholtz resonator to study the A--B phase transition of $^3$He confined to a $1.8\,μ$m cavity after preplating the internal surfaces with $\sim4$ atomic layers of $^4$He. In contrast to our previous fourth-sound measurements, which showed no resolvable hysteresis in the transition temperature, the preplated device exhibits a clear separation between cooling and warming transition temperatures together with stochastic run-to-run variations. The hysteresis decreases toward the highest pressures studied, consistent with previous observations of the pressure dependence of $^4$He-mediated quasiparticle boundary scattering. These results demonstrate that surface preparation can qualitatively modify first-order transition kinetics in confined $^3$He, making boundary conditions an experimentally accessible control parameter for metastability and for future studies of reduced-dimension topological superfluid states.

title: Higher-Order Interactions in Complex Systems: Mechanisms, Behaviour, Representation and Reducibility
summary: Higher-order interactions couple three or more elements in ways that cannot be decomposed into pairwise contributions. In diverse complex systems they produce striking collective behaviours such as explosive synchronization, discontinuous transitions and altered stability. Neither such behaviour nor a description written in many-body terms establishes a many-body mechanism, since both depend on how the system is represented. This review distinguishes three questions: what mechanism governs the system, what behaviour does it produce, and how is either represented? Representation covers both which variables are included and how relations among them are encoded. We examine direct many-body mechanisms, nonlinear but pairwise mechanisms that mimic them, and indirect routes through shared environments or eliminated variables, together with temporal aggregation, an artefact of observation rather than a mechanism. The same behaviour can arise from different mechanisms, and a given higher-order mechanism has no universal behavioural consequence. We then formulate reducibility, the question of whether a higher-order model can be replaced by a lower-order one, as a comparison between a source model and an admissible class of lower-order models, relative to a target and a tolerance. The target may be a microscopic rule, an observable or a qualitative feature. Information-theoretic and inferential methods are reviewed as complementary tools for detecting higher-order dependence, testing lower-order alternatives and reconstructing interaction structure. However, observational data alone generally cannot establish the mechanism. We close by identifying open problems in linking mechanisms to measurable signatures, coarse-graining, identifiability and causality, and in extending reductions beyond mean field. (Abridged)

AI.tldr: This review argues that higher-order interactions require distinguishing mechanism, behaviour, and representation, and formulates reducibility as a model-comparison problem relative to a target and tolerance.
AI.motivation: Higher-order interactions produce striking collective behaviours such as explosive synchronization and discontinuous transitions, but neither the behaviour nor a many-body description alone establishes a genuine many-body mechanism, since both depend on representation. The paper aims to disentangle what governs a system from what it produces and how it is represented.
AI.method: The review distinguishes three questions—mechanism, behaviour, and representation (which variables are included and how relations are encoded). It examines direct many-body mechanisms, nonlinear pairwise mechanisms that mimic them, indirect routes via shared environments or eliminated variables, and temporal aggregation as an observational artefact. It formulates reducibility as comparison between a source model and an admissible class of lower-order models relative to a target (microscopic rule, observable, or qualitative feature) and a tolerance, and reviews information-theoretic and inferential methods.

Information-theoretic and inferential methods serve as complementary tools for detecting higher-order dependence, testing lower-order alternatives, and reconstructing interaction structure, yet observational data alone generally cannot establish the mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Open problems remain in linking mechanisms to measurable signatures, coarse-graining, identifiability, causality, and extending reductions beyond mean field.

title: Energy Harvesting for Self-Powered Microsystems: A Critical Review of Materials, Power Management, and System Integration
summary: The relentless proliferation of the Internet of Things (IoT), wearable bioelectronics, and cyber-physical infrastructure has rendered the conventional electrochemical battery the single most prohibitive bottleneck to long-term, maintenance-free autonomous microsystems. Energy harvesting, i.e. the conversion of ambient mechanical, thermal, and radiative energy into usable electrical power, has consequently emerged as a transformative paradigm to realize perpetual, battery-independent operation. This review critically synthesizes the most significant advances in energy harvesting technologies over the recent period, with a focus on triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs), piezoelectric and pyroelectric transducers, indoor photovoltaics, radio-frequency (RF) rectennas, and their multi-source hybrid integrations. We highlight paradigm-shifting breakthroughs, including liquid-solid TENGs that eliminate mechanical wear, nonlinear piezoelectric oscillators that broaden operational bandwidth by over 300%, machine-learning-accelerated material discovery for high charge-density dielectrics, and multiband and broadband RF harvesting enabled by metamaterial architectures. Crucially, we move beyond conventional materials-centric narratives to critically interrogate the "unseen" system-level bottlenecks: ultra-low-voltage cold-start power management integrated circuits (PMICs), the impedance-matching challenges of hybrid energy sources, and the persistent degradation of micro-supercapacitors and thin-film batteries under realistic field conditions.

AI.tldr: This review synthesizes recent advances in energy harvesting for battery-free IoT microsystems, covering TENGs, piezoelectric/pyroelectric transducers, indoor photovoltaics, RF rectennas, and hybrid integration, while critically addressing overlooked system-level bottlenecks such as cold-start PMICs, impedance matching, and storage degradation.
AI.motivation: The proliferation of IoT, wearable bioelectronics, and cyber-physical infrastructure has made conventional electrochemical batteries the key bottleneck to long-term, maintenance-free autonomous microsystems. Energy harvesting is positioned as a transformative path to perpetual, battery-independent operation, motivating a critical synthesis of the field.
AI.method: A critical review approach that synthesizes recent advances across triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs), piezoelectric and pyroelectric transducers, indoor photovoltaics, RF rectennas, and multi-source hybrid integrations, with deliberate attention to system-level rather than purely materials-centric analysis.
AI.result: Paradigm-shifting breakthroughs are highlighted: liquid-solid TENGs that eliminate mechanical wear, nonlinear piezoelectric oscillators broadening operational bandwidth by over 300%, machine-learning-accelerated discovery of high charge-density dielectrics, and metamaterial-enabled multiband/broadband RF harvesting.
AI.conclusion: The field must move beyond materials-centric narratives to confront 'unseen' system-level bottlenecks: ultra-low-voltage cold-start power management ICs (PMICs), impedance-matching challenges in hybrid energy sources, and degradation of micro-supercapacitors and thin-film batteries under realistic field conditions.

title: Efficient tensorized evaluation of permutation invariant polynomials for representing potential energy surfaces
summary: Permutation invariant polynomials (PIPs), together with related polynomial-based invariant descriptors such as fundamental invariants (FIs), are widely used in constructing high-fidelity global potential energy surfaces (PESs) of molecules that contain identical atoms. Although the monomial symmetrization approach (MSA) enables fast evaluation of PIPs through recursive factorization, it leads to deeply nested computational graphs that may require large memory and are inefficient in modern automatic differentiation frameworks. In this work, we introduce JaxPIP, a JAX-based implementation that reformulates PIP/FI evaluation into tensorized linear algebra operations. By replacing recursive factorization with dense matrix operations combined with log-exp transformation and segmented summation, the evaluation becomes regular and GPU-friendly. This allows efficient execution with just-in-time compilation and enables large-scale batch evaluation of energies and forces (as well as higher-order derivatives). The resulting architecture supports ensemble simulations such as quasi-classical trajectory (QCT), path-integral molecular dynamics (PIMD), and diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) in a fully vectorized manner. As demonstrated in examples, JaxPIP provides a practical route for efficient simulations of molecular systems with scalable GPU execution.

AI.tldr: JaxPIP reformulates permutation invariant polynomial (PIP)/fundamental invariant (FI) evaluation into tensorized linear algebra operations on GPUs, replacing recursive factorization with dense matrix ops, log-exp transforms, and segmented summation to enable fast, scalable, vectorized molecular simulations.
AI.motivation: PIPs and FIs are widely used to build high-fidelity global potential energy surfaces (PESs) for molecules with identical atoms. The monomial symmetrization approach (MSA) enables fast PIP evaluation via recursive factorization, but produces deeply nested computational graphs that demand large memory and are inefficient in modern automatic differentiation frameworks.
AI.method: JaxPIP, a JAX-based implementation, reformulates PIP/FI evaluation as tensorized linear algebra. It replaces recursive factorization with dense matrix operations combined with log-exp transformation and segmented summation, yielding regular, GPU-friendly computation executable via just-in-time compilation. This supports large-scale batch evaluation of energies, forces, and higher-order derivatives, and enables fully vectorized ensemble simulations (QCT, PIMD, DMC).
AI.result: The evaluation becomes regular and GPU-friendly, allowing efficient JIT-compiled execution and large-scale batch computation of energies, forces, and higher-order derivatives. The architecture supports fully vectorized ensemble simulations including quasi-classical trajectory (QCT), path-integral molecular dynamics (PIMD), and diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC).
AI.conclusion: JaxPIP provides a practical route for efficient simulations of molecular systems with scalable GPU execution.

title: How durable are high-performance racing shoes?
summary: High-performance racing shoes rely on ultra-low-density elastomeric foams that undergo large, repeated deformations during running. Yet little is known about how their mechanical properties vary throughout the shoe or change with repeated use. Here, we characterize the midsole foam in an elite-level racing shoe from the heel, midfoot, and toe of a new shoe and a shoe worn for 300 miles. Microscopy reveals a characteristic pore length scale of 128+/-18 um and supports an approximately isotropic continuum description. We then quantify the mechanical response under tension, compression, and shear. Remarkably, despite 300 miles of real-world use, the foam retains its mechanical response across all three loading modes and shoe regions. Energy return remains largely unchanged, with values of 85-93% in tension and compression and 64-71% in shear. At the same time, we observe strong regional variations, with tensile and compressive stiffnesses 38-51% lower in the toe than in the heel. The foam also exhibits a pronounced tension-compression asymmetry in Poisson's ratio. Together, these findings reveal a spatially structured and mode-dependent mechanical response that remains largely preserved after 300 miles of use. This mechanical resilience may extend the functional lifetime of racing shoes, with implications for runners, replacement recommendations, and sustainability.

AI.tldr: The midsole foam of an elite racing shoe retains its mechanical response after 300 miles of real-world use, but exhibits strong spatial and mode-dependent variations.
AI.motivation: Ultra-low-density elastomeric foams in high-performance racing shoes undergo large repeated deformations, yet how their mechanical properties vary across the shoe and change with repeated use is poorly understood.
AI.method: The midsole foam of a new shoe and one worn for 300 miles was characterized from heel, midfoot, and toe regions. Microscopy established pore length scale (128+/-18 um) and approximately isotropic continuum behavior, followed by quantification of mechanical response under tension, compression, and shear.
AI.result: The foam retained its mechanical response across all three loading modes and all shoe regions after 300 miles. Energy return was 85-93% in tension and compression and 64-71% in shear. Tensile and compressive stiffnesses were 38-51% lower in the toe than the heel, and a pronounced tension-compression asymmetry in Poisson's ratio was observed.
AI.conclusion: The foam shows a spatially structured, mode-dependent mechanical response that is largely preserved after 300 miles of use, suggesting mechanical resilience that may extend the functional lifetime of racing shoes, with implications for runners, replacement recommendations, and sustainability.

title: Electron $g$-value comparison of paramagnetic muonium and hydrogen centers in rutile TiO$_2$
summary: Muonium (Mu) is widely used as a model for isolated hydrogen in condensed matter, but whether its electronic state is truly equivalent to that of hydrogen remains to be tested with an orbital-sensitive probe. Here we use double electron-muon resonance to determine the electron $g$ values of the paramagnetic Mu center in rutile TiO$_2$ for magnetic fields along [100], [110], and [001] directions. The obtained $g$ values closely follow those of the H-related Ti$^{3+}$ paramagnetic center in both magnitude and anisotropy. This agreement tests the Mu--H correspondence at the level of the Ti $3d$ electronic state and supports a common localized Ti$^{3+}$ electronic core for the two centers.

AI.tldr: Double electron-muon resonance measures the electron g values of the paramagnetic muonium center in rutile TiO2 along three crystallographic directions, and the results match the H-related Ti3+ center, validating the Mu-H correspondence at the Ti 3d electronic level.
AI.motivation: Muonium (Mu) is widely used as a model for isolated hydrogen in condensed matter, but whether its electronic state is truly equivalent to that of hydrogen had not been tested with an orbital-sensitive probe.
AI.method: Double electron-muon resonance was used to determine the electron g values of the paramagnetic Mu center in rutile TiO2 for magnetic fields along the [100], [110], and [001] directions.
AI.result: The obtained g values closely follow those of the H-related Ti3+ paramagnetic center in both magnitude and anisotropy.
AI.conclusion: The agreement between the Mu and H-related centers tests the Mu-H correspondence at the level of the Ti 3d electronic state and supports a common localized Ti3+ electronic core for the two centers.

title: Transport Relaxation Mechanisms in Bilayer Graphene: Effects of Pauli Blocking
summary: We present a unified analytical treatment of carrier transport relaxation in bilayer graphene (BLG), including scattering by surface roughness, charged and neutral impurities, acoustic and optical phonons, and substrate polar phonons. The calculation is formulated within the low-energy two-band approximation using Fermi's golden rule and the semiclassical Boltzmann transport equation. Closed-form expressions for the transport relaxation rates are derived and verified by numerical evaluation of the corresponding scattering integrals. Particular attention is given to Pauli blocking, whose influence becomes important under degenerate carrier conditions owing to the approximately parabolic low-energy dispersion and nearly constant density of states of BLG. We find that Pauli blocking modifies the relaxation rates in a mechanism- and energy-dependent manner for both suspended and substrate-supported BLG. For the parameters considered, neutral-impurity scattering provides the dominant contribution over a substantial energy range, while acoustic-phonon and charged-impurity scattering remain important competing mechanisms. Optical-phonon scattering is suppressed below its emission threshold, whereas substrate polar phonons provide an additional relaxation channel in supported BLG. Comparison with monolayer graphene and a conventional two-dimensional electron gas highlights the role of band dispersion, density of states, screening, and chirality in determining the distinct scattering behavior of BLG. These results provide analytical insight into the relative importance of the principal momentum-relaxation mechanisms and the role of Pauli blocking in BLG transport.

AI.tldr: The paper derives closed-form transport relaxation rates for bilayer graphene across six scattering mechanisms within the two-band model and Boltzmann formalism, showing that Pauli blocking modulates rates in a mechanism- and energy-dependent way, with neutral-impurity scattering dominating over a wide energy range for the studied parameters.
AI.motivation: Carrier transport relaxation in bilayer graphene involves multiple competing scattering channels, yet a unified analytical treatment with closed-form relaxation rates—and a clear account of how Pauli blocking affects each mechanism—was lacking. The work aims to quantify the relative importance of these mechanisms and to contrast BLG with monolayer graphene and a conventional 2D electron gas.
AI.method: A low-energy two-band (approximately parabolic) approximation of BLG is used with Fermi's golden rule and the semiclassical Boltzmann transport equation. Scattering by surface roughness, charged and neutral impurities, acoustic and optical phonons, and substrate polar phonons is treated. Closed-form transport relaxation rates are derived and validated against numerical evaluation of the scattering integrals, with explicit handling of Pauli blocking under degenerate conditions. Both suspended and substrate-supported BLG are considered.
AI.result: Pauli blocking alters relaxation rates in a mechanism- and energy-dependent manner, enabled by BLG's near-parabolic low-energy dispersion and nearly constant density of states. For the parameters considered, neutral-impurity scattering dominates over a substantial energy range, with acoustic-phonon and charged-impurity scattering as important competitors. Optical-phonon scattering is suppressed below its emission threshold, while substrate polar phonons add a relaxation channel in supported BLG. Comparisons with monolayer graphene and a 2D electron gas underscore the roles of band dispersion, density of states, screening, and chirality.
AI.conclusion: The analysis provides closed-form, analytically transparent metrics for the relative strength of momentum-relaxation mechanisms in BLG and clarifies the role of Pauli blocking in BLG transport for both suspended and supported samples.

title: Pressure induced structural phase transition and magneto-elastic coupling in Eu doped LaCrO$_3$
summary: In this study, we have carried out a detailed high pressure investigation on 5$\%$ Eu doped LaCrO$_3$ (ELCO) using synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD), micro Raman spectroscopy, and low-temperature magnetization measurements to correlate the structural and magnetic properties under pressure. The high pressure XRD reveals the orthorhombic to rhombohedral structural phase transition around 10.6 GPa. The high pressure Raman data corroborate this result and indicate that the lattice instabilities associated with the low-frequency soft modes play a crucial role in driving this transition. In addition, a pronounced anomaly in the Raman shift and integrated intensity of several Raman modes is observed around 4.5 GPa. By combining the low-temperature magnetization measurements with the anomalies observed in the XRD and Raman data and by comparing with the similar results in LaCrO$_3$ (LCO), a pressure-induced change in the magnetic ground state to antiferromagnetic ordering is predicted.

AI.tldr: High-pressure XRD, Raman, and magnetization studies on 5% Eu-doped LaCrO3 reveal an orthorhombic-to-rhombohedral transition near 10.6 GPa, soft-mode-driven lattice instabilities, an additional anomaly near 4.5 GPa, and a predicted pressure-induced change of the magnetic ground state to antiferromagnetic order.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to establish a correlation between structural and magnetic properties of 5% Eu-doped LaCrO3 under pressure, and to clarify how doping and compression together influence its structural stability and magnetic ground state.
AI.method: The authors performed high-pressure synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD), micro-Raman spectroscopy, and low-temperature magnetization measurements on 5% Eu-doped LaCrO3 (ELCO), and compared the results with those of undoped LaCrO3 (LCO).
AI.result: High-pressure XRD shows an orthorhombic-to-rhombohedral structural phase transition around 10.6 GPa, corroborated by Raman data indicating that lattice instabilities linked to low-frequency soft modes drive the transition. A pronounced anomaly in Raman shift and integrated intensity of several modes appears near 4.5 GPa. Combining magnetization with the XRD/Raman anomalies and comparison to LaCrO3 predicts a pressure-induced change of the magnetic ground state to antiferromagnetic ordering.
AI.conclusion: Pressure drives a structural transition near 10.6 GPa mediated by soft-mode lattice instabilities, alongside an anomaly near 4.5 GPa; together these results predict a pressure-induced antiferromagnetic ground state in Eu-doped LaCrO3, highlighting strong coupling between structure and magnetism under compression.

title: Pairing symmetry and superconductivity from long-range Coulomb interactions in the extended t-t'-t''-Jz model for cuprates
summary: We investigate the pairing symmetry of the ground-state phase diagram of an extended two-dimensional $t$-$t'$-$t''$-$J_z$ model, in which the first-, second-, and third-nearest neighbor electron hopping terms ($t,t'$ and $t''$) and an anisotropic Ising-like antiferromagnetic interaction $J_z$ are treated on the same framework. We find that the dominant pairing symmetry depends sensitively on the sign and magnitude of the hopping parameters $t'$ and $t''$, showing pure $p$-wave, pure $d$-wave, or coexisting pairing channels, highlighting the decisive role of these terms. We further explore the role of the long-range and short-range repulsive interactions in the formation of pairs and analyze the specific case of hole-doped cuprates. Our results indicate that repulsive interactions favors hole pair escaping of the stripe domains. Furthermore, pairing correlation calculations strongly suggest that repulsive Coulomb interactions drive reentrant superconducting behavior at experimentally observed underdoped regime ($δ\approx0.07$ to $0.15$), as in Neodymium-based cuprates.

AI.tldr: The pairing symmetry of an extended 2D t-t'-t''-Jz model is studied, showing that p-wave, d-wave, or coexisting channels emerge depending on the sign and magnitude of t' and t'', with repulsive interactions driving reentrant superconductivity in the underdoped regime.
AI.motivation: To understand how first-, second-, and third-nearest neighbor hopping terms (t, t', t'') and an anisotropic Ising-like antiferromagnetic interaction Jz jointly govern the ground-state pairing symmetry, and to clarify the role of repulsive interactions in pair formation, particularly for hole-doped cuprates.
AI.method: Ground-state phase diagram calculation of an extended two-dimensional t-t'-t''-Jz model treating hopping terms and Jz on the same footing; analysis of pairing symmetry, pairing correlation calculations, and examination of long-range and short-range repulsive interactions, with a specific application to hole-doped cuprates.
AI.result: The dominant pairing symmetry depends sensitively on the sign and magnitude of t' and t'', yielding pure p-wave, pure d-wave, or coexisting pairing channels. Repulsive interactions favor hole pairs escaping stripe domains. Pairing correlation calculations suggest repulsive Coulomb interactions drive reentrant superconducting behavior in the underdoped regime (δ ≈ 0.07–0.15), as observed in Neodymium-based cuprates.
AI.conclusion: Hopping parameters t' and t'' play a decisive role in selecting the pairing symmetry. Repulsive Coulomb interactions are essential for pair formation and can induce reentrant superconductivity in the underdoped regime, consistent with experimental observations in Neodymium-based cuprates.

title: Landau diamagnetism and the de Haas-van Alphen effect from a single geometric construction
summary: Landau diamagnetism is usually derived from the grand canonical potential, a calculation that yields the correct susceptibility but little physical insight, while the rule that extremal cross sections govern the de Haas-van Alphen (dHvA) oscillations is commonly asserted rather than exhibited. We present an elementary zero-temperature construction in which the occupied states of a free-electron gas are grouped, interval by interval along the field direction, into the Landau levels onto which they condense. Within each interval the field-induced energy cost reduces to a transfer of states between two congruent triangles, and center-of-mass arithmetic yields the Landau susceptibility. The construction fails only in a narrow neighborhood of an extremal cross section of the Fermi surface; there the contribution oscillates with the dHvA period, one oscillation for each Landau level that passes through the extremal cross section. Direct zero-temperature state counting locates the oscillation: the residual is concentrated in the few intervals nearest the extremal cross section, the summed contribution of the distant ones being negligible on the scale of the peak oscillation amplitude.

AI.tldr: An elementary zero-temperature geometric construction derives Landau diamagnetism via center-of-mass arithmetic of two congruent triangles, and explains the dHvA oscillations as arising from the narrow neighborhood of an extremal Fermi-surface cross section.
AI.motivation: Standard derivations of Landau diamagnetism from the grand canonical potential give the correct susceptibility but little physical insight, and the rule that extremal cross sections govern de Haas-van Alphen oscillations is typically asserted rather than demonstrated.
AI.method: A zero-temperature construction groups the occupied states of a free-electron gas, interval by interval along the field direction, into the Landau levels they condense onto. In each interval the field-induced energy cost becomes a transfer of states between two congruent triangles, so the susceptibility follows from center-of-mass arithmetic.
AI.result: The construction yields the Landau susceptibility and fails only in a narrow neighborhood of an extremal cross section of the Fermi surface, where the contribution oscillates with the dHvA period, one oscillation per Landau level passing through that cross section. Zero-temperature state counting shows the residual is concentrated in the few intervals nearest the extremal cross section, while the summed contribution of distant intervals is negligible relative to the peak oscillation amplitude.
AI.conclusion: The geometric triangle-transfer picture reproduces the Landau susceptibility and makes the extremal-cross-section origin of dHvA oscillations explicit, with the oscillation localized to intervals near the extremal cross section.

title: Three-dimensional vector waves in time-variant materials, with applications in time-reversed focusing and Green's function retrieval
summary: The behavior of wave propagation and scattering in time-variant materials has been studied by many authors, for electromagnetic as well as for mechanical waves. Most studies consider two-dimensional waves, governed by scalar wave equations. Here we introduce a unified wave equation for three-dimensional electromagnetic and elastodynamic vector-wave propagation and scattering in homogeneous, time-variant materials. Using the symmetry properties of this equation, we establish the conservation of net field-momentum density, and a reciprocity relation between causal and acausal Green's functions. The latter relation is exploited in the derivation of the counterparts of classical time-reversed focusing and Green's function retrieval for time-variant materials.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a unified wave equation for 3D electromagnetic and elastodynamic vector-wave propagation/scattering in homogeneous time-variant materials, and uses its symmetries to derive net field-momentum conservation, a reciprocity relation between causal and acausal Green's functions, and counterparts of time-reversed focusing and Green's function retrieval.
AI.motivation: Prior studies on wave propagation and scattering in time-variant materials mostly rely on two-dimensional waves governed by scalar wave equations, and are typically limited to either electromagnetic or mechanical waves separately. A general, unified framework covering three-dimensional vector-wave propagation and scattering in homogeneous time-variant media is lacking, limiting the extension of classical time-symmetry-based concepts to such media.
AI.method: The authors introduce a unified wave equation governing three-dimensional electromagnetic and elastodynamic vector-wave propagation and scattering in homogeneous, time-variant materials. They exploit the symmetry properties of this equation to establish the conservation of net field-momentum density and a reciprocity relation between causal and acausal Green's functions. This reciprocity relation is then used to derive counterparts of classical time-reversed focusing and Green's function retrieval for time-variant materials.
AI.result: A unified wave equation for 3D electromagnetic and elastodynamic vector waves in homogeneous time-variant materials is established. Conservation of net field-momentum density is proven. A reciprocity relation between causal and acausal Green's functions is derived, and from it, generalized counterparts of classical time-reversed focusing and Green's function retrieval are obtained for time-variant media.
AI.conclusion: The proposed unified equation and its symmetry properties extend classical time-symmetry-based results—field-momentum conservation, Green's function reciprocity, time-reversed focusing, and Green's function retrieval—from time-invariant to homogeneous time-variant materials, providing a general framework applicable to both electromagnetic and elastodynamic vector waves in three dimensions.

title: FOSY: Segmental Backbone Assignment in Intrinsically Disordered Proteins
summary: Backbone resonance assignment is a prerequisite for most biomolecular NMR applications, yet conventional multidimensional strategies frequently fail for intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and regions (IDRs) because of severe spectral overlap, rapid amide proton exchange with water, and missing sequential correlations. In many biological applications, however, complete protein assignment is unnecessary, as only a limited sequence segment surrounding a functional site is required. Here we introduce segmental backbone assignment, an assignment strategy implemented by FOcused SpectroscopY (FOSY), which concentrates experimental effort on relatively short regions while retaining the high-dimensional sequential connectivity needed for unambiguous assignments. We present a self-consistent suite of selective two-dimensional FOSY experiments that enables bidirectional assignment walks along the protein sequence through complementary forward and backward transfer schemes. The methodology employs frequency-selective polarisation transfer to replace high-dimensional experiments with sensitive and readily interpretable 2D spectra while preserving the information content of multidimensional correlation experiments. The approach is demonstrated by completing the assignment of G302-K311 segment, which is missing in the published assignment of the 441-residue human Tau protein. The approach complements conventional multidimensional or residue type-selective assignment strategies by providing an efficient means of traversing assignment interruptions and rapidly characterising functionally important segments in intrinsically disordered proteins.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces segmental backbone assignment via FOcused SpectroscopY (FOSY), a suite of selective 2D experiments using frequency-selective polarisation transfer that assigns only a short region of interest. It is validated by completing the missing G302-K311 assignment in the 441-residue human Tau protein.
AI.motivation: Conventional multidimensional backbone assignment fails for intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and regions (IDRs) due to severe spectral overlap, rapid amide proton exchange with water, and missing sequential correlations. Since complete assignment is often unnecessary—only a limited segment around a functional site is needed—a method targeting short regions while retaining unambiguous sequential connectivity is required.
AI.method: Segmental backbone assignment implemented by FOcused SpectroscopY (FOSY). A self-consistent suite of selective 2D FOSY experiments enables bidirectional assignment walks along the sequence via complementary forward and backward transfer schemes. Frequency-selective polarisation transfer replaces high-dimensional experiments with sensitive, readily interpretable 2D spectra while preserving the information content of multidimensional correlation experiments.
AI.result: The approach completes assignment of the G302-K311 segment, which was missing in the published assignment of the 441-residue human Tau protein.
AI.conclusion: FOSY-based segmental backbone assignment complements conventional multidimensional and residue type-selective strategies, providing an efficient means to traverse assignment interruptions and rapidly characterise functionally important segments in intrinsically disordered proteins.

title: How Does Distribution Shift Shape Pretraining Gains in Neural PDE Surrogates?
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures. Representations for the Physical Sciences Workshop, NeurIPS 2026
summary: Pretraining a neural PDE surrogate can reduce the amount of new CFD data needed when geometry or modeled physics changes. However, it remains unclear how different components of distribution shift affect this benefit. We pretrain a surrogate on 254,909 RANS solutions from one airfoil family and fine-tune it on a new family under two target settings with matched freestream ranges: the same Spalart-Allmaras (SA) modeling and SA with added $e^N$ transition modeling. At $N=1000$, the pretrained model matches the accuracy of a model trained from scratch on $3.25\times$ as many samples for the same-SA target, but $2.58\times$ as many for the transition-modeled target. By $N=5000$, this ordering reverses ($1.56\times$ versus $1.86\times$). At $N=1000$, sampling more distinct airfoils lowers error on both targets, but only for the same-SA target is the gain increase larger than the observed draw-to-draw variation ($3.3\times$ to $4.0\times$). These results show that pretraining value depends jointly on target-data budget, target-data coverage, and whether source and target differ in modeled physics.

AI.tldr: Pretraining a neural PDE surrogate on one airfoil family reduces new CFD data needs, but the benefit depends jointly on target-data budget, target-data coverage, and whether source and target differ in modeled physics.
AI.motivation: Pretraining can reduce the amount of new CFD data needed when geometry or modeled physics changes, but it is unclear how the different components of distribution shift (geometry vs. modeled physics) affect this benefit.
AI.method: Pretrain a surrogate on 254,909 RANS solutions from one airfoil family, then fine-tune it on a new family under two target settings with matched freestream ranges: the same Spalart-Allmaras (SA) modeling and SA with added e^N transition modeling.
AI.result: At N=1000, the pretrained model matches from-scratch accuracy using 3.25x fewer samples for the same-SA target but 2.58x for the transition-modeled target. By N=5000, the ordering reverses (1.56x vs. 1.86x). At N=1000, sampling more distinct airfoils lowers error on both targets, but only for the same-SA target is the gain larger than draw-to-draw variation (3.3x to 4.0x).
AI.conclusion: The value of pretraining depends jointly on target-data budget, target-data coverage, and whether source and target differ in modeled physics, with the relative benefit of same-SA vs. transition-modeled targets reversing between small and larger data budgets.

title: Pressure-dependent melting and crystallization of B2-NiAl from neural-network molecular dynamics
summary: We investigate pressure-dependent melting of ordered B2-NiAl using neural-network molecular dynamics with a Deep Potential interatomic model. Melting temperatures are determined from two-phase solid-liquid coexistence simulations over a broad pressure range, yielding the melting curve $T_m(P)$. Relative to available experimental and previous molecular-dynamics results, the present calculations predict a stronger increase of the melting temperature with pressure at elevated compression. To assess the thermodynamic consistency of the calculated melting line, we evaluate the enthalpy and volume changes upon melting and compare the Clapeyron slope with the derivative of the fitted $T_m(P)$ curve. The two estimates are in good agreement over most of the investigated pressure range, supporting the internal consistency of the coexistence results. To probe the character of melting, we perform a layer-resolved composition analysis of the coexistence configurations and find that the coexisting liquid remains essentially equiatomic at all studied pressures, with deviations of the aluminum fraction from the stoichiometric value not exceeding $5\times10^{-3}$. This provides direct atomistic evidence that melting of B2-NiAl remains congruent within the present model. Together, these results establish a thermodynamically consistent pressure-dependent melting description of B2-NiAl and clarify the character of its melting under compression.

AI.tldr: Using a Deep Potential neural-network molecular-dynamics model, the authors map the B2-NiAl melting curve over a broad pressure range, verify its thermodynamic consistency via Clapeyron analysis, and show that melting remains congruent (equiatomic liquid, Al-fraction deviation < 5×10⁻³).
AI.motivation: The pressure dependence and the character (congruent vs. incongruent) of melting in ordered B2-NiAl are not well established, and existing experimental and molecular-dynamics results for the melting curve show discrepancies, particularly at elevated compression.
AI.method: Neural-network molecular dynamics with a Deep Potential interatomic model. Melting temperatures are obtained from two-phase solid-liquid coexistence simulations across a broad pressure range to construct Tm(P). Thermodynamic consistency is checked by comparing enthalpy and volume changes upon melting (Clapeyron slope) with the derivative of the fitted Tm(P). Melting character is probed by layer-resolved composition analysis of the coexistence configurations.
AI.result: The calculated melting curve predicts a stronger increase of Tm with pressure at high compression than prior experimental and molecular-dynamics results. The Clapeyron slope from enthalpy/volume changes agrees well with the derivative of the fitted Tm(P) over most of the pressure range. The coexisting liquid remains essentially equiatomic at all studied pressures, with Al-fraction deviations from stoichiometry not exceeding 5×10⁻³.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a thermodynamically consistent, pressure-dependent melting description of B2-NiAl and gives direct atomistic evidence that its melting remains congruent under compression within the present model.

title: Observation of Dyakonov-Perel-type magnon spin relaxation in uniaxial antiferromagnetic insulators
summary: Long-distance transport of magnon spin currents in antiferromagnetic (AFM) insulators has attracted tremendous attention recently, however, the AFM magnon spin relaxation mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we report that the Dyakonov-Perel-type magnon spin relaxation mechanism governs the spin current transport along the easy axis in two prototypical uniaxial AFM insulators, Cr2O3 and alpha-Fe2O3. First, an over 450% enhancement of the first-harmonic nonlocal signal induced by a magnetic field is observed prior to the spin-flop transition, which can be well-interpreted by our model incorporating Dyakonov-Perel-type magnon spin relaxation. Secondly, we find that the magnon spin diffusion length in both crystals increases with magnetic field and saturates at fields above 0.8 T, consistent with our model. Finally, the temperature dependence of the zero-field magnon spin diffusion length in both AFM insulators can be qualitatively explained through our model. These findings are valuable for the development of low-dissipation antiferromagnetic spintronic devices.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that Dyakonov-Perel-type magnon spin relaxation governs spin current transport along the easy axis in uniaxial antiferromagnetic insulators Cr2O3 and alpha-Fe2O3, explaining field- and temperature-dependent magnon spin diffusion.
AI.motivation: Long-distance magnon spin current transport in antiferromagnetic insulators has drawn strong interest, yet the underlying magnon spin relaxation mechanisms remain elusive.
AI.method: The authors measured nonlocal magnon spin transport in two prototypical uniaxial AFM insulators, Cr2O3 and alpha-Fe2O3, and modeled the data with a Dyakonov-Perel-type magnon spin relaxation mechanism.
AI.result: A over 450% enhancement of the first-harmonic nonlocal signal induced by magnetic field was observed prior to the spin-flop transition, matching the model. The magnon spin diffusion length in both crystals increased with magnetic field and saturated above 0.8 T. The temperature dependence of the zero-field magnon spin diffusion length was also qualitatively explained.
AI.conclusion: Dyakonov-Perel-type magnon spin relaxation governs spin current transport along the easy axis in uniaxial AFM insulators, offering insights for low-dissipation antiferromagnetic spintronic devices.

title: Tunable flat band on the surface of a rhombohedral kagome ferromagnet
summary: A central goal in the exploration of kagome-based materials is the realization of a flat band that has meV bandwidth and lies close to the Fermi energy. The prevailing assumption is that band flattening originates from destructive hopping processes on the kagome lattice. We perform scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) on the layered kagome ferromagnet Fe$_3$Sn$_2$ and show that it indeed hosts a flat band near the Fermi energy, which is manifested as a sharp peak in the differential tunneling conductance. First-principles slab calculations reveal, however, that this band is flattened not by the destructive interference of intralayer hopping, but by interlayer hopping between rhombohedral-stacked kagome planes in Fe$_3$Sn$_2$, and is confined to the surface layer. This surface band, forming in the vicinity of the Brillouin zone corners $\bar{K}$ and $\bar{K'}$, exhibits rich magnetic-field dependence, including fine structure due to valley-symmetry breaking by rotated Fe moments, as well as a persistent diamagnetic shift associated with orbital magnetic moments, all reproduced by our calculations. Our results, highlighting the crucial role of layer stacking on the band structure of kagome magnets, demonstrate experimentally an alternative mechanism of generating magnetically tunable flat bands in atomically thin volumes of topological magnets.

AI.tldr: STM on the kagome ferromagnet Fe3Sn2 reveals a flat band near the Fermi energy, but first-principles slab calculations show it arises from interlayer hopping between rhombohedral-stacked kagome planes rather than intralayer destructive interference, forming a surface-confined, magnetically tunable band near the Brillouin zone corners.
AI.motivation: A central goal in kagome materials research is realizing a flat band with meV bandwidth near the Fermi energy. The prevailing assumption attributes band flattening to destructive hopping (interference) on the kagome lattice itself, motivating a direct experimental and theoretical test of the true origin of flat bands in a layered kagome magnet.
AI.method: Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and differential tunneling conductance spectroscopy on the layered kagome ferromagnet Fe3Sn2, combined with first-principles slab calculations, to identify the band origin, its layer confinement, and its magnetic-field dependence (valley-symmetry breaking, diamagnetic shift).
AI.result: STM shows a sharp peak in the differential conductance, confirming a flat band near the Fermi energy. Slab calculations reveal the band is flattened by interlayer hopping between rhombohedral-stacked kagome planes, not by intralayer destructive interference, and is confined to the surface layer. It forms near the Brillouin zone corners K-bar and K'-bar and exhibits rich magnetic-field dependence: fine structure from valley-symmetry breaking by rotated Fe moments and a persistent diamagnetic shift from orbital magnetic moments, both reproduced by calculations.
AI.conclusion: Layer stacking plays a crucial role in the band structure of kagome magnets. The work experimentally demonstrates an alternative mechanism for generating magnetically tunable flat bands in atomically thin volumes of topological magnets, revising the prevailing view that flat bands in kagome systems stem from intralayer destructive hopping.

title: Crystallographic imperfections and exotic superconductivity of UBe$_{13}$
comment: Accepted for publication in Physical Review B
summary: The symmetry of the superconducting gap is related to the symmetry of the crystal structure. In unconventional superconductors, big changes of the critical temperature, critical field or even the gap structure can happen even for small perturbations of the lattice. In this letter, we use microstructuring to study aluminium-free crystals of UBe$_{13}$ which are expected to be closer to "perfect" material than previously studied aluminium-grown single crystals. We compare the effect of minuscule imperfections on the value of the critical temperature and critical field, which, in the case of UBe$_{13}$, has drastic effects, supporting its unconventional nature. We conjecture that this likely arises from the oxidation state of uranium, which is sensitive to its crystal environment. Our findings suggests that uranium-based materials provide not only an excellent reservoir of new unconventional phenomena, but also a way to identify the gap symmetry of unconventional superconductors.

AI.motivation: In unconventional superconductors the gap symmetry is tied to crystal symmetry, so tiny lattice perturbations can dramatically alter T_c, H_c, or the gap structure. Prior UBe₁₃ studies relied on aluminium-grown single crystals; removing aluminium contamination and probing near-"perfect" crystals is needed to test how intrinsic this fragility is and to clarify the link between lattice environment and superconducting properties.
AI.method: The authors apply microstructuring to aluminium-free UBe₁₃ crystals, which are expected to be closer to ideal than previously studied aluminium-grown single crystals. They then compare how minuscule imperfections affect the critical temperature and the critical field.
AI.result: Even small imperfections produce drastic changes in the critical temperature and critical field of UBe₁₃, confirming strong sensitivity to lattice perturbations and supporting the material's unconventional nature. The effect is conjectured to originate from the oxidation state of uranium, which is sensitive to its crystal environment.
AI.conclusion: Uranium-based materials are not only a rich reservoir of new unconventional phenomena but also offer a route to identify the gap symmetry of unconventional superconductors. The crystal-environment sensitivity of uranium's oxidation state provides a mechanism for tuning and probing this symmetry.

title: Universal 1/f Noise in the Power Spectra of Energy Time-series in Solvated DNA Dynamics
summary: We investigate energy fluctuations of solvated DNA in three conformations: G-quadruplex, Hairpin, and Duplex. Our comprehensive molecular dynamics (MD) simulations demonstrate that the time-series of interaction energies for DNA self, DNA-water and DNA-ion show 1/f noise with a universal decay exponent $β\simeq 0.90$. We show that DNA topology and structural rigidity modulate its dynamic coupling with the surrounding hydration shell and mobile counter-ions. This coupling critically shapes the 1/f noise profile: DNA self energies in flexible structures (G-quadruplex, Hairpin) display pronounced low-frequency modes absent in the rigid Duplex. These findings reveal how the interplay between DNA topology and environmental coupling governs different stochastic behavior in biologically relevant forms of DNA.

AI.tldr: MD simulations show DNA interaction-energy time series (self, water, ion) exhibit universal 1/f noise with decay exponent β≈0.90, where DNA topology and rigidity modulate coupling to the hydration shell and counter-ions, introducing low-frequency modes in flexible conformations.
AI.motivation: To understand how DNA topology and structural rigidity influence its dynamic coupling with the surrounding hydration shell and mobile counter-ions, and how this coupling governs stochastic energy fluctuations in biologically relevant DNA forms.
AI.method: Comprehensive molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of solvated DNA in three conformations: G-quadruplex, Hairpin, and Duplex. Analysis of time series of interaction energies for DNA self, DNA-water, and DNA-ion, characterizing their spectral noise (1/f) behavior and decay exponents.
AI.result: All three interaction-energy time series exhibit 1/f noise with a universal decay exponent β≈0.90. DNA topology and structural rigidity modulate the dynamic coupling with the hydration shell and counter-ions. Flexible structures (G-quadruplex, Hairpin) display pronounced low-frequency modes in DNA self energies, which are absent in the rigid Duplex.
AI.conclusion: The interplay between DNA topology and environmental coupling governs distinct stochastic behavior in biologically relevant DNA conformations, with flexibility playing a key role in shaping the 1/f noise profile.

title: Collective Ion Dynamics from Finite-Volume Fluctuations in Model Explicit-Solvent Electrolytes
summary: Understanding how collective ion transport emerges from equilibrium fluctuations is central to electrolyte statistical mechanics. Finite-volume fluctuations provide an accessible route to this information, but their interpretation is complicated because they mix wave numbers and collective fields. Here, we extend the finite-volume counting framework for inferring collective ion diffusion by combining the exact window projection with an inertial independent-particle reference, and apply it to a symmetric 1:1 solvent primitive model. The growth of ion-number fluctuations between the ballistic and plateau regimes appears nearly ideal, but this apparent ideality results from compensation between negative structural and positive dynamical excess contributions. The coupled ion-number--solvent relaxation further reveals a signed redistribution between solvent-associated and solvent-orthogonal projections that is largely hidden in the total response. The inferred collective diffusion depends on observation length and dynamical closure: measured structure alone does not systematically improve the estimate, whereas the coupled-field description reduces the high-concentration discrepancy. These results provide a basis for analyzing more realistic electrolytes with mutually coupled ion-number, charge, and solvent fluctuations.

AI.tldr: This work extends a finite-volume counting framework to infer collective ion diffusion in a symmetric 1:1 solvent primitive model by combining exact window projection with an inertial independent-particle reference, revealing that apparent ideal fluctuation growth masks compensating excess contributions and that coupled-field descriptions improve estimates at high concentration.
AI.motivation: Understanding how collective ion transport emerges from equilibrium fluctuations is central to electrolyte statistical mechanics. Finite-volume fluctuations offer an accessible probe, but their interpretation is difficult because they convolve wave numbers and collective fields, obscuring the physical origin of the observed behavior.

They decompose ion-number fluctuation growth across ballistic and plateau regimes and analyze the coupled ion-number--solvent relaxation into solvent-associated and solvent-orthogonal projections.

The coupled ion-number--solvent relaxation reveals a signed redistribution between solvent-associated and solvent-orthogonal projections that is largely hidden in the total response.
