title: The Origin of the Observed Raman Peaks in α-MnTe
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, plus Supporting Information (8 figures, 1 table)
summary: The Raman spectrum of the room-temperature altermagnet $α$-MnTe is reported to contain unassigned peaks at 120(3) cm$^{-1}$ and 140(3) cm$^{-1}$, absent from the predicted phonon spectrum of the material. This has generated considerable debate within the altermagnet community and necessitates urgent resolution. This work establishes that these peaks, together with the 90(5) cm$^{-1}$ peak that matches a theoretically predicted mode, are all extrinsic, originating from elemental tellurium formed during air exposure of the surface. Raman spectra of MBE-grown thin films show that these peaks closely match those of elemental tellurium, emerge soon after air exposure, and are absent in AlO$_x$-capped films. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy shows that air exposure breaks Mn--Te bonds and oxidizes Mn within a minute. Cross-sectional scanning transmission electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy reveals that the oxidation leads to Mn out-diffusion, forming a few-nanometer-thick oxide layer above a buried, Te-enriched region, likely responsible for the anomalous Raman peaks. Additionally, no sample exhibited the 175 cm$^{-1}$ Raman peak which is commonly attributed to MnTe$_2$. The aggressive surface oxidation and associated elemental Te formation in MnTe have important implications for any surface-sensitive and optical characterization of MnTe (and other similar Te-containing materials) involving even the briefest air exposure.

AI.tldr: The Raman peaks at 120, 140, and 90 cm⁻¹ in α-MnTe are extrinsic, arising from elemental tellurium formed during air oxidation, not intrinsic to the altermagnet.
AI.motivation: Unassigned Raman peaks at 120(3) and 140(3) cm⁻¹ in room-temperature altermagnet α-MnTe, absent from predicted phonon spectra, have sparked debate in the altermagnet community and require urgent resolution to correctly interpret its vibrational properties.
AI.method: MBE-grown α-MnTe thin films were studied with Raman spectroscopy comparing air-exposed versus AlOₓ-capped films; X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy probed chemical bonding/oxidation; cross-sectional STEM with EDS mapped the oxidation-induced structural and compositional changes.
AI.result: The 120, 140, and 90 cm⁻¹ peaks closely match elemental tellurium, emerge soon after air exposure, and are absent in AlOₓ-capped films. XPS shows air exposure breaks Mn–Te bonds and oxidizes Mn within a minute. STEM-EDS reveals Mn out-diffusion forming a few-nanometer oxide layer above a buried Te-enriched region likely responsible for the anomalous Raman peaks. No sample exhibited the 175 cm⁻¹ peak commonly attributed to MnTe₂.
AI.conclusion: The disputed Raman peaks in α-MnTe are extrinsic, originating from elemental Te formed by aggressive surface oxidation during air exposure, with important implications for any surface-sensitive or optical characterization of MnTe and similar Te-containing materials.

title: Highly uniform first-electron position in qubit arrays fabricated on dedicated QSOI(R) 300mm commercial platform
summary: We report progress toward the development of a quantum silicon-on-insulator (QSOI(R)) technology compatible with 300mm CMOS fabrication and adapted from the 28nm Fully-Depleted SOI (28nm FD-SOI) platform for scalable quantum computing. We compare quantum devices fabricated with standard 28nm FD-SOI and QSOI(R) technologies, and show striking improvements of room temperature electrostatic properties of the individual device. Moreover, the QSOI(R) technology has significantly reduced the device variability and the dispersion of device properties at the wafer level. Transistor metrics are reproduced by TCAD simulations showing that the electrostatics of the devices behave as expected for QSOI(R) technology. Wafer-scale measurements at sub-2K show reproducible quantum dots down to the few-electron regime with 69\% yield for successful charge detection of the first electron and a dispersion of the first electron position of $\mathrm{\pm 35 mV}$ over 377 quantum dots. These results establish QSOI(R) as a promising platform for CMOS-compatible quantum device co-integration.

AI.tldr: QSOI(R), a 300mm CMOS-compatible quantum SOI technology adapted from 28nm FD-SOI, achieves significantly improved room-temperature electrostatics, reduced wafer-level variability, and reproducible few-electron quantum dots with 69% first-electron charge-detection yield.
AI.motivation: Scalable quantum computing requires a quantum device platform that is compatible with mature, high-volume CMOS fabrication and can be co-integrated with classical control electronics. Existing standard 28nm FD-SOI technology suffers from inferior electrostatic properties and large device-to-device and wafer-level variability, which limits reproducibility of quantum dots.

They compared quantum devices fabricated with standard 28nm FD-SOI and QSOI(R), characterized room-temperature electrostatic properties and wafer-level dispersion, reproduced transistor metrics using TCAD simulations, and performed wafer-scale measurements at sub-2K to assess quantum dot reproducibility.
AI.result: QSOI(R) shows striking improvements in room-temperature electrostatics of individual devices, significantly reduced device variability and dispersion of device properties at wafer level. TCAD simulations confirm the expected electrostatics. Sub-2K wafer-scale measurements yield reproducible quantum dots down to the few-electron regime, with 69% yield for successful first-electron charge detection and a first-electron position dispersion of ±35 mV across 377 quantum dots.
AI.conclusion: QSOI(R) is established as a promising platform for CMOS-compatible quantum device co-integration, offering improved electrostatics and reduced variability suitable for scalable quantum computing.

title: Corner entanglement scaling with projected entangled pair states
summary: Entanglement scaling provides a powerful probe of universal properties at quantum critical points. In two dimensions, contributions originating from a corner-shaped bipartition exhibit a universal scaling, which is determined by the underlying conformal field theory. We develop a method to extract this corner entanglement entropy from projected entangled pair states directly in the thermodynamic limit. When applied to models at a quantum critical point, we show that the corner contribution exhibits scaling with the effective correlation length, in agreement with the hypothesis of finite-entanglement scaling. Our results for the corner coefficients are consistent with other methods, demonstrating the efficiency of our method for diagnosing strongly-correlated quantum critical points in two dimensions.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a method to extract corner entanglement entropy from projected entangled pair states (PEPS) directly in the thermodynamic limit, showing that the corner contribution scales with the effective correlation length in agreement with finite-entanglement scaling.
AI.motivation: Entanglement scaling is a powerful probe of universal properties at quantum critical points. In two dimensions, corner-shaped bipartitions yield universal contributions governed by the underlying conformal field theory, but extracting these corner contributions efficiently in the thermodynamic limit remains a challenge.
AI.method: The authors develop a method to extract corner entanglement entropy from projected entangled pair states (PEPS) directly in the thermodynamic limit.
AI.result: Applied to models at a quantum critical point, the corner contribution exhibits scaling with the effective correlation length, consistent with the finite-entanglement scaling hypothesis. The corner coefficients agree with results from other methods.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the efficiency of this PEPS-based method for diagnosing strongly-correlated quantum critical points in two dimensions.

title: Superconductivity at the metal-insulator phase boundary in a bulk nickelate at ambient pressure
summary: The discovery of superconductivity in nickelates has seeded a new field for exploring unconventional superconductivity in transition metal oxides. However, to date superconductivity has only been realized in thin films or under extreme pressure in the bulk. Here we report signatures of superconductivity at ambient pressure in bulk nickelate single crystals of (La1-xPrx)4Ni3O8 and (La1-xYx)4Ni3O8, whose crystal structure comprises interleaving trilayers of square-planar nickel oxide and fluorite-like spacer layers. The parent compound La4Ni3O8 exhibits an insulating ground state, where electrons order into intertwined, insulating charge/spin stripes. Substitution of smaller lanthanide ions disrupts this order, eventually leading to a metallic ground-state. We find that superconductivity emerges in a narrow window proximate to the insulator-metal phase boundary, where both metallic and charge-stripe phases co-exist. The observed low volume-fraction superconductivity is non-percolative, suggesting the prospect of filamentary superconductivity nucleated at the boundary between these phases. However, intergrowth defects that approximate the known infinite layer nickelates are observed in TEM, leaving open the possibility that superconductivity resides here rather than in the trilayer matrix. Remarkably, the electronic phase diagrams of both the Y and Pr series coincide when parameterized by the volume of the fluorite like spacer layers, revealing that this steric parameter profoundly modifies the nickel oxide trilayer electronic structure. Our results identify better understanding of the co-existence region between metallic and charge-ordered phases as a priority for expanding the range of bulk, ambient-pressure nickelate superconductivity and establish spacer-layer engineering as a design tool for exploring this regime of phase competition.

AI.tldr: Signatures of ambient-pressure superconductivity are reported in bulk nickelate single crystals (La1-xPrx)4Ni3O8 and (La1-xYx)4Ni3O8, emerging in a narrow, non-percolative window near the insulator-metal boundary, with fluorite spacer-layer volume acting as a unifying control parameter.
AI.motivation: Superconductivity in nickelates had only been realized in thin films or under extreme pressure in the bulk, so extending it to ambient-pressure bulk crystals and understanding the electronic phase competition is a key open challenge.
AI.method: Bulk single crystals of (La1-xPrx)4Ni3O8 and (La1-xYx)4Ni3O8 were synthesized; the parent La4Ni3O8 is insulating with intertwined charge/spin stripes, and smaller lanthanide substitution was used to tune the ground state through an insulator-metal transition. Transport measurements identified superconductivity, and TEM was used to examine intergrowth defects.
AI.result: Superconductivity emerges in a narrow window proximate to the insulator-metal phase boundary where metallic and charge-stripe phases coexist. The observed superconductivity has a low volume fraction and is non-percolative, suggesting filamentary superconductivity nucleated at phase boundaries. TEM reveals intergrowth defects approximating infinite-layer nickelates, leaving open whether superconductivity resides there instead of the trilayer matrix. AI.conclusion: Understanding the coexistence region between metallic and charge-ordered phases is a priority for expanding bulk, ambient-pressure nickelate superconductivity, and spacer-layer engineering is established as a design tool for exploring this regime of phase competition. However, the exact location of the superconducting phase (phase boundary vs. intergrowth defects) remains unresolved.

title: Khinchin's ergodicity and typicality in statistical mechanics
summary: The formulation of statistical mechanics in terms of ensembles, originally proposed by Gibbs, has proved to be extremely effective in describing the equilibrium state of many-particle systems, in the most diverse contexts (critical phenomena, quantum mechanics, biophysics, just to mention a few). The reasons of this success are still debated, and the connection between dynamics and probability in large systems remains somehow elusive. Indeed, in order to derive the main results of equilibrium statistical mechanics, strong assumptions on the ergodicity of the dynamics are usually required. Nonetheless, empirical observations seem to suggest that the predictions of the theory hold true even when such assumptions are not verified. In this paper we reconsider the point of view put forward by Khinchin, stating that the only relevant ingredients for the validity of statistical mechanics are the large number of degrees of freedom in the system and the choice of extensive observables, irrespectively of the details of the microscopic dynamics. In particular, the presence of dynamical chaos is not required. To this aim, we discuss some analytical and numerical results on a couple of classical integrable systems, the harmonic chain and the Toda model, showing that many important features predicted by equilibrium statistical mechanics, as for instance Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, are found even in absence of chaos.

AI.tldr: The paper revisits Khinchin's viewpoint that statistical mechanics is valid due to large system size and extensive observables rather than ergodicity or chaos, using analytical and numerical studies of the integrable harmonic chain and Toda model to show that equilibrium predictions like the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution emerge even without chaos.
AI.motivation: The success of Gibbsian ensemble statistical mechanics is widely recognized, but its foundations remain debated since deriving its main results typically requires strong ergodicity assumptions on the dynamics. Empirical evidence suggests the theory works even when ergodicity fails, motivating a reassessment of what conditions are truly necessary for statistical mechanics to hold.
AI.method: The authors adopt Khinchin's perspective, arguing that the key ingredients are the large number of degrees of freedom and the choice of extensive observables, independent of microscopic dynamical details or dynamical chaos. They support this with analytical and numerical investigations of two classical integrable systems: the harmonic chain and the Toda model.
AI.result: Analytical and numerical results on the harmonic chain and Toda model show that many central predictions of equilibrium statistical mechanics, such as the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, are recovered even in the complete absence of chaos.
AI.conclusion: The validity of equilibrium statistical mechanics does not require ergodicity or dynamical chaos; instead, it relies on the large number of degrees of freedom and extensive observables, supporting Khinchin's viewpoint.

title: Truncated automatic sparse differentiation for machine learning interatomic potentials
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables (7 pages main text). Additional information at https://marcel.science/tasd4mlip
summary: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) learn the mapping from atomic positions to potential energy. The forces, the negative gradient of this energy, drive molecular dynamics and are readily obtained using automatic differentiation. Higher-order derivatives, most notably the Hessian, describe collective motion and allow the direct prediction of experimental observables, but are considered computationally inaccessible for large systems. We suggest a solution: in physical systems, interactions decay with distance, and most MLIPs build on this locality through message passing up to a finite receptive field. This implies both sparsity of higher-order derivatives and their decay with distance. This structure can be exploited using automatic sparse differentiation (ASD). We explain how to compute the sparsity pattern for MLIP derivatives and demonstrate that, for multiple foundation MLIPs, ASD computes full Hessians of large porous materials exactly, but with modest speedups at best. The larger gains come from truncated ASD: discarding small, but nonzero, Hessian entries between distant atoms yields order-of-magnitude speedups with negligible impact on predicted observables.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes exploiting locality in machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) to compute higher-order derivatives, especially Hessians, via automatic sparse differentiation (ASD). While exact ASD gives only modest speedups, truncating small distant-atom Hessian entries yields order-of-magnitude speedups with negligible impact on predicted observables.
AI.motivation: MLIPs readily provide forces (the negative energy gradient) through automatic differentiation, but higher-order derivatives such as the Hessian—essential for describing collective motion and directly predicting experimental observables—are considered computationally inaccessible for large systems. A method is needed to make Hessian computation tractable at scale.
AI.method: The authors leverage the physical fact that interactions decay with distance and that most MLIPs enforce locality through message passing within a finite receptive field. This implies sparsity and distance decay of higher-order derivatives. They exploit this structure with automatic sparse differentiation (ASD), explain how to compute the sparsity pattern for MLIP derivatives, and additionally introduce truncated ASD that discards small but nonzero Hessian entries between distant atoms.
AI.result: For multiple foundation MLIPs, ASD computes full Hessians of large porous materials exactly, but achieves only modest speedups. Truncated ASD delivers order-of-magnitude speedups with negligible impact on predicted observables.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the locality-induced sparsity and distance decay of MLIP higher-order derivatives makes Hessian computation feasible; truncating negligible long-range Hessian entries provides large practical speedups while preserving accuracy of predicted observables.

title: ALIGNN 2.0: A Unified Line-Graph Neural Network Framework for Materials Screening, Force Fields, Inverse Design, Spectroscopy, and Microscopy
summary: Graph neural networks are central to materials property prediction and machine-learning interatomic potentials, yet their reliance on specialized graph libraries hampers portability and reproducibility, and property and force-field models have historically required separate graph pipelines. We present ALIGNN 2.0, a dependency-free, pure-PyTorch reimplementation of the Atomistic Line Graph Neural Network, with the line graph and its batching built from scratch, running on current-generation accelerators and unifying scalar, spectral, tensorial, per-atom, and force-field prediction behind a single graph, a combination that to our knowledge no existing framework provides. Comparing radius and k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) graphs, the wider kNN graph is more accurate for properties while the smoothly varying radius graph is required for energy-conserving molecular dynamics. On the JARVIS-Leaderboard, ALIGNN 2.0 leads on 26 of 30 single-property benchmarks against the original ALIGNN, with large gains for piezoelectric and dielectric maxima, exfoliation energy, moduli, and superconducting Tc. The LAMMPS- and OpenMM-compatible ALIGNN-FF matches leading universal potentials on the Matbench-Discovery and CHIPS-FF benchmarks at a small fraction of their parameters while scaling to hundred-thousand-atom cells. We further use ALIGNN 2.0 as the denoiser in a conditional crystal-diffusion model, where explicit line-graph message passing consistently lowers structural denoising loss. We also show, as work in progress, that an independently diffused, redundant bond-angle state is learnable but does not uniformly improve reconstruction or combine additively with the line graph. Finally, from a single relaxed structure the same framework reconstructs infrared, Raman, optical-dielectric, and neutron spectra in agreement with experiment and DFT, and drives frozen-phonon electron-microscopy image simulation.

There is a need for a unified, portable framework that handles all these tasks within one graph representation.
AI.method: ALIGNN 2.0 is a dependency-free, pure-PyTorch reimplementation of ALIGNN with the line graph and its batching built from scratch. It runs on current-generation accelerators and unifies scalar, spectral, tensorial, per-atom, and force-field prediction behind a single graph. The authors compare radius and k-nearest-neighbor graphs, and use ALIGNN 2.0 as a denoiser in a conditional crystal-diffusion model. They also explore an independently diffused, redundant bond-angle state.

On the JARVIS-Leaderboard, ALIGNN 2.0 leads on 26 of 30 single-property benchmarks over the original ALIGNN, with large gains for piezoelectric and dielectric maxima, exfoliation energy, moduli, and superconducting Tc. The LAMMPS- and OpenMM-compatible ALIGNN-FF matches leading universal potentials on Matbench-Discovery and CHIPS-FF at a small fraction of their parameters while scaling to hundred-thousand-atom cells. Explicit line-graph message passing consistently lowers structural denoising loss. title: Plasmons in twisted bilayer graphene across dispersive and flat bands
summary: The dynamical dielectric response of twisted bilayer graphene is explored in large-angle dispersive-band and small-angle quasi-flat-band regimes using time-dependent density-functional theory within the random-phase approximation. At the reference bilayer-graphene interlayer distance, weak coupling in the largest-angle structures preserves Dirac dispersions and the intrinsic $π$ plasmon. Electron doping activates a two-dimensional Dirac plasmon with energies obeying approximate geometric twist-angle scaling, while acoustic-like branches remain embedded in the single-particle continuum. The prohibitively large first-magic-angle supercell is represented by a tractable cell with its interlayer separation reduced to the angle-dependent magic distance, where four quasi-flat bands emerge around the Fermi level. Their partial occupation produces a dispersive low-energy plasmon-like excitation without a clear dielectric zero at resonance. A distinct interband plasmon is instead identified, supported by transitions involving the quasi-flat manifold and neighboring high-density-of-states regions. Band-energy rescaling places its characteristic energy in the mid-infrared range of interband collective excitations measured near the magic angle.

AI.tldr: The dielectric response of twisted bilayer graphene is studied via TDDFT-RPA in both large-angle dispersive and small-angle quasi-flat-band regimes, revealing Dirac plasmons with twist-angle scaling at large angles and a distinct interband plasmon in the quasi-flat-band regime.
AI.motivation: Twisted bilayer graphene hosts distinct electronic phases depending on twist angle, but its dynamical dielectric response across large-angle dispersive and small-angle quasi-flat-band regimes remains insufficiently understood, particularly near the magic angle.
AI.method: Time-dependent density-functional theory within the random-phase approximation is used. Large-angle structures are treated with dispersive Dirac bands at the reference interlayer distance, while the intractable first-magic-angle supercell is modeled by a tractable cell with interlayer separation reduced to the angle-dependent magic distance, yielding four quasi-flat bands near the Fermi level.
AI.result: At large angles, weak coupling preserves Dirac dispersions and the intrinsic π plasmon; electron doping activates a 2D Dirac plasmon with approximate geometric twist-angle energy scaling, while acoustic-like branches remain embedded in the single-particle continuum. In the quasi-flat-band regime, partial occupation produces a dispersive low-energy plasmon-like excitation without a clear dielectric zero at resonance, and a distinct interband plasmon arises from transitions involving the quasi-flat manifold and neighboring high-DOS regions.
AI.conclusion: Band-energy rescaling places the characteristic energy of the interband plasmon in the mid-infrared range of interband collective excitations measured near the magic angle, linking the model calculations to experimental observations.

title: When Is Kramers-Wannier Duality Invertible?
summary: {\it Kramers-Wannier} duality of the quantum Ising chain is naturally realized as a noninvertible transformation on a finite periodic chain. Upon incorporating appropriate symmetry-twisted sectors, however, the duality can be promoted to an invertible unitary transformation. In this Letter, we classify when the Kramers-Wannier duality admits an invertible realization on a finite Hilbert space. We show that this is determined by the representation of the Ising bond algebra and establish a necessary and sufficient condition in terms of its two central elements. This representation-theoretic criterion unifies the conventional noninvertible realization with invertible constructions involving symmetry-twisted sectors and applies equally to other models with the same underlying bond algebra. As an explicit example, we find an order-disorder duality in a non-trivial realization of the Ising bond algebra that admits an invertible Kramers-Wannier duality.

AI.tldr: The paper classifies when the Kramers-Wannier duality of the quantum Ising chain can be realized as an invertible unitary transformation on a finite Hilbert space, providing a representation-theoretic criterion based on the Ising bond algebra's two central elements.
AI.motivation: Kramers-Wannier duality on a finite periodic Ising chain is naturally noninvertible, but can become invertible upon including symmetry-twisted sectors. A unified understanding of when such an invertible realization is possible was lacking.
AI.method: The authors analyze the representation of the Ising bond algebra and derive a necessary and sufficient condition, expressed in terms of its two central elements, for the existence of an invertible realization of the Kramers-Wannier duality.
AI.result: The criterion unifies the conventional noninvertible realization with invertible constructions involving symmetry-twisted sectors, and extends to other models sharing the same bond algebra. An explicit example is found: an order-disorder duality in a nontrivial realization of the Ising bond algebra admitting an invertible Kramers-Wannier duality.
AI.conclusion: A representation-theoretic criterion on the Ising bond algebra's central elements determines when the Kramers-Wannier duality admits an invertible realization, generalizing beyond the standard Ising chain.

title: Vortex-mediated spin current injection into two-dimensional superconductor NbSe2
summary: Injection of pure spin current into superconductors remains a major challenge in superconducting spintronics. Previous studies have primarily focused on spin-polarized quasiparticles and spin-triplet supercurrents, while vortices, ubiquitous topological defects in type-2 superconductors, have been theoretically proposed as alternative carriers of spin angular momentum, yet direct experimental evidence is still lacking. Here, we report the vortex-mediated spin current injection in NbSe2/LiAl2Fe3O8(LAFO) bilayer, an Ising superconductor/ferrimagnetic insulator heterostructure. Under an out-of-plane temperature gradient and an in-plane magnetic field, the NbSe2/LAFO bilayer shows a pronounced thermoelectric peak near the upper critical magnetic field, which has the opposite sign to the conventional vortex Nernst signal observed in a single-layer NbSe2. The sign reversal suggests that the vortex flow induced by spin current injection is opposite to the flow driven by the temperature gradient, which is consistent with theoretical mechanisms including spin-vorticity transmutation and the inverse vortex spin Hall effect. By mapping the field temperature phase diagram, we reveal that the spin current injection occurs exclusively in the vortex liquid phase of NbSe2. Absence of the thermoelectric signal above the superconducting transition temperature further rules out the quasiparticle contribution. Our results establish vortices as efficient carriers of spin information in superconductors, opening a new route towards vortex-mediated superconducting spintronic devices.

AI.tldr: The paper reports experimental evidence of vortex-mediated spin current injection in a NbSe2/LAFO (Ising superconductor/ferrimagnetic insulator) bilayer, evidenced by a sign-reversed thermoelectric peak near the upper critical field that persists only in the vortex liquid phase.
AI.motivation: Injecting pure spin current into superconductors is a central challenge in superconducting spintronics. Prior work focused on spin-polarized quasiparticles and spin-triplet supercurrents, while vortices—ubiquitous topological defects in type-2 superconductors—were only theoretically proposed as spin angular momentum carriers, lacking direct experimental evidence.
AI.method: The authors fabricated a NbSe2/LAFO heterostructure (Ising superconductor/ferrimagnetic insulator bilayer) and measured its thermoelectric response under an out-of-plane temperature gradient and an in-plane magnetic field, mapping the field–temperature phase diagram and comparing against single-layer NbSe2.
AI.result: The bilayer exhibits a pronounced thermoelectric peak near the upper critical magnetic field with a sign opposite to the conventional vortex Nernst signal in single-layer NbSe2. The sign reversal indicates vortex flow induced by spin current injection opposing the temperature-gradient-driven flow, consistent with spin-vorticity transmutation and the inverse vortex spin Hall effect. The signal occurs exclusively in the vortex liquid phase, and its absence above Tc rules out quasiparticle contributions.
AI.conclusion: Vortices act as efficient carriers of spin information in superconductors, establishing a new route toward vortex-mediated superconducting spintronic devices.

title: Formal Fluctuation-Response Relations for Non-Stationary Systems: The Dynamic Conjugate Variable
summary: Fluctuation-response relations (FRRs) connect the linear response of a system to an external perturbation with properties of spontaneous fluctuations in the unperturbed system. We provide a simple derivation of FRRs for non-stationary dynamics following an almost standard way based on introducing a variable conjugated to perturbation (a dynamic conjugate). The derivation relies solely on the Markovianity of the underlying dynamics, with the only additional assumption that the transition PDF of the process is differentiable with respect to the strength of a constant, time- independent perturbation. The structure of this conjugate variable is however unusual: it is a two-time one, and reduces to a usual single-time conjugate in stationary situations. We show how several known results follow from this approach.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a simple derivation of fluctuation-response relations (FRRs) for non-stationary dynamics, relying only on Markovianity and differentiability of the transition PDF, using a novel two-time conjugate variable that reduces to the standard single-time conjugate in the stationary case.
AI.motivation: FRRs link the linear response of a system to an external perturbation with the properties of spontaneous fluctuations in the unperturbed system. Extending these relations to non-stationary dynamics is important, and the authors seek a derivation that is simple and grounded in minimal assumptions.
AI.method: The derivation follows an almost standard route based on introducing a variable conjugated to the perturbation (a dynamic conjugate). It relies solely on the Markovianity of the underlying dynamics, with the only additional assumption that the transition PDF of the process is differentiable with respect to the strength of a constant, time-independent perturbation. The conjugate variable introduced is a two-time one, which reduces to a usual single-time conjugate in stationary situations.
AI.result: The approach yields FRRs for non-stationary dynamics and is shown to reproduce several known results as special cases.
AI.conclusion: FRRs for non-stationary dynamics can be derived simply from Markovianity and differentiability of the transition PDF, using a two-time conjugate variable that generalizes the standard single-time conjugate. This unified framework recovers several known results.

title: Anharmonic Phonon Renormalization and Defect Tolerance of the Thermoelectric Power Factor in Monolayer SnSe
summary: Monolayer tin selenide (SnSe) exhibits phase-dependent anharmonic lattice dynamics, yet their consequences for the thermoelectric power factor (PF) and point-defect tolerance remain unresolved. We combine density functional theory, the stochastic self-consistent harmonic approximation (SSCHA), and Boltzmann transport calculations including electron-phonon and electron-defect scattering to investigate monolayer $α$-SnSe (Pnma) and $β$-SnSe (Cmcm). In dynamically stable $α$-SnSe, SSCHA renormalizes the finite-temperature phonons without changing the qualitative n-type transport picture. In $β$-SnSe, SSCHA removes the harmonic soft-mode instability of the Cmcm phase at 800-1000 K, and thereby enables high-temperature transport calculations; LO/TO-2 is the principal electron-scattering channel. In the lower-density window near $10^{12}$ cm$^{-2}$, the n-type PF reaches 15-19 $μ\mathrm{W}/(\mathrm{K}^{2}\cdot\mathrm{cm})$ at 800-900 K and exceeds the p-type PF primarily because of the higher electrical conductivity. Se vacancies ($V_{\mathrm{Se}}$) produce weaker electron-defect scattering than Sn vacancies ($V_{\mathrm{Sn}}$), and p-type transport is less defect tolerant than n-type transport in both phases. We define an operational critical defect concentration, $C_{\mathrm{crit}}$, at which the PF decreases by 15% relative to the corresponding defect-free value. The lowest $C_{\mathrm{crit}}$ is $8.841\times10^{-5}$ (approximately 88 ppm) for p-type $α$-SnSe with $V_{\mathrm{Sn}}$; for n-type $β$-SnSe with $V_{\mathrm{Se}}$, the 15% threshold is not reached up to $5\times10^{-3}$ (5000 ppm). These results distinguish finite-temperature phonon renormalization in stable $α$-SnSe from anharmonic stabilization in $β$-SnSe and provide defect-concentration limits for preserving the PF.

AI.tldr: This work uses DFT, SSCHA, and Boltzmann transport to show how phase-dependent anharmonic phonon renormalization governs the thermoelectric power factor and point-defect tolerance of monolayer α- and β-SnSe, establishing operational critical defect concentrations.
AI.motivation: Monolayer SnSe has phase-dependent anharmonic lattice dynamics, but the resulting effects on thermoelectric power factor (PF) and point-defect tolerance have not been resolved. The study aims to clarify how finite-temperature phonon renormalization versus anharmonic stabilization influence high-temperature transport and defect tolerance.
AI.method: The authors combine density functional theory (DFT), the stochastic self-consistent harmonic approximation (SSCHA), and Boltzmann transport calculations that include both electron-phonon and electron-defect scattering. They study monolayer α-SnSe (Pnma) and β-SnSe (Cmcm), introducing an operational critical defect concentration C_crit defined by a 15% PF reduction.
AI.result: In stable α-SnSe, SSCHA renormalizes finite-temperature phonons without qualitatively altering n-type transport. In β-SnSe, SSCHA removes the Cmcm harmonic soft-mode instability at 800–1000 K, enabling high-temperature transport calculations, with LO/TO-2 as the dominant electron-scattering channel. Near 10^12 cm^-2, n-type PF reaches 15–19 μW/(K^2·cm) at 800–900 K and exceeds p-type PF due to higher electrical conductivity. Se vacancies (V_Se) cause weaker electron-defect scattering than Sn vacancies (V_Sn), and p-type transport is less defect tolerant than n-type in both phases. The lowest C_crit is 8.841×10^-5 (~88 ppm) for p-type α-SnSe with V_Sn; for n-type β-SnSe with V_Se, the 15% threshold is not reached up to 5×10^-3 (5000 ppm).
AI.conclusion: The study distinguishes finite-temperature phonon renormalization in stable α-SnSe from anharmonic stabilization in β-SnSe and provides quantitative defect-concentration limits for preserving the thermoelectric PF in monolayer SnSe.

title: Molecular Geometry Understanding Has Unintendedly Emerged in Frontier Large Language Models
comment: 28 pages, 3 figures, 6 extended data figures. Supplementary Information included. Code and data available at https://github.com/TheorChemGroup/LLMConfBench
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have already shown strong capabilities in solving complex chemical problems expressed in natural language. Yet, many tasks performed by chemists require understanding of 3D structures of chemical compounds and reasoning about them -- abilities, which, to the best of our knowledge, were neither intended by LLM developers nor tested in contemporary models. Such understanding is essential for autonomous molecular discovery and drug development, which is one of the Holy Grails of AI application to chemistry. We tested this capability in modern LLMs on 810 geometries and DFT energies of 27 small organic molecules. Strikingly, while models released before July 2025 struggled to rank conformers by stability, many recent frontier models, including GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi K3, and Gemini 3.6 Flash achieved competitive accuracy, outperforming the Universal Force Field, and GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 came very close to a modern GFN-FF force field. Analysis of models' explanations for their rankings suggests that they perform best for molecules with well-defined intramolecular interactions -- hydrogen bonds -- which are well quantified in scientific language; at the same time all models except the two newest -- GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 -- struggle with molecules governed by loosely defined concepts (e.g., ring strain), where force fields excel, suggesting that the scientific language itself might impose constraints on LLMs. Notably, a model's ability to rank conformers is strongly associated with its performance on scientific, coding, and abstract-reasoning benchmarks, suggesting that it emerged unintendedly from models training on linked but conceptually different tasks. Thanks to this generalization of mere scientific knowledge into understanding molecular structures, current frontier models offer a realistic starting point for AI-driven molecular design.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates whether modern LLMs can reason about 3D molecular structure by testing them on conformer stability ranking across 810 geometries of 27 small organic molecules, finding that recent frontier models now rival or approach classical force fields and that this ability appears to emerge unintentionally from general scientific and reasoning training.
AI.motivation: LLMs have demonstrated strong performance on chemically oriented natural-language problems, but many real chemical tasks demand understanding of and reasoning about 3D molecular structures—capabilities that were neither explicitly intended by LLM developers nor previously benchmarked. Such structural understanding is considered essential for autonomous molecular discovery and drug development, a major goal of AI in chemistry, so the authors aimed to test whether this capability exists in contemporary models.
AI.method: The authors probed modern LLMs on 810 geometries and corresponding DFT energies drawn from 27 small organic molecules, using conformer stability ranking as the task. They compared model accuracy against classical force fields (Universal Force Field and GFN-FF), and analyzed the models' explanations for their rankings to identify which molecular features drive success or failure. They also correlated conformer-ranking performance with results on scientific, coding, and abstract-reasoning benchmarks.
AI.result: Models released before July 2025 struggled to rank conformers by stability. In contrast, many recent frontier models, including GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi K3, and Gemini 3.6 Flash, reached competitive accuracy and outperformed the Universal Force Field, while GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 came very close to a modern GFN-FF force field. Explanation analysis showed models perform best on molecules with well-defined intramolecular interactions such as hydrogen bonds, which are well quantified in scientific language, whereas all models except GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 struggled with molecules governed by loosely defined concepts like ring strain, where force fields excel. Conformer-ranking ability was strongly associated with performance on scientific, coding, and abstract-reasoning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Current frontier LLMs exhibit an emergent, unintended ability to reason about 3D molecular structure, apparently generalizing from training on linked but conceptually different tasks. This capability, however, remains uneven—strong where scientific language precisely captures the governing interactions and weak where concepts are loosely defined, hinting that scientific language itself may constrain models. Because of this generalization from mere scientific knowledge into structural understanding, frontier models offer a realistic starting point for AI-driven molecular design and autonomous molecular discovery.

title: The Roadmap of Inorganic Computational Materials Databases: Capabilities, Credibility, Coverage, and the Open Frontier
summary: Computational materials databases have become central infrastructure for data-driven discovery of inorganic materials, yet their growth remains strikingly uneven across property families. This perspective synthesizes a systematic survey of mainstream density functional theory (DFT) software, the computational cost and credibility of nineteen material-property families, and the coverage of existing computational databases, into a coherent picture of where the field stands and where it should go. We show that the ecosystem of first-principles codes is methodologically mature: for nearly every property of technological interest, at least one production-grade code can compute it.The binding constraint is no longer methodological capability but the economics of trust - which properties can be computed cheaply enough, and accurately enough, to be harvested at database scale. Mapping database coverage onto a Gartner-style readiness cycle reveals a sharp divide: ground-state structure, energetics, elasticity, and topology have reached routine production, while nine property families - including NMR/EPR parameters, core-level spectra, electron-phonon properties, thermal conductivity, and quantum transport - remain without any systematic computational database. We argue that these blank zones define the scientific opportunity of the next decade, and we propose a three-horizon roadmap: consolidating coverage and interoperability in the near term, industrializing mid-cost properties through surrogate-accelerated workflows in the medium term, and conquering the high-cost frontier through machine-learned interatomic potentials, autonomous computing infrastructure, and community governance in the long term.

AI.tldr: This perspective surveys DFT codes, property families, and database coverage, showing that computational infrastructure is methodologically mature but coverage is limited by "economics of trust"; nine property families lack systematic databases, and a three-horizon roadmap is proposed to close these gaps.
AI.motivation: Computational materials databases are central to data-driven inorganic materials discovery, yet their growth is uneven across property families. The authors aim to explain why this imbalance persists and to chart a direction for the field.
AI.method: Systematic survey of mainstream DFT software, assessment of computational cost and credibility across nineteen material-property families, and evaluation of existing computational database coverage, analyzed through a Gartner-style readiness cycle.
AI.result: The first-principles code ecosystem is methodologically mature—nearly every property of technological interest can be computed by at least one production-grade code. The binding constraint is the economics of trust. Database coverage splits sharply: ground-state structure, energetics, elasticity, and topology are in routine production, while nine families (including NMR/EPR parameters, core-level spectra, electron-phonon properties, thermal conductivity, and quantum transport) have no systematic computational database.
AI.conclusion: The uncovered "blank zones" represent the major scientific opportunity of the next decade. A three-horizon roadmap is proposed: near-term consolidation of coverage and interoperability; medium-term industrialization of mid-cost properties via surrogate-accelerated workflows; long-term conquest of the high-cost frontier using machine-learned interatomic potentials, autonomous computing infrastructure, and community governance.

title: Portfolio-Based Constrained Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization for Materials Design
summary: Materials discovery and design campaigns can be formulated as constrained multi-objective Bayesian optimization (CMOBO) problems, within which each experimental decision negotiates between two coupled but competing goals: discovering feasible candidates and refining the underlying Pareto front. Here we recast acquisition-function choice as an adaptive policy-selection problem over a portfolio of conventional and feasibility-focused acquisition functions. This was done using two controllers: UCB-Bandit, a modified UCB multi-armed bandit, and Agentic-Switch, a multi-agent decision system driven by a large language model (LLM). Both were evaluated against fixed-policy baselines in silico across five synthetic benchmark functions and two materials design case studies. The adaptive policies performed competitively in terms of both cumulative feasibility count and feasible hypervolume improvement, while each individual acquisition function performed well for only one metric, suggesting that adaptive policies are better suited for constrained materials science problems.

AI.tldr: Acquisition-function choice in constrained multi-objective Bayesian optimization is recast as an adaptive policy-selection problem, solved via a UCB bandit controller and an LLM-driven multi-agent controller, which outperform fixed acquisition policies on synthetic and materials design benchmarks by balancing feasibility discovery with Pareto front refinement.
AI.motivation: Materials discovery and design campaigns are naturally formulated as constrained multi-objective Bayesian optimization (CMOBO) problems, where each experimental decision must trade off two coupled but competing goals: discovering feasible candidates and refining the underlying Pareto front. Conventional practice relies on a single, fixed acquisition function, which cannot adequately balance these dual objectives. This motivates treating acquisition-function selection as an adaptive policy-selection problem over a portfolio of acquisition functions.
AI.method: The authors formulate acquisition-function choice as adaptive policy selection over a portfolio of conventional and feasibility-focused acquisition functions. Two controllers are proposed: UCB-Bandit, a modified UCB multi-armed bandit, and Agentic-Switch, a multi-agent decision system driven by a large language model (LLM). Both controllers adaptively select among the acquisition functions during the optimization campaign.
AI.result: The adaptive policies were evaluated against fixed-policy baselines in silico across five synthetic benchmark functions and two materials design case studies.
AI.conclusion: The adaptive policies (UCB-Bandit and Agentic-Switch) performed competitively on both cumulative feasibility count and feasible hypervolume improvement, whereas each individual fixed acquisition function excelled on only one metric. This indicates that adaptive policies are better suited for constrained materials science problems than any single fixed acquisition function.

title: Predictive Structure to Thermal Conductivity Modeling Framework for BEOL Interconnect Stacks in Advanced Technology Nodes Enabled by Extensive Layer Resolved Thermal Measurements
summary: The increasing structural complexity of BEOL interconnect stacks in advanced integrated circuits demands a structure-aware thermal conductivity (\k{appa}) modeling framework. However, generalizable models derived from layer-resolved thermal measurements that quantitatively capture the dependence of \k{appa} on interconnect structures remain lacking, limiting predictive thermal analysis. Here, we establish an experimentally derived, structure-aware \k{appa} modeling framework enabled by time-domain thermoreflectance measurements with ~100 nm depth resolution. Statistical analysis of a compiled dataset comprising over 40 experimentally measured layer-resolved \k{appa} values across diverse BEOL layers reveals a generalizable empirical structure-to-\k{appa} relationship, enabling predictive modeling based on interconnect structure. An intra-layer three-dimensional \k{appa} distribution model based on effective medium theory and realistic layouts further resolves spatial \k{appa} variations within practical interconnect layers. Together, these models establish an experimentally derived, structure-aware \k{appa} modeling framework for predictive and generalizable thermal analysis of advanced interconnect stacks and 3D ICs.

AI.tldr: This work presents an experimentally derived, structure-aware thermal conductivity (\k{appa}) modeling framework for BEOL interconnect stacks, built on time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) measurements with ~100 nm depth resolution, yielding a generalizable structure-to-\k{appa} relationship and an intra-layer 3D \k{appa} distribution model.
AI.motivation: Advanced integrated circuits feature increasingly complex BEOL interconnect stacks, which demand structure-aware \k{appa} modeling for predictive thermal analysis. However, generalizable models that are derived from layer-resolved thermal measurements and quantitatively capture how \k{appa} depends on interconnect structures remain lacking.
AI.method: Time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) measurements with ~100 nm depth resolution are used to obtain layer-resolved \k{appa} values. A compiled dataset of over 40 experimentally measured layer-resolved \k{appa} values across diverse BEOL layers is statistically analyzed to extract a generalizable empirical structure-to-\k{appa} relationship. An intra-layer 3D \k{appa} distribution model is constructed using effective medium theory combined with realistic interconnect layouts.
AI.result: Statistical analysis of the 40+ layer-resolved \k{appa} dataset reveals a generalizable empirical structure-to-\k{appa} relationship enabling predictive modeling from interconnect structure. The effective-medium-theory-based model further resolves spatial \k{appa} variations within practical interconnect layers.
AI.conclusion: The combined empirical structure-to-\k{kappa} relationship and intra-layer 3D \k{appa} distribution model form an experimentally derived, structure-aware \k{appa} modeling framework that supports predictive and generalizable thermal analysis of advanced interconnect stacks and 3D ICs.

title: Pressure-induced electronic and structural evolution of EuIrGe3
summary: We investigated the pressure-induced evolution of the electronic and crystal structure of the noncentrosymmetric BaNiSn3-type antiferromagnet EuIrGe3 using x-ray absorption spectroscopy, synchrotron x-ray diffraction complemented by density functional theory calculations, and electrical resistivity measurements. The Eu L3-edge spectra reveal a continuous increase in the mean Eu valence under compression, accompanied by modifications of the Ge and Ir electronic states. High- pressure x-ray diffraction shows anisotropic lattice compression in the tetragonal (I4mm) phase and provides evidence for a structural phase transition above 38 GPa. The experimentally deter- mined lattice and equation-of-state parameters are in good agreement with the DFT calculations. Electrical resistivity measurements reveal a monotonic increase in the antiferromagnetic ordering temperatures up to 18 GPa, indicating that the antiferromagnetic ground state remains robust despite the increasing contribution of the nonmagnetic Eu3+ configuration to the intermediate va- lence state. These results demonstrate that EuIrGe3 exhibits a pressure response distinct from EuCoGe3 and EuRhGe3, highlighting the important role of the transition metal d-electron states in the pressure-induced electronic and structural evolution of the EuT Ge3 family

AI.tldr: Pressure drives a continuous increase in Eu valence, anisotropic lattice compression, and a structural transition above 38 GPa in EuIrGe3, yet the antiferromagnetic order strengthens up to 18 GPa, unlike EuCoGe3 and EuRhGe3.
AI.motivation: The EuTGe3 family offers a platform to study how pressure tunes the interplay between Eu intermediate valence, magnetism, and crystal structure, but the specific role of transition-metal d-electron states in these pressure responses remains unclear, motivating a comparison of EuIrGe3 with EuCoGe3 and EuRhGe3.
AI.method: X-ray absorption spectroscopy at the Eu L3-edge, synchrotron x-ray diffraction complemented by density functional theory calculations, and electrical resistivity measurements were applied to the noncentrosymmetric BaNiSn3-type antiferromagnet EuIrGe3 under compression.
AI.result: Eu L3-edge spectra show a continuous increase in mean Eu valence with pressure, accompanied by changes in Ge and Ir electronic states. X-ray diffraction reveals anisotropic lattice compression in the tetragonal I4mm phase and a structural phase transition above 38 GPa. Experimental lattice and equation-of-state parameters agree well with DFT. Resistivity measurements show antiferromagnetic ordering temperatures increasing monotonically up to 18 GPa, so the antiferromagnetic ground state persists despite a growing nonmagnetic Eu3+ contribution.
AI.conclusion: EuIrGe3 exhibits a pressure response distinct from EuCoGe3 and EuRhGe3, underscoring the important role of transition-metal d-electron states in the pressure-induced electronic and structural evolution of the EuTGe3 family.

title: Generic thermodynamics of condensates with extremely small superfluid density ---Application to UTe$_2$ and hidden second phase transition---
summary:
Motivated by recent experimental findings on UTe$_2$ via NMR and specific heat experiments, we theoretically explore the thermodynamic signatures of condensates with small superfluid density and characterize their physical properties. We identify the hidden superconducting phase $A_2$ composed of spin-up Cooper pairs
  at lower temperature ($T$) and field ($H$) under ambient pressure of UTe$_2$ and show that $A_2$ reappears at higher $H$ for all three principal field directions, $a$, $b$, and $c$-axis. The phase transition lines from the $A_1$ phase with spin down pairs to the $A_2$ phase in the $H$-$T$ plane are all horizontal in common, implying a universal physical origin due to the originating from the magnetic-energy gain of the spin-up pairing state with increasing magnetic field. This multiple-phase diagram is extended to these under pressure ($P$), resulting in a simple picture based on non-unitary spin-triplet pairing symmetry $^3B_{3u}$, which enables us to consistently capture the evolution of the superconducting phases throughout the entire $H$-$T$-$P$ phase space.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically identifies a hidden superconducting phase A2 (spin-up Cooper pairs) in UTe2, showing it reappears at higher magnetic fields for all principal directions and constructing a unified H-T-P phase diagram based on non-unitary spin-triplet pairing symmetry.
AI.motivation: Recent NMR and specific heat experiments on UTe2 revealed unusual thermodynamic behavior suggesting condensates with small superfluid density, motivating a theoretical exploration of the thermodynamic signatures and physical properties of such superconducting states.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze condensates with small superfluid density, characterize their thermodynamic signatures, and construct phase transition lines in the H-T plane and extended H-T-P phase space, invoking non-unitary spin-triplet pairing symmetry (3B3u).
AI.result: The hidden superconducting phase A2, composed of spin-up Cooper pairs, appears at lower temperature and field under ambient pressure and reappears at higher fields for all three principal field directions (a, b, c-axis). Phase transition lines from A1 (spin-down pairs) to A2 in the H-T plane are universally horizontal, reflecting a magnetic-energy gain origin for spin-up pairing with increasing field.
AI.conclusion: The multiple-phase diagram extends to pressure, yielding a simple picture based on non-unitary spin-triplet pairing symmetry 3B3u that consistently captures the evolution of superconducting phases throughout the entire H-T-P phase space.

title: Martingale theory for heat and phase-space contraction in heterogeneous diffusions
summary: We investigate martingale properties of heat dissipated by generic non-equilibrium overdamped Langevin dynamics with multiple dimensions and transport coefficients that may depend explicitly on time and/or space. We find quantitative criteria that establish that heat dissipation may exhibit transient martingale (time-conserved), submartingale (time increasing), and supermartingale (time decreasing) properties in Langevin dynamics with drift coefficients with spatial non-linear dependencies. Furthermore, we reveal a tight link between the heat statistics at stopping (e.g. first-passage) times with that of a functional quantifying the phase-space contraction in the system dynamics. The theoretical results are used to predict the statistical properties of the heat dissipated by a spherical microscopic particle subject to gravity and double-layer forces and hydrodynamically interacting with a rigid wall, whose validity is confirmed by numerical simulations. These results extend the scope of stochastic energetics by revealing a non-trivial relation between heat fluctuations' statistical properties and the non-linear features of non-equilibrium processes.

AI.tldr: This paper studies martingale properties of heat dissipation in multi-dimensional, time/space-dependent non-equilibrium overdamped Langevin dynamics, establishing criteria for transient martingale, submartingale, and supermartingale behavior, linking heat statistics at stopping times to a phase-space contraction functional, and validating predictions via a microscopic particle simulation.
AI.motivation: Stochastic energetics typically characterizes heat fluctuations in non-equilibrium processes, but the martingale structure of dissipated heat—particularly under non-linear spatial drift and time/space-dependent transport coefficients—remains underexplored. A quantitative framework connecting heat fluctuation statistics to non-linear features of non-equilibrium dynamics is needed.
AI.method: The authors analyze generic non-equilibrium overdamped Langevin dynamics with multiple dimensions and transport coefficients depending explicitly on time and/or space. They derive quantitative criteria for transient martingale, submartingale, and supermartingale properties of heat dissipation under spatially non-linear drift. They further relate heat statistics at stopping (first-passage) times to a functional quantifying phase-space contraction, and apply the theory to a spherical microscopic particle under gravity, double-layer forces, and hydrodynamic interaction with a rigid wall, corroborated by numerical simulations.
AI.result: Quantitative criteria are established showing that heat dissipation can exhibit transient martingale, submartingale, and supermartingale behavior in Langevin dynamics with non-linear spatial drift. A tight link is revealed between heat statistics at stopping times and the phase-space contraction functional. Theoretical predictions for the spherical particle's dissipated heat statistics are confirmed by numerical simulations.
AI.conclusion: The work extends stochastic energetics by revealing a non-trivial relation between the statistical properties of heat fluctuations and the non-linear features of non-equilibrium processes, providing criteria for martingale behavior and stopping-time heat statistics in generic overdamped Langevin systems.

title: Divergent Solid-state Conversion Pathways in Evaporated All-perovskite Tandem Solar Cells
comment: 54 pages (main text: 20 pages, 5 figures; Supplementary Information: 34 pages, 30 figures, 2 tables)
summary: Sequential thermal evaporation (sTE) is emerging as a solvent-free route to high-quality mid-bandgap perovskites, but its extension to mixed-halide wide-bandgap (WBG) and Sn-Pb narrow-bandgap (NBG) absorbers for all-perovskite tandem solar cells (TSCs) remains limited by an incomplete understanding of solid-state conversion. Here, using time-sliced ex situ analysis, we reveal divergent solid-state conversion mechanisms in sequentially evaporated WBG and NBG precursor stacks. In WBG stacks, formamidinium (FA)-containing species penetrate the inorganic template and Br/I redistribution precedes substantial three-dimensional perovskite formation. The photoactive phase then crystallizes from a chemically mixed reservoir, and absolute PbBr$_2$ thickness, rather than nominal PbBr$_2$/PbI$_2$ ratio, determines the final bandgap. In NBG stacks, by contrast, an early Pb-rich perovskite phase forms upon formamidinium iodide deposition, restricting further FA penetration into the buried SnI$_2$ precursor. Subsequent annealing promotes rapid lattice reorganization faster than Sn/Pb interdiffusion, leaving vertical compositional gradients. Guided by these insights, we develop sTE absorbers with bandgaps spanning 1.26-1.96 eV and demonstrate the first evaporated all-perovskite TSC, reaching a power conversion efficiency of 19.2%. Encapsulated tandems retain on average 80% of their initial efficiency after 1,200 h at 65 $^\circ$C (ISOS-D-2). These results establish bandgap-specific control of solid-state conversion as a design principle for sequentially evaporated perovskite tandem photovoltaics.

AI.tldr: Time-sliced ex situ analysis reveals distinct solid-state conversion mechanisms in sequentially evaporated wide-bandgap and Sn-Pb narrow-bandgap perovskite stacks, enabling tunable bandgaps (1.26-1.96 eV) and the first evaporated all-perovskite tandem solar cell with 19.2% efficiency and good thermal stability.
AI.motivation: Sequential thermal evaporation (sTE) is a promising solvent-free route to high-quality mid-bandgap perovskites, but its extension to mixed-halide wide-bandgap (WBG) and Sn-Pb narrow-bandgap (NBG) absorbers for all-perovskite tandem solar cells (TSCs) is hindered by an incomplete understanding of the solid-state conversion process.
AI.method: The authors employed time-sliced ex situ analysis to track the solid-state conversion of sequentially evaporated WBG and NBG precursor stacks, identifying mechanism-specific intermediate phases, elemental redistribution, and crystallization pathways. Guided by these insights, they engineered sTE absorbers across a wide bandgap range and fabricated evaporated all-perovskite tandem solar cells.
AI.result: WBG and NBG stacks exhibit divergent conversion mechanisms: in WBG stacks, FA-containing species penetrate the inorganic template with Br/I redistribution preceding 3D perovskite formation, and absolute PbBr2 thickness (not the nominal PbBr2/PbI2 ratio) sets the final bandgap; in NBG stacks, an early Pb-rich perovskite phase upon FAI deposition restricts FA penetration into buried SnI2, and annealing drives rapid lattice reorganization outpacing Sn/Pb interdiffusion, leaving vertical compositional gradients. The resulting sTE absorbers span bandgaps of 1.26-1.96 eV, and the first evaporated all-perovskite TSC achieves 19.2% PCE, with encapsulated tandems retaining on average 80% of initial efficiency after 1,200 h at 65 °C (ISOS-D-2).
AI.conclusion: Bandgap-specific control of solid-state conversion is established as a design principle for sequentially evaporated perovskite tandem photovoltaics, enabling high-performance, thermally stable evaporated all-perovskite tandem solar cells.

title: Hydrogen Reorganization in Hot Dense Ammonia
summary: Hydrogen is known to form stable compounds with a variety of simple molecular solids under high pressure. However, ammonia hydride has not been experimentally observed. Here, through a series of laser-heating diamond anvil cell (LHDAC) experiments, we observed the transparent ionic ammonia transformed into an opaque phase above 150 GPa and 1000 K. Raman spectroscopy reveals a pronounced structural change, accompanied by the emergence of two distinct asymmetric H$_2$ vibrons ($ν_1$ and $ν_2$). A new ionic phase produced following thermally induced dissociation and hydrogen reorganization in hot dense ammonia. The combination of experimental results and first-principles calculations identify this phase as the theoretically predicted ionic $P4_12_12$ phase of NH$_7$ , which consists of NH$_4^+$, H$^-$and H$_2$ units. Our results suggest that the formation of ammonia hydrides follows a thermodynamic pathway distinct from those of other H$_2$-containing mixtures, revealing a new ionic transformation pathway driven by hydrogen reorganization in hot dense ammonia.

AI.tldr: This study reports the first experimental observation of an ionic ammonia hydride (NH₇) formed via laser heating of ammonia above 150 GPa and 1000 K, identified as the theoretically predicted ionic P4₁2₁2 phase.
AI.motivation: Hydrogen forms stable compounds with many simple molecular solids at high pressure, but ammonia hydride has never been experimentally observed. The motivation is to probe whether ammonia can form hydrides under extreme conditions and to understand the transformation pathway.
AI.method: Laser-heating diamond anvil cell (LHDAC) experiments combined with Raman spectroscopy and first-principles calculations.
AI.result: Transparent ionic ammonia transformed into an opaque phase above 150 GPa and 1000 K. Raman spectroscopy revealed a pronounced structural change with two distinct asymmetric H₂ vibrons (ν₁ and ν₂). Experiment and calculations jointly identify the phase as the ionic P4₁2₁2 phase of NH₇, composed of NH₄⁺, H⁻, and H₂ units.
AI.conclusion: The formation of ammonia hydrides follows a thermodynamic pathway distinct from other H₂-containing mixtures, revealing a new ionic transformation pathway driven by hydrogen reorganization in hot dense ammonia.

title: Coplanar Lateral Gating MoS2 on SrTiO3: A Unified Platform for Classical and Quantum Devices
summary: Atomically thin transition-metal dichalcogenides, such as MoS2, offer a promising route to surpass the scaling limits of silicon owing to their excellent electrostatic control and resilience to short-channel effects. Realizing this potential depends critically on gate-stack engineering, where strong gate coupling must be achieved without compromising the pristine two-dimensional interface. Here, we demonstrate a coplanar lateral-gating architecture for MoS2 field-effect transistors fabricated directly on single-crystal SrTiO3. The exceptionally high permittivity of SrTiO3 enhances gate-channel coupling. The coplanar geometry eliminates the need for a separate gate insulator, reducing interface disorder. Owing to the quantum paraelectric nature, the SrTiO3 dielectric constant increases upon cooling, enhancing the gate coupling, leading to a decrease in threshold voltage and subthreshold swing an effect that contrasts with conventional FET architectures. The dielectric-free MoS2 surface, combined with enhanced electrostatic control, makes this architecture a promising platform for low-power two-dimensional electronics and cryogenic quantum devices.

AI.tldr: A coplanar lateral-gating MoS2 FET on single-crystal SrTiO3 achieves strong gate coupling without a separate gate insulator, exploiting SrTiO3's high permittivity and quantum paraelectric behavior to improve subthreshold performance upon cooling.
AI.motivation: Atomically thin transition-metal dichalcogenides like MoS2 can surpass silicon scaling limits due to excellent electrostatic control and short-channel resilience, but this requires gate-stack engineering that provides strong gate coupling without degrading the pristine 2D interface.
AI.method: Fabricated MoS2 field-effect transistors directly on single-crystal SrTiO3 using a coplanar lateral-gating architecture, eliminating the separate gate insulator and leaving a dielectric-free MoS2 surface, while leveraging SrTiO3's high permittivity for gate-channel coupling.
AI.result: Enhanced gate-channel coupling was achieved; the coplanar geometry reduced interface disorder. Due to SrTiO3's quantum paraelectric nature, its dielectric constant increased upon cooling, strengthening gate coupling and lowering both threshold voltage and subthreshold swing—opposite to conventional FET behavior.
AI.conclusion: The dielectric-free MoS2 surface combined with enhanced electrostatic control makes this architecture a promising platform for low-power 2D electronics and cryogenic quantum devices.

title: Emergent Surface Kondo Flat Band Driven by Competing Interactions in a Topological Ferromagnet
summary: A central goal of modern condensed matter physics is to uncover new quantum states of matter arising from the intertwined effects of strong electron correlations, magnetism, and band topology. Heavy-fermion phases, generated by Kondo interactions, represent one of the most remarkable manifestations of electronic correlations, and topological heavy-fermion states have been identified in several non-magnetic materials. Yet, the consequences of their competition with magnetic order have remained largely unexplored. Here, we reveal a new phenomenon: the spontaneous spatial separation of correlated quantum phases. By showing that magnetism can drive distinct strongly correlated electronic states to coexist in different regions of a single material, our work establishes a previously unknown mechanism for organizing quantum matter and opens a new direction in the study of correlated topological systems. Using \emph{bulk-sensitive} probes, we show that UAsS crystals are, in the bulk, metallic ferromagnets with only moderate correlation-driven band renormalizations. First-principles calculations reveal a topological electronic structure hosting both nodal lines and Weyl points, pointing to a rich underlying topology. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) measurements are consistent with these predictions, resolving the nodal lines and Weyl crossings. In striking contrast, \emph{surface-sensitive} ARPES and scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy (STM/STS) measurements reveal a pronounced flat band pinned at the Fermi level, accompanied by a sharp resonance -- hallmarks of an emergent, strongly correlated Kondo state not captured by first-principles calculations.

AI.tldr: UAsS crystals exhibit a spontaneous spatial separation of quantum phases: a bulk metallic ferromagnet with topological nodal lines/Weyl points, coexisting with a surface-layer strongly correlated Kondo state marked by a Fermi-level flat band.
AI.motivation: Topological heavy-fermion states from Kondo interactions are known in non-magnetic materials, but how they compete with magnetic order remains largely unexplored. The paper aims to investigate the interplay of strong correlations, magnetism, and band topology.
AI.method: Bulk-sensitive probes plus first-principles calculations; ARPES to resolve nodal lines and Weyl crossings; surface-sensitive ARPES and STM/STS to probe the surface electronic structure.
AI.result: Bulk UAsS is a metallic ferromagnet with moderate correlation-driven band renormalization and a topological electronic structure hosting nodal lines and Weyl points, consistent with ARPES. Surface-sensitive ARPES and STM/STS reveal a pronounced flat band pinned at the Fermi level with a sharp resonance, indicating an emergent strongly correlated Kondo state absent from first-principles calculations.
AI.conclusion: Magnetism can drive distinct strongly correlated electronic states to coexist in different regions of one material, establishing a new mechanism for organizing quantum matter and a new direction for correlated topological systems.

title: Type-I superconductivity in a quasi-2D topologically nontrivial YbBi$_2$
summary: Intrinsic superconductivity in stoichiometric materials with nontrivial electronic topology remains uncommon, limiting opportunities to investigate how these two phenomena coexist within a single electronic system. Here, we report bulk type-I superconductivity below $T_c$ $\sim$ 0.9~K in YbBi$_2$, a layered rare-earth compound with a nonsymmorphic crystal structure and a quasi-two-dimensional Fermi surface. Thermodynamic and transport measurements establish the superconducting ground state, while quantum oscillations reveal exceptionally light carriers, with a cyclotron mass as low as 0.07 $m_e$, and a nonzero Berry phase of approximately 0.82 $π$. The latter closely matches the calculated value of the corresponding Wilson phase 0.99 $π$ for the corresponding orbit near a symmetry-protected band degeneracy. ARPES measurements show good agreement with key features of the calculated electronic structure, providing complementary experimental constraints on the normal-state band structure. The combination of intrinsic type-I superconductivity, light quasi-two-dimensional carriers, and signatures of nontrivial electronic topology identifies YbBi$_2$ as a distinct stoichiometric platform for investigating superconductivity in a topologically nontrivial electronic environment.

AI.tldr: YbBi₂, a stoichiometric nonsymmorphic layered rare-earth compound, hosts intrinsic bulk type-I superconductivity below ~0.9 K coexisting with topologically nontrivial electronic features, including extremely light carriers and a nonzero Berry phase.
AI.motivation: Intrinsic superconductivity in stoichiometric materials with nontrivial electronic topology is uncommon, which limits studies of how superconductivity and band topology interact within a single electronic system. The work aims to identify a stoichiometric platform where both phenomena coexist.
AI.method: The study combines thermodynamic and transport measurements to establish the superconducting ground state; quantum oscillation measurements to extract cyclotron masses and the Berry phase; first-principles calculations of the Wilson phase and band structure; and ARPES to experimentally constrain the normal-state band structure.
AI.result: Bulk type-I superconductivity is observed below Tc ~ 0.9 K in YbBi₂, which adopts a nonsymmorphic crystal structure with a quasi-two-dimensional Fermi surface. Quantum oscillations reveal exceptionally light carriers with a cyclotron mass as low as 0.07 me and a nonzero Berry phase of ~0.82π, close to the calculated Wilson phase of 0.99π for the corresponding orbit near a symmetry-protected band degeneracy. ARPES results agree well with key features of the calculated electronic structure.
AI.conclusion: YbBi₂ is identified as a distinct stoichiometric platform combining intrinsic type-I superconductivity, light quasi-two-dimensional carriers, and signatures of nontrivial electronic topology, enabling investigation of superconductivity in a topologically nontrivial electronic environment.

title: Global Minima of the Thomson Problem in a Disk: A Molecular Dynamics Approach with Fixed Border Charges
summary: We report improved global-minimum configurations for the classical Thomson problem of $N=60$, $61$, $92$, and $99$ repulsive Coulomb charges confined to a disk. By combining the quenched molecular dynamics (QMD) method with the fixed-border heuristic introduced by Amore and Zarate, we systematically obtain configurations with energies $E_{\mathrm{QMD}}(60)=2159.3584240930$, $E_{\mathrm{QMD}}(61)=2237.19264190$, $E_{\mathrm{QMD}}(92)=5358.35353314$, and $E_{\mathrm{QMD}}(99)=6254.83029083$, which improve upon the previously best-known values. For $N=60$, the Voronoi diagram of our configuration differs from the one reported earlier. The symmetries for $N=61$ $(C_{2})$ and $N=99$ $(D_{1})$ are confirmed and are consistent with the known symmetry patterns for these configurations. For $N=92$, whereas the previously reported Voronoi diagram has lower symmetry, our solution exhibits a clear $D_{1}$ (axial) symmetry of defects. The results are highly reproducible across multiple independent runs, providing strong evidence that these configurations are robust global-minimum candidates.

AI.tldr: The paper reports improved global-minimum configurations for the classical Thomson problem (repulsive Coulomb charges confined to a disk) at N=60, 61, 92, and 99, using a combination of quenched molecular dynamics and the fixed-border heuristic, achieving lower energies than previously known and confirming or revising symmetry and Voronoi-diagram properties.
AI.motivation: The classical Thomson problem seeks the global-minimum energy arrangement of repulsive charges on a confining surface, and finding true global minima is computationally hard because the energy landscape has many local minima. Prior best-known configurations for disk-confined systems at certain N (notably 60, 61, 92, 99) left room for improvement and uncertainty about their symmetries and defect structures.
AI.method: The authors combine the quenched molecular dynamics (QMD) method with the fixed-border heuristic of Amore and Zarate. QMD quenches trajectories to nearby local minima, while the fixed-border heuristic constrains border particles, together efficiently exploring the configurational space. Configurations are obtained for N=60, 61, 92, and 99, then characterized via energy values, Voronoi diagrams, and symmetry analysis, with reproducibility tested across multiple independent runs.
AI.result: Improved energies are obtained: E_QMD(60)=2159.3584240930, E_QMD(61)=2237.19264190, E_QMD(92)=5358.35353314, and E_QMD(99)=6254.83029083, all beating previous best-known values. For N=60 the Voronoi diagram differs from the earlier reported one. Symmetries for N=61 (C2) and N=99 (D1) are confirmed and consistent with known symmetry patterns. For N=92, the previously reported Voronoi diagram has lower symmetry, whereas the new solution shows a clear D1 (axial) symmetry of defects. Results are highly reproducible across independent runs.
AI.conclusion: The combined QMD plus fixed-border approach yields lower-energy configurations for the disk-confined Thomson problem at N=60, 61, 92, and 99, revising prior best-known results and clarifying their symmetries and defect/Voronoi structures. The high reproducibility across multiple runs provides strong evidence that these configurations are robust global-minimum candidates.

title: Grain Boundary Distortion Reorients the Local 4f Easy Axis and Splits Light from Heavy Lanthanides in Nd2Fe14B
summary: The coercivity of rare-earth permanent magnets originates from the crystal field acting on localized 4f electrons, yet how grain boundaries modify the underlying single-ion Hamiltonian remains largely unknown.
