Here we determine the 4f crystal field in bulk and grain-boundary environments of Nd2Fe14B using embedded multireference electronic-structure calculations for the substitutional series Ce, Pr, Nd, Gd, Tb, and Dy. Grain-boundary distortion produces a crossover across the lanthanide series: the crystal field weakens by up to 36% for light lanthanides but strengthens by about 25% for heavy lanthanides, with Nd marking the crossover. The ground-state doublet of Dy becomes more isolated and axial, whereas Ce exhibits a collapsed low-lying excitation that suppresses anisotropy. The local easy axis rotates from the bulk c axis toward the basal plane, identifying grain-boundary sites as favorable nucleation centers for magnetization reversal. These results provide an atomistic basis for heavy rare-earth grain-boundary diffusion and furnish transferable single-ion parameters for spin-lattice simulations.

AI.tldr: Grain boundaries in Nd2Fe14B reverse the crystal-field trend across the lanthanide series: it weakens for light rare earths (up to 36%) but strengthens for heavy ones (~25%), rotating the local easy axis toward the basal plane and marking boundary sites as nucleation centers for reversal.
AI.motivation: Coercivity in rare-earth permanent magnets arises from crystal fields acting on localized 4f electrons, but how grain boundaries alter the underlying single-ion Hamiltonian is largely unknown.
AI.method: Embedded multireference electronic-structure calculations determine the 4f crystal field in bulk and grain-boundary environments of Nd2Fe14B across the substitutional series Ce, Pr, Nd, Gd, Tb, and Dy.
AI.result: Grain-boundary distortion creates a crossover: the crystal field weakens by up to 36% for light lanthanides but strengthens by ~25% for heavy ones, with Nd at the crossover. Dy's ground-state doublet becomes more isolated and axial, while Ce gains a collapsed low-lying excitation suppressing anisotropy. The local easy axis rotates from the bulk c axis toward the basal plane.
AI.conclusion: The results give an atomistic basis for heavy rare-earth grain-boundary diffusion and provide transferable single-ion parameters for spin-lattice simulations.

title: Non-Thermal Effects in Fermionic Atoms Coupled to Open Cavities
summary: We study a Fermi-Hubbard model coupled to a open dissipative single cavity mode. Using Keldysh diagrammatics we derive and solve the quantum kinetic equations for the fermions, taking the bosonic cavity mode as a source of non-equilibrium noise and dissipation. In absence of Hubbard interactions we show that the fermions reach generically a non-equilibrium steady-state, characterized by a non-thermal distribution function. Quite interestingly we demonstrate that the latter exactly nullifies the heat-current between fermions and cavity mode. We discuss the regimes of parameters where a low-frequency effective temperature description emerges and how the fluctuations affect the mean-field phase diagram for the superradiance phase transition. Finally we include Hubbard interaction in the weak-coupling regime and show that it leads to a crossover towards a full equilibrium distribution.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes quantum kinetic equations for fermions in a Fermi-Hubbard model coupled to a dissipative cavity mode via Keldysh diagrammatics. Without interactions, fermions reach a non-equilibrium steady state with a non-thermal distribution that nullifies the fermion-cavity heat current; a low-frequency effective temperature regime emerges. Hubbard interactions at weak coupling drive a crossover toward full equilibrium.
AI.motivation: Cavity-coupled Fermi-Hubbard systems are platforms where non-equilibrium noise and dissipation from a bosonic mode coexist with strong electronic correlations, yet a controlled quantum-kinetic description of how cavity fluctuations shape fermionic steady states and the superradiance transition is needed.
AI.method: Keldysh diagrammatics (non-equilibrium field theory) is used to derive and solve quantum kinetic equations for the fermions, treating the single bosonic cavity mode as a source of non-equilibrium noise and dissipation. The analysis proceeds first without Hubbard interactions, then extends to the weak-coupling Hubbard regime, including a mean-field treatment of the superradiance phase transition.
AI.result: In the absence of Hubbard interactions, fermions generically reach a non-equilibrium steady state with a non-thermal distribution function, and this distribution exactly nullifies the heat current between fermions and the cavity mode. A low-frequency effective-temperature description emerges in certain parameter regimes. Cavity fluctuations modify the mean-field phase diagram of the superradiance transition. Adding weak Hubbard interactions produces a crossover toward a full equilibrium distribution.
AI.conclusion: Dissipative cavity fluctuations alone drive fermions to a distinct non-equilibrium steady state that is heat-current-free yet non-thermal, while weak Hubbard interactions restore equilibration, revealing a competition between cavity-induced non-equilibrium behavior and interaction-driven relaxation that shapes both transport and the superradiance phase diagram.

title: Superconductivity in Pb2-xBixPd Single Crystals
summary: Chemical substitution provides an effective route to tune the structural and superconducting properties and to explore the evolution of superconductivity across related materials. In this work, we investigate the effect of Pb/Bi mixing on superconductivity in possible topological superconductors \ch{Pb2Pd} and $β$-\ch{Bi2Pd}, by synthesizing and characterizing single crystals of \ch{Pb_{2-x}Bi_{x}Pd} ($0.2\le x\le1.8$). Increasing Bi content triggers a structural phase transition from non-symmorphic ($I4/mcm$, $x<1$) to layered ($I4/mmm$, $x\ge1$) and induces a monotonic expansion of the lattice parameters. Across the doped range, all superconducting samples behave as weakly-coupled type-II superconductors exhibiting isotropic s-wave superconducting gaps.

AI.tldr: A solid-solution series Pb$_{2-x}$Bi$_x$Pd ($0.2\le x\le1.8$) was synthesized and characterized, revealing a Bi-driven structural transition and weakly-coupled, isotropic s-wave superconductivity throughout the doped range.
AI.motivation: Chemical substitution offers a tunable route to modify structural and superconducting properties and to track the evolution of superconductivity between related materials, which is desirable for probing possible topological superconductors such as Pb$_2$Pd and β-Bi$_2$Pd.
AI.method: Single crystals of Pb$_{2-x}$Bi$_x$Pd ($0.2\le x\le1.8$) were synthesized and characterized via structural and superconducting measurements.
AI.result: Increasing Bi content induces a structural phase transition from the non-symmorphic I4/mcm phase ($x<1$) to a layered I4/mmm phase ($x\ge1$) and causes monotonic lattice expansion. All superconducting samples are weakly-coupled type-II superconductors with isotropic s-wave gaps.
AI.conclusion: Pb/Bi mixing tunes the structure and lattice parameters of Pb$_2$Pd–β-Bi$_2$Pd while preserving robust, isotropic s-wave superconductivity across the doped range.

title: Coherent and ultra-low-power EDSR with a flopping-mode spin qubit in germanium
summary: Hole spin qubits in semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) enable high-fidelity all-electric control, but conventional electric dipole spin resonance (EDSR) can require substantial rf drive power at the low magnetic fields that are favorable for qubit coherence and readout. In planar Ge hole spin qubits, this can reach -27 dBm at the device, posing challenges for scalable architectures due to heating and crosstalk. Here, we demonstrate a flopping-mode (FM) qubit in Ge, where a single spin is delocalized in a double QD, combining first-order protection against charge noise with exceptionally efficient electric driving. By mapping out coherence sweet-spots as a function of magnetic field orientation we achieve $T_2^*= 1.4μ\mathrm{s}$, $T_2^{\mathrm{Hahn}}= 11.5 μ\mathrm{s}$, $T^{φ, \mathrm{CPMG32}}_2= 130 μ\mathrm{s}$, and $T_1= 226 μ\mathrm{s}$, and a single-qubit gate fidelity of up to 99.76$\%$ for a gate time $t_{Xπ} = 88$ ns. Importantly, these results are obtained at a nearly in-plane magnetic field of 5 mT using only -52 dBm drive power at the device. We further find that qubit relaxation in this regime is consistent with a two-photon Orbach process, providing a route for further optimization. Our results demonstrate that FM-EDSR supports ultra-low-power, high-fidelity single-qubit operations, improvements that could benefit scalable hole-spin-based architectures and hybrid spin-photon interfaces.

AI.tldr: A flopping-mode hole spin qubit in planar Ge is demonstrated, achieving high-fidelity single-qubit gates at 5 mT using only -52 dBm drive power, enabled by efficient flopping-mode EDSR and charge-noise protection.
AI.motivation: Hole spin qubits in semiconductor quantum dots allow all-electric control, but conventional EDSR at low magnetic fields (favorable for coherence and readout) demands high rf drive power, reaching -27 dBm in planar Ge, which causes heating and crosstalk problems for scalable architectures. A more power-efficient driving scheme is needed.
AI.method: The authors implement a flopping-mode (FM) qubit in Ge, delocalizing a single spin in a double quantum dot to combine first-order protection against charge noise with efficient electric driving. They map coherence sweet spots versus magnetic field orientation and characterize coherence times and gate fidelity, using nearly in-plane magnetic field of 5 mT and -52 dBm drive power.
AI.result: Coherence metrics: T2* = 1.4 μs, T2 Hahn = 11.5 μs, T2^{φ,CPMG32} = 130 μs, T1 = 226 μs. Single-qubit gate fidelity up to 99.76% for gate time t_Xπ = 88 ns. These achieved at 5 mT nearly in-plane field with only -52 dBm drive power. Relaxation in this regime is consistent with a two-photon Orbach process.
AI.conclusion: FM-EDSR enables ultra-low-power, high-fidelity single-qubit operations, potentially benefiting scalable hole-spin-based architectures and hybrid spin-photon interfaces, with the identified Orbach relaxation providing a route for further optimization.

title: Collective Charge-\(2e\) Bosonic Excitations in Charge-Ordered Systems
summary: Charge order is conventionally characterized by a static modulation of the electronic density, while its collective excitations remain less developed from a quasiparticle perspective than those of spin-ordered systems. Here, we formulate the collective excititations of charge order within an effective charge-pseudospin model, in which the charge-ordered ground state is represented by staggered pseudospin order. Quantizing fluctuations around this ordered state via a Holstein--Primakoff transformation, we reveal two branches of bosonic quasiparticles with degenerate, gapped dispersions that carry opposite quantized electric charges $\pm 2e$. We therefore term these charge-$2e$ bosons ``\textit{bichargons},'' closely paralleling the two magnon branches of a bipartite antiferromagnet that carry opposite spin angular momenta. We show that a temperature gradient drives the diffusion of thermally excited bichargons, generating a charge Seebeck response when the degeneracy between the oppositely charged branches is lifted by tuning the chemical potential away from the charge-neutrality point. In contrast, despite carrying finite electric charges, a thermal bichargon gas remains electrically insulating under a static electric field because bichargon quasiparticle number is not conserved. An ac electric field, however, can parametrically generate coherent pairs of oppositely charged bichargons that support a finite dc drift current in the presence of a bias electric field, offering a bosonic analogue of photoconductivity mediated by photoexcited electron--hole pairs in semiconductors. Our results establish bichargons as a new class of collective bosonic charge carriers in charge-ordered systems and extend the quasiparticle paradigm of magnons in spin-ordered systems to the charge sector, with electric charge replacing spin angular momentum as the transported quantity.

AI.tldr: This work develops a charge-pseudospin model for collective excitations of charge order, identifying "bichargons"—two bosonic quasiparticle branches with opposite quantized charges ±2e—and showing they yield charge Seebeck and a bosonic analogue of photoconductivity.
AI.motivation: Charge order is conventionally described by static electronic density modulation, and its collective excitations remain underdeveloped as quasiparticles compared to the well-established magnons of spin-ordered systems.
AI.method: The authors formulate collective excitations within an effective charge-pseudospin model, representing the charge-ordered ground state as staggered pseudospin order. They quantize fluctuations via a Holstein–Primakoff transformation and analyze transport responses (temperature gradient, static and ac electric fields).
AI.result: Two bosonic quasiparticle branches emerge with degenerate, gapped dispersions carrying opposite quantized electric charges ±2e (termed bichargons), paralleling the two magnon branches of a bipartite antiferromagnet. A temperature gradient drives bichargon diffusion, producing a charge Seebeck response when degeneracy is lifted by tuning chemical potential off charge neutrality. The bichargon gas is electrically insulating under a static field (number not conserved), but an ac field can parametrically generate coherent bichargon pairs supporting a finite dc drift current under bias.
AI.conclusion: Bichargons constitute a new class of collective bosonic charge carriers in charge-ordered systems, extending the magnon quasiparticle paradigm to the charge sector with electric charge replacing spin angular momentum as the transported quantity.

title: Orbital fingerprinting of magnetism across the Mn-Ni-Ga Heusler ternary
summary: In Mn--Ni--Ga Heusler alloys, the competing magnetic states are separated by differences of a few meV per atom, so the ground state has to be resolved from the electronic structure and cannot be read off the composition. Moving away from the stoichiometric compounds, where the established rules for Heusler magnetism fall short, increases this difficulty. To overcome it, we introduce orbital fingerprints taken from the projected density of states, and use them as the input to machine-learning models for classification of the magnetic ordering, for the magnetic moment amplitude, for the spin polarization at the Fermi level and for interpolation of the phase diagram. The models are trained on a dataset of 370 spin-polarized first-principles calculations of quasirandom structures covering the ternary, which show good agreement with the magnetic ground states and lattice parameters available in the literature. For magnetic ordering, the top-ranked descriptor is the same quantity found by first-principles calculations to distinguish the phases, suggesting that the fingerprints capture the underlying physics.

AI.tldr: Orbital fingerprints from projected density of states serve as machine-learning inputs to classify magnetic ordering, predict moment amplitude, spin polarization at the Fermi level, and interpolate the phase diagram of Mn-Ni-Ga Heusler alloys.
AI.motivation: In Mn-Ni-Ga Heusler alloys, competing magnetic states differ by only a few meV per atom, so the ground state must be resolved from electronic structure. Established Heusler magnetism rules fall short away from stoichiometry, and this off-stoichiometric regime remains difficult to characterize.
AI.method: The authors introduce orbital fingerprints extracted from the projected density of states and use them as inputs to machine-learning models for four tasks: magnetic ordering classification, magnetic moment amplitude prediction, spin polarization at the Fermi level, and phase-diagram interpolation. Models are trained on 370 spin-polarized first-principles calculations of quasirandom structures spanning the ternary composition space.
AI.result: The models achieve good agreement with magnetic ground states and lattice parameters reported in the literature. For magnetic ordering, the top-ranked descriptor coincides with the quantity identified by first-principles calculations as distinguishing the phases.
AI.conclusion: Orbital fingerprints from the projected density of states capture the underlying physics governing magnetism in off-stoichiometric Mn-Ni-Ga Heusler alloys, enabling reliable machine-learning prediction of magnetic ordering, moments, spin polarization, and phase-diagram interpolation.

title: Unconstrained compact lattice QED$_{2+1}$ coupled to phonons: Gauss sectors, orthogonal semimetal, and deconfined criticality
summary: Gauge theoretic descriptions of 2D quantum magnets are defined on a restricted physical Hilbert space by imposing Gauss's law. In this work, we study an unconstrained compact lattice QED$_{2+1}$ coupled to bond phonons, in which local Gauss operators are conserved, but their eigenvalues are not a priori fixed. Using exact auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations at $N_f = 2$, we investigate how the physical Gauss sector becomes energetically favourable, and how this process is connected to confinement and symmetry breaking. We identify an orthogonal semimetallic (OSM) phase, in which fermions striped off their gauge charge and form a Dirac liquid. This phase mixes various Gauss sectors, and becomes unstable when Gauss's law is explicitly enforced. Upon the imposition of Gauss's law, compactness allows for monopole excitations carrying antiferromagnetic (AFM) and valence-bond-solid (VBS) quantum numbers. Gauge field fluctuations and spinon-phonon coupling tune between the competition of such monopoles and generate a phase diagram with OSM, AFM and VBS orders. The transitions out of the OSM phase coincide with the dynamical generation of Gauss's law, while the competition between AFM and VBS charged monopoles produces a transition consistent with deconfined quantum criticality. Thus our results establish that upon the projection to the physical Hilbert space, deconfinement in compact lattice QED$_{2+1}$ is always unstable towards either AFM or VBS order.

AI.tldr: This work studies an unconstrained compact lattice QED$_{2+1}$ coupled to bond phonons, using exact auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo at $N_f = 2$. It identifies an orthogonal semimetallic (OSM) phase that mixes Gauss sectors, and shows that enforcing Gauss's law dynamically generates monopole excitations carrying AFM and VBS quantum numbers, yielding a phase diagram with OSM, AFM, and VBS orders.
AI.motivation: Gauge-theoretic descriptions of 2D quantum magnets are conventionally defined on a restricted physical Hilbert space via Gauss's law. This work asks how the physical Gauss sector becomes energetically favourable and how this process connects to confinement and symmetry breaking, addressing whether deconfinement in compact lattice QED$_{2+1}$ survives projection to the physical Hilbert space.
AI.method: Exact auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations at $N_f = 2$ on an unconstrained compact lattice QED$_{2+1}$ coupled to bond phonons, where local Gauss operators are conserved but their eigenvalues are not fixed a priori. The study analyzes the energetics of Gauss sectors, the imposition of Gauss's law, monopole excitations, and the tuning via gauge field fluctuations and spinon-phonon coupling.
AI.result: An orthogonal semimetallic (OSM) phase is identified, in which fermions shed their gauge charge and form a Dirac liquid; this phase mixes Gauss sectors and becomes unstable when Gauss's law is explicitly enforced. Upon imposing Gauss's law, compactness permits monopole excitations carrying AFM and VBS quantum numbers. Gauge field fluctuations and spinon-phonon coupling tune the competition among these monopoles, producing a phase diagram with OSM, AFM, and VBS orders. Transitions out of the OSM phase coincide with dynamical generation of Gauss's law, and the AFM-VBS monopole competition yields a transition consistent with deconfined quantum criticality.
AI.conclusion: Upon projection to the physical Hilbert space, deconfinement in compact lattice QED$_{2+1}$ is always unstable toward either AFM or VBS order.

title: Machine Learning for High-Entropy Catalysts: Methods and Applications
summary: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) exhibit exceptional catalytic performance in various reactions due to their high configurational entropy, synergistic elemental effects, tunable electronic structures, and excellent structural stability. However, the vast compositional space of HEA catalysts makes traditional experimental and theoretical design costly and inefficient. In recent years, data-driven machine learning (ML) methods have emerged as powerful tools for studying HEAs in catalysis. Through predictive models and ML surrogates, researchers can decipher the intricate composition-structure-performance relationships of these materials. In addition, by leveraging large language models (LLMs) for knowledge extraction, hypothesis generation and validation, and as a foundation to build integrated design workflows, ML approaches can significantly accelerate the design of novel HEA catalysts. This review systematically summarizes the latest methodological advances and applications of ML methods for HEAs in catalysis, discusses the challenges, and offers insights into future research directions to support the rational design and efficient development of catalysts.

AI.tldr: This review summarizes recent advances in applying machine learning and large language models to high-entropy alloy (HEA) catalyst design, covering predictive models, composition-structure-performance mapping, and integrated design workflows.
AI.motivation: HEAs show exceptional catalytic performance due to high configurational entropy, synergistic elemental effects, tunable electronic structures, and structural stability, but their vast compositional space makes traditional experimental and theoretical design costly and inefficient, motivating data-driven alternatives.
AI.method: The review systematically surveys machine learning approaches for HEA catalysis, including predictive models and ML surrogates for deciphering composition-structure-performance relationships, alongside large language models used for knowledge extraction, hypothesis generation and validation, and as a foundation for integrated design workflows.
AI.result: ML methods, particularly predictive models and surrogates, enable researchers to decode intricate composition-structure-performance relationships of HEA catalysts, while LLMs facilitate knowledge extraction and hypothesis generation/validation within integrated workflows.
AI.conclusion: Machine learning can significantly accelerate the design of novel HEA catalysts; the review outlines challenges and future directions to support rational design and efficient catalyst development.

title: Multiconfigurational Analysis of Local Electronic Structure of $\mathrm{RuO_2}$ Using Relativistic Embedded Clusters
summary: We present a multiconfigurational, relativistic embedded-cluster study of the local electronic structure of ruthenium dioxide ($\mathrm{RuO_2}$), a candidate altermagnetic material. Starting from free $\mathrm{Ru}$ ions, we progressively build up the local environment through a $\mathrm{Ru+Q_6}$ electrostatic model, a bare $\mathrm{[RuO_6]^{8-}}$ ligand model, and finally a high-accuracy $\mathrm{RuO_6}$@CTEP embedded cluster that reproduces the crystalline surroundings. All systems are treated at the SA-CASSCF and NEVPT2+SOC levels of theory to capture strong electron correlation and spin-orbit coupling on an equal footing. While the formal local site symmetry of the $\mathrm{Ru}$ sites in $\mathrm{RuO_2}$ is orthorhombic ($D_{2h}$), we find that the calculated $4d$-orbital energy spectrum and its splitting pattern behave much closer to the higher tetragonal ($D_{4h}$) symmetry, preserving a strong quasi-degeneracy among the relevant $4d$ orbitals. Since the local $xy$ quadrupolar order responsible for altermagnetic spin splitting in independent-particle models relies on this symmetry reduction, its suppression by orbital quasi-degeneracy offers a natural explanation for why altermagnetism is not observed in bulk $\mathrm{RuO_2}$ experiments, in contrast to the robust altermagnetic signatures reported in strained thin films.

AI.tldr: A multiconfigurational relativistic embedded-cluster study finds that the local 4d orbital spectrum of Ru in RuO2 behaves closer to tetragonal (D4h) than orthorhombic (D2h) symmetry, with strong quasi-degeneracy that suppresses the xy quadrupolar order needed for altermagnetic spin splitting, explaining the absence of bulk altermagnetism.
AI.motivation: RuO2 is a widely discussed candidate altermagnet, yet bulk experiments fail to observe the altermagnetic spin splitting seen in strained thin films. The origin of this discrepancy is unresolved, motivating a closer look at the local electronic structure and orbital symmetry at the Ru sites.
AI.method: The authors perform a multiconfigurational relativistic embedded-cluster study, progressively building the local environment from free Ru ions via a Ru+Q6 electrostatic model and a bare [RuO6]8- ligand model to a high-accuracy RuO6@CTEP embedded cluster reproducing the crystalline surroundings, all treated at the SA-CASSCF and NEVPT2+SOC levels to treat strong correlation and spin-orbit coupling on equal footing.
AI.result: Although the formal local site symmetry is orthorhombic (D2h), the calculated 4d-orbital energy spectrum and splitting pattern resemble the higher tetragonal (D4h) symmetry, preserving a strong quasi-degeneracy among the relevant 4d orbitals.
AI.conclusion: The local xy quadrupolar order underlying altermagnetic spin splitting in independent-particle models depends on the orthorhombic symmetry reduction; its suppression by orbital quasi-degeneracy provides a natural explanation for the absence of altermagnetism in bulk RuO2, in contrast to strained thin films.

title: Lyapunov-controlled thermalization: an exact real-time example
summary: A verified Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (KMS) relation, after a drive has ceased, is not sufficient evidence to prove equilibrium. We demonstrate this in a large-$N$ large-$q$ Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) quench protocol. Although all post-quench fermion correlators are exactly thermal, a second quench back to the initial Hamiltonian reveals hidden memory of the initial state. It is encoded in correlators connecting to times before the first quench. This memory is an extensive nonequilibrium (NEQ) witness with its decay rate being the Lyapunov exponent $λ_L$. Thus $λ_L$ sets the rate at which the state becomes effectively indistinguishable from a Gibbs state. Despite being a unitary interacting many-body system, the complete NEQ real-time evolution is obtained exactly in the large-$N$, large-$q$ limit, making the setup ideal for analytically studying thermalization.

AI.tldr: A verified KMS relation after a drive ceases does not guarantee equilibrium: in a large-N, large-q SYK quench protocol, all post-quench correlators are exactly thermal, yet a second quench reveals hidden memory of the initial state whose decay rate equals the Lyapunov exponent.
AI.motivation: Equilibrium is often inferred from the Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (KMS) relation once a drive stops. The paper questions whether satisfying the KMS relation is truly sufficient to prove equilibrium, and seeks a counterexample in a solvable many-body system.
AI.method: A quench protocol in the large-N, large-q Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model: a first quench drives the system, then a second quench returns it to the initial Hamiltonian. Correlators connecting to times before the first quench are computed exactly in the large-N, large-q limit.
AI.result: Although all post-quench fermion correlators are exactly thermal (obeying KMS), the second quench exposes hidden memory of the initial state encoded in correlators linking to pre-first-quench times. This memory is an extensive nonequilibrium witness whose decay rate is the Lyapunov exponent λ_L, which thus sets the rate at which the state becomes effectively indistinguishable from a Gibbs state.
AI.conclusion: KMS relation alone is insufficient evidence of equilibrium. The exactly solvable large-N, large-q SYK quench setup makes the full nonequilibrium real-time evolution accessible, providing an ideal framework for analytically studying thermalization.

title: Modeling Dynamic Magnetic Response of Spinel Soft Ferrites with the Steepest-Entropy-Ascent Quantum Thermodynamics Formalism
summary: Selecting soft ferrites for alternating-field applications requires balancing magnetic response, dissipation, nonlinearity, and heating. We use a field-driven steepest-entropy-ascent quantum thermodynamic (SEAQT) model to compare the electron, phonon, and magnon responses of Fe$_3$O$_4$, MnFe$2$O$4$, and (Mn${0.5}$Zn${0.5}$)Fe$_2$O$_4$ within a common first-principles framework. The model treats spatially uniform longitudinal relaxation and neglects domain-wall motion, transverse rotation, resonance, eddy-current effects, and heat removal. We use $τ_e=0.05$ ps and $τ_p=3$ ps for all three materials, with effective longitudinal magnon relaxation times of 500, 200, and 85 ps, respectively; these literature-motivated values are model inputs, not fits to measured losses. Within this framework, the Mn--Zn ferrite gives the largest peak longitudinal magnetization change, retains its response best at high frequency, and shows the largest work per cycle and peak-to-peak magnon temperature change, whereas MnFe$_2$O$_4$ gives the largest normalized $χ''$ peak. Thus, no single ferrite ranks highest across all metrics: the preferred material depends on the property, frequency, field amplitude, and cation configuration of interest. The model therefore provides a spectrum- and kinetics-resolved screening tool for engineering comparison of ferrites rather than a prediction of total core loss.

AI.tldr: A field-driven steepest-entropy-ascent quantum thermodynamic model compares electron, phonon, and magnon responses of three soft ferrites, showing that no single material ranks best across all metrics and that material choice depends on the target property and operating conditions.
AI.motivation: Selecting soft ferrites for alternating-field (AC) applications requires balancing magnetic response, dissipation, nonlinearity, and heating. A common first-principles framework is needed to compare candidate materials on a consistent basis, since conventional loss measurements do not resolve the underlying electron, phonon, and magnon kinetics.
AI.method: A field-driven steepest-entropy-ascent quantum thermodynamic (SEAQT) model is applied to Fe3O4, MnFe2O4, and (Mn0.5Zn0.5)Fe2O4. The model treats spatially uniform longitudinal relaxation and neglects domain-wall motion, transverse rotation, resonance, eddy-current effects, and heat removal. Fixed relaxation times are used: tau_e = 0.05 ps and tau_p = 3 ps for all materials, with effective longitudinal magnon relaxation times of 500, 200, and 85 ps respectively. These literature-motivated values serve as model inputs rather than fits to measured losses.
AI.result: The Mn-Zn ferrite exhibits the largest peak longitudinal magnetization change, retains its response best at high frequency, and shows the largest work per cycle and peak-to-peak magnon temperature change. MnFe2O4 yields the largest normalized chi'' peak. Therefore, no single ferrite ranks highest across all metrics.
AI.conclusion: The preferred ferrite depends on the property, frequency, field amplitude, and cation configuration of interest. The SEAQT model functions as a spectrum- and kinetics-resolved screening tool for engineering comparison of ferrites, not as a prediction of total core loss.

title: Ultralow-Tensile Strain Enables Exciton Funneling and Energy Transfer to Boost MoSe2 Photoluminescence Quantum Yield
summary: Strain engineering is a powerful route for controlling the exciton dynamics in van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures (HSs). The interlayer energy transfer (ET) process is another key factor in controlling the photocarrier relaxation pathways in vdW HSs. In this work, we combine these two processes to achieve an 8-fold enhancement to the relative photoluminescence (PL) quantum yield (QY) in a HS formed from monolayers of ReS2 and MoSe2, separated by a thin hBN interlayer, placed onto an hBN bubble. We achieve this enhancement by applying only 0.1% biaxial tensile strain, which results in efficient exciton funneling and an increased transition dipole moment. Our experimental data are supported by first-principles density-functional theory and coherent transfer-matrix method calculations, ruling out optical interference as the dominant origin of the enhancement. This work provides an innovative route for enhancing the PL QY of vdW materials via interplay between the tensile strain and the ET process.

AI.tldr: Combining strain engineering with interlayer energy transfer yields an 8-fold enhancement of the relative photoluminescence quantum yield in a ReS2/MoSe2 van der Waals heterostructure separated by thin hBN and placed on an hBN bubble, achieved with only 0.1% biaxial tensile strain.
AI.motivation: Strain engineering and interlayer energy transfer are both key routes for controlling exciton dynamics and photocarrier relaxation pathways in van der Waals heterostructures, but their combined effect on photoluminescence quantum yield had not been exploited.
AI.method: The authors fabricated a heterostructure from monolayers of ReS2 and MoSe2 separated by a thin hBN interlayer and placed onto an hBN bubble, applying 0.1% biaxial tensile strain. Experimental measurements were supported by first-principles density-functional theory and coherent transfer-matrix method calculations.
AI.result: An 8-fold enhancement of the relative photoluminescence quantum yield was obtained, attributed to efficient exciton funneling and an increased transition dipole moment. Calculations ruled out optical interference as the dominant origin of the enhancement.
AI.conclusion: The interplay between tensile strain and the interlayer energy transfer process provides an innovative route for enhancing the photoluminescence quantum yield of van der Waals materials.

title: Engineering Weak Universality with Quantum Dots
summary: Quantum critical theories with continuously varying critical exponents remain challenging to access experimentally. Here, we propose quantum-dot architectures for realizing the quantum Ashkin-Teller and XYZ/eight-vertex models using resonator-mediated and direct Coulomb interactions, respectively. We focus on the Ashkin-Teller and eight-vertex critical lines, which are connected by a non-local duality relating local order parameters to topological string operators. The resulting platforms provide microscopic control over the parameters explicitly controlling critical exponents, with the Coulomb-based implementation enabling stronger interaction regimes. We demonstrate that continuously varying critical behavior can already be resolved in short chains. For experimentally realistic parameters, the accessible interaction range is expected to produce changes in the critical exponents of order $10\%$ for the Ashkin-Teller model and substantially larger changes for the eight-vertex model. In both cases, the predicted variations lie well above the estimated measurement uncertainties.

AI.tldr: The authors propose quantum-dot architectures to realize the quantum Ashkin-Teller and XYZ/eight-vertex models, enabling experimental access to quantum critical theories with continuously varying critical exponents.
AI.motivation: Quantum critical theories with continuously varying critical exponents are difficult to access experimentally, so a controllable platform is needed to tune and resolve these exponents.
AI.method: Proposes quantum-dot architectures based on resonator-mediated interactions (Ashkin-Teller) and direct Coulomb interactions (XYZ/eight-vertex), exploiting a non-local duality linking local order parameters to topological string operators.
AI.result: Continuously varying critical behavior is resolvable in short chains; realistic parameters yield critical-exponent changes of order 10% for the Ashkin-Teller model and substantially larger changes for the eight-vertex model, exceeding estimated measurement uncertainties.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-dot platforms provide microscopic control over parameters governing critical exponents, offering a viable route to experimentally probe continuously varying quantum criticality.

title: Coherent antiferromagnetic resonance in MnO driven by impulsive terahertz excitation
summary: Antiferromagnets (AFMs) offer a promising platform for ultrafast information processing owing to their intrinsically fast spin dynamics and vanishing net magnetization. Realizing this potential, however, requires understanding how terahertz fields excite coherent magnons and how the resulting spin motion is transduced into an optical signal. Here we report impulsive terahertz (THz) excitation and time-domain detection of the antiferromagnetic resonance (AFMR) in single-crystal manganese(II) oxide. Time-resolved birefringence measurements reveal long-lived coherent spin oscillations in the AFM phase. The resonance softens and becomes strongly damped upon warming toward the Néel temperature. Despite this similar excitation behavior, the detected birefringence in MnO is markedly weaker than in NiO. We associate this suppressed optical visibility with the weak spin--orbit-mediated magneto-optical coupling of orbital-singlet, high-spin Mn$^{2+}$. These results demonstrate that coherent magnon excitation and its optical detection are governed by distinct microscopic interactions.

AI.tldr: Impulsive THz excitation and time-domain detection of antiferromagnetic resonance in single-crystal MnO reveal long-lived coherent spin oscillations, a softening and strong damping near the Néel temperature, and markedly weaker birefringence than NiO due to weak spin-orbit magneto-optical coupling of orbital-singlet high-spin Mn²⁺.
AI.motivation: Antiferromagnets are attractive for ultrafast information processing thanks to intrinsically fast spin dynamics and vanishing net magnetization, but exploiting this requires understanding how terahertz fields excite coherent magnons and how the resulting spin motion is transduced into an optical signal.
AI.method: Impulsive terahertz (THz) excitation combined with time-domain detection of the antiferromagnetic resonance (AFMR) in single-crystal manganese(II) oxide (MnO), using time-resolved birefringence measurements across temperatures up to the Néel temperature, with comparison to NiO.
AI.result: Time-resolved birefringence reveals long-lived coherent spin oscillations in the AFM phase. The resonance softens and becomes strongly damped upon warming toward the Néel temperature. Despite similar excitation behavior, the detected birefringence in MnO is markedly weaker than in NiO, attributed to weak spin-orbit-mediated magneto-optical coupling of orbital-singlet, high-spin Mn²⁺.
AI.conclusion: Coherent magnon excitation and its optical detection are governed by distinct microscopic interactions, as evidenced by the contrast between similar excitation behavior and strongly suppressed optical visibility in MnO relative to NiO.

title: Spacetime Dynamics of Altermagnetic Magnons
summary: Distinguishing altermagnetism from conventional ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism typically relies on momentum-space probes. Here, we show that the real-space spreading of a localized spin excitation provides a distinctive dynamical fingerprint of altermagnetic order. Using linear spin-wave theory on a two-dimensional checkerboard lattice with nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor couplings J_1 and J_2, we demonstrate that finite J_2 produces direction-dependent magnon group velocities and splits the two magnon branches. The resulting propagation remains closer to that of an antiferromagnet than a ferromagnet, retaining an approximately circular outer wavefront, while the direction-dependent magnon velocities produce a pronounced cross-like spatial structure inside this front. We further show that changing the sign of J_2 to enter the unfrustrated regime (J_2<0) increases the characteristic propagation velocities and interchanges the diagonal directions of enhanced propagation, corresponding to a pi/2 rotation of the anisotropic spatial pattern. These results establish spacetime dynamics as a complementary probe of altermagnetic magnons, providing a route to identifying unconventional magnetic order through real-space propagation patterns in solid-state and synthetic quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that the real-space spreading pattern of a localized spin excitation, governed by direction-dependent magnon group velocities in a J1-J2 checkerboard lattice, serves as a distinctive dynamical fingerprint of altermagnetic order.
AI.motivation: Identifying altermagnetism conventionally requires momentum-space probes, which is experimentally demanding; a complementary, real-space diagnostic is therefore desirable.
AI.method: Linear spin-wave theory is applied to a two-dimensional checkerboard lattice with nearest-neighbor (J1) and next-nearest-neighbor (J2) couplings to compute magnon dispersions and the spacetime propagation of a localized spin excitation.
AI.result: Finite J2 induces direction-dependent magnon group velocities and splits the two magnon branches. The propagation retains an approximately circular outer wavefront (closer to antiferromagnetic than ferromagnetic behavior), while anisotropic velocities create a pronounced cross-like internal spatial structure. Reversing the sign of J2 (unfrustrated regime, J2<0) increases characteristic propagation velocities, interchanges the enhanced-propagation diagonal directions, and rotates the anisotropic pattern by pi/2.
AI.conclusion: Spacetime dynamics offer a complementary probe of altermagnetic magnons, enabling identification of unconventional magnetic order through real-space propagation patterns in solid-state and synthetic quantum systems.

title: Statistics, 't Hooft Anomaly, and the Else-Nayak Index: a careful comparison of concepts
summary: Generalized symmetries and topological excitations, as well as symmetry anomalies and the statistics of topological excitations, are widely believed to be related. There are, however, pitfalls in how this relation is established. A lattice truncation of a symmetry transformation to a finite patch gives a symmetry patch operator that creates symmetry defects at its boundary. This geometric picture resembles a hopping operator creating topological excitations at the boundary of its support, but does not provide well-defined statistics, let alone guarantee agreement with the symmetry anomaly. A more natural and robust relation is that the hopping operators of topological excitations are symmetric: they commute with symmetry transformations. Under suitable assumptions, this condition yields a one-to-one correspondence between statistics and anomalies. We further couple boundary matter to a DW gauge field in one higher dimension to explain this relation from the perspective of gauging. A hopping operator is, in essence, a gauge-invariant operator acting on the physical degrees of freedom after gauging. Once the gauge-field background is fixed, global symmetry comes from gauge transformations that preserve that background, while the symmetric condition on hopping is precisely the remaining gauge invariance. This distinction clarifies potential misconceptions in the literature and provides a more reliable framework for comparing symmetries and topological excitations.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that the correct, robust relation between symmetry anomalies and the statistics of topological excitations is that hopping operators commute with symmetry transformations, and explains this via a gauging perspective using a DW gauge field in one higher dimension.
AI.motivation: The widely believed relation between generalized symmetries, symmetry anomalies, and the statistics of topological excitations is often established through a flawed geometric picture: truncating a symmetry transformation to a finite patch yields a symmetry patch operator that creates symmetry defects at its boundary. This resembles a hopping operator creating topological excitations, but does not provide well-defined statistics nor guarantee agreement with the anomaly. The work aims to clarify these pitfalls and correct misconceptions in the literature.
AI.method: The authors replace the flawed patch-operator analogy with a more natural and robust condition: the hopping operators of topological excitations must be symmetric, i.e., commute with symmetry transformations. Under suitable assumptions this condition yields a one-to-one correspondence between statistics and anomalies. They further couple boundary matter to a DW (domain-wall) gauge field in one higher dimension to explain the relation from the perspective of gauging.
AI.result: Under suitable assumptions, the symmetry condition on hopping operators gives a one-to-one correspondence between the statistics of topological excitations and symmetry anomalies. In the gauging picture, a hopping operator is essentially a gauge-invariant operator acting on the physical degrees of freedom after gauging; once the gauge-field background is fixed, the global symmetry arises from gauge transformations preserving that background, and the symmetric condition on hopping is precisely the remaining gauge invariance.
AI.conclusion: The distinction between symmetry patch operators and symmetric hopping operators clarifies potential misconceptions and provides a more reliable framework for comparing symmetries with topological excitations.

title: A Computational Method to Simulate Electrostatic Actuation in Polycatenated Architected Materials
summary: A novel class of polycatenated architected materials (PAMs) has recently emerged, exhibiting distinctive mechanical properties such as stress-strain hysteresis and a geometry-driven transition between solid-like and fluid-like behavior. Although finite element models exist for conventional PAMs, none currently account for electrostatic effects. Here, we propose and qualitatively validate a computational framework to simulate the structure, dynamics, and mechanical response of electrostatically charged PAMs. Our approach successfully reproduces electrostatic actuation in close agreement with experiments, and reveals that electrostatic charges enable a reversible fluid-to-solid transition while also providing a means to estimate electrostatic stiffness. Notably, stiffness enhancements of up to sevenfold are achieved upon charging. This work expands the design space of PAMs and offers a predictive tool for actively controllable mechanical metamaterials.

AI.tldr: The authors propose and qualitatively validate a computational framework to simulate structure, dynamics, and mechanical response of electrostatically charged polycatenated architected materials (PAMs), reproducing electrostatic actuation and revealing a reversible fluid-to-solid transition with up to sevenfold stiffness enhancement upon charging.
AI.motivation: Existing finite element models for conventional PAMs do not account for electrostatic effects, leaving a gap in predictive tools despite PAMs' distinctive mechanical properties (stress-strain hysteresis, geometry-driven solid-like/fluid-like transitions) and the potential of active controllability.
AI.method: A computational framework is proposed to simulate the structure, dynamics, and mechanical response of electrostatically charged PAMs; it is qualitatively validated against experiments on electrostatic actuation, and further used to estimate electrostatic stiffness and analyze charging-induced transitions.
AI.result: The framework reproduces electrostatic actuation in close agreement with experiments, reveals that electrostatic charges enable a reversible fluid-to-solid transition, and provides a means to estimate electrostatic stiffness, with stiffness enhancements of up to sevenfold upon charging.
AI.conclusion: The work expands the design space of PAMs and offers a predictive tool for actively controllable mechanical metamaterials.

title: Tuning the Coercive Field in Ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2-Al2O3 Heterostructures via Interfacial Charge Dynamics
comment: 35 manuscript pages, 7 figures, 12 supplemental pages, 17 supplemental figures
summary: Interleaving dielectric layers into ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 (HZO) films increases the memory window (MW) beyond what is accounted for by the dielectric constants. Determining the physical mechanisms behind these MW improvements is critical to reaching the full potential of HZO FeNAND. Here, we show that MW improvements stem from the interfacial charge dynamics enabled by oxygen vacancies at the interlayer interface. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy(XPS) etching experiments demonstrate increased off-stoichiometry at the interface, with a 2.3x increase in oxygen vacancies. Polarization-dependent XPS and first-order reversal curves(FORC) show that tunneling between interfacial defect states causes a bidirectional internal bias of 0.56MV/cm. The impact of defects is further corroborated through phase-field modeling(PFM), which only recreates the coercive fields, FORC, and internal bias for defect densities and tunneling barrier heights that are consistent with experiment, quantitatively capturing an internal electric field of 0.55 MV/cm. The phase field models are then used to simulate 36 devices with varied charge densities and dielectric thickness to provide a predictive framework for further improvements in the MW of interlayer HZO. These findings redefine the role of defects in ferroelectric HZO from deleterious to engineerable and provide critical insights into how to tune ferroelectric device architectures for improved memory.

AI.tldr: Interfacial oxygen vacancies and tunneling between defect states, not dielectric constants, drive the memory window improvements in interlayer ferroelectric HZO films.
AI.motivation: Interleaving dielectric layers into ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 (HZO) films improves the memory window (MW) beyond what dielectric constants alone can explain. Identifying the underlying physical mechanisms is critical to realizing the full potential of HZO FeNAND.
AI.method: X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) etching experiments, polarization-dependent XPS, first-order reversal curves (FORC), and phase-field modeling (PFM) were combined to probe interfacial charge dynamics and defect behavior. PFM simulations were extended to 36 devices with varied charge densities and dielectric thicknesses.
AI.result: XPS etching revealed increased off-stoichiometry at the interlayer interface with a 2.3x increase in oxygen vacancies. Polarization-dependent XPS and FORC showed that tunneling between interfacial defect states induces a bidirectional internal bias of 0.56 MV/cm. PFM reproduced the coercive fields, FORC, and internal bias only for defect densities and tunneling barrier heights consistent with experiment, quantitatively capturing an internal electric field of 0.55 MV/cm.

These findings redefine defects in ferroelectric HZO from deleterious to engineerable and provide a predictive framework for tuning ferroelectric device architectures to enhance memory performance.

title: Strain-Induced Metal-to-Insulator Transition in Antiferromagnetic SrCrO$_3$ Thin Films
comment: 10 Pages, 4 figures, Supplement Information with additional 5 pages, 7 figures
summary: Antiferromagnetic (AF) metals are rare, yet they combine properties attractive for spintronic devices like robustness against stray fields and electrical readout. Among AF metal oxide candidates, SrCrO$_3$ remains largely unexplored due to its notoriously difficult synthesis. In this paper, we demonstrate the growth of high-quality SrCrO$_3$ thin films by magnetron sputtering on substrates that impose a wide range of tensile and compressive strains. Muon spin relaxation experiments, supported by x-ray magnetic dichroism, unveil the emergence of an AF phase with dilute magnetic disorder at low temperatures, while resistivity measurements confirm the simultaneous metallic ground state of SrCrO$_3$ under low strain. As both compressive and tensile strain increase, a metal-to-insulator transition is induced in the films, while the onset of the magnetic transition temperature remains unchanged. Moreover, an intriguing resistivity upturn, accompanied by a change in the dominant charge-carrier type, occurs at a temperature that correlates with strain. These observations suggest a complex strain-dependent band structure, with strain-induced Jahn-Teller distortions or tilting of the CrO$_6$ octahedra that emerge depending on the sign of the strain, as inferred from density functional theory calculations.

AI.tldr: High-quality SrCrO3 thin films grown by magnetron sputtering across a range of strains reveal a dilute-disorder AF phase coexisting with a metallic ground state at low strain, while increasing compressive or tensile strain drives a metal-to-insulator transition without changing the magnetic ordering temperature.
AI.motivation: Antiferromagnetic metals are rare but attractive for spintronics (stray-field robustness, electrical readout). SrCrO3 is a promising AF metal oxide candidate but remains largely unexplored because of its notoriously difficult synthesis.
AI.method: Magnetron sputtering growth of high-quality SrCrO3 thin films on substrates imposing a wide range of tensile and compressive strains; muon spin relaxation (μSR) supported by x-ray magnetic dichroism to probe magnetism; resistivity measurements for transport/ground state; density functional theory calculations to interpret band structure and structural distortions.
AI.result: An AF phase with dilute magnetic disorder emerges at low temperatures, with a simultaneous metallic ground state under low strain. Increasing compressive or tensile strain induces a metal-to-insulator transition while the magnetic transition onset temperature stays unchanged. A resistivity upturn accompanied by a change in dominant charge-carrier type occurs at a strain-correlated temperature.
AI.conclusion: The observations indicate a complex strain-dependent band structure, with strain-induced Jahn-Teller distortions or tilting of CrO6 octahedra emerging depending on the sign of the strain, as inferred from DFT calculations.

title: Magnon-Phonon Dynamics in Multidimensional Antiferromagnetic Oxides
summary: Antiferromagnetic oxides offer a compelling paradigm for magnonics. Combining ab initio and spin Hamiltonian modeling, we map Cr2O3 from bulk to monolayer limits, verifying stability via phonon spectra. Contrary to previously predicted half-metallic ferromagnetic monolayer phases, we conclusively demonstrate that monolayer and bilayer configurations preserve an antiferromagnetic semiconductor ground state despite systematic gap narrowing. Intersecting magnon and phonon branches drive strong hybridization, establishing low-dimensional Cr2O3 as an ideal platform for quantum spintronics.

AI.tldr: Monolayer and bilayer Cr2O3 retain an antiferromagnetic semiconducting ground state (not the previously predicted half-metallic ferromagnetic phase) despite gap narrowing; strong magnon–phonon hybridization makes low-dimensional Cr2O3 a promising quantum spintronics platform.
AI.motivation: Antiferromagnetic oxides are attractive for magnonics, but prior predictions suggested that low-dimensional Cr2O3 could host half-metallic ferromagnetic phases, leaving the true ground state of monolayer/bilayer Cr2O3 unclear.
AI.method: Combined ab initio calculations with spin Hamiltonian modeling, mapping Cr2O3 from bulk to monolayer, with phonon spectra used to verify structural/dynamical stability.
AI.result: Monolayer and bilayer Cr2O3 preserve an antiferromagnetic semiconductor ground state with systematic gap narrowing, contradicting earlier half-metallic ferromagnetic predictions. Magnon and phonon branches intersect, producing strong magnon–phonon hybridization.
AI.conclusion: Low-dimensional Cr2O3 is established as an ideal platform for quantum spintronics, driven by its stable antiferromagnetic semiconducting character and pronounced magnon–phonon hybridization.

title: Spin-Lattice Dynamics and Interactions in Magnonic Spinels
summary: Minimizing magnetic damping while understanding spin-lattice interactions remains a key challenge for magnonics. We show site-specific Al/Li ordering in spinel ferrites drives a ferrimagnetic insulating state, quenching the Fermi-level density of states. \textit{Ab initio} calculations reveal collective acoustic modes alongside sub-lattice-selective optical modes on tetrahedral and octahedral networks, providing a microscopic understanding of substitution-driven spin dynamics. Crucially, the low-frequency magnon and acoustic phonon modes intersect, driving strong hybridization for low-loss technologies.

AI.tldr: Site-specific Al/Li ordering in spinel ferrites induces a ferrimagnetic insulating state and enables magnon–phonon hybridization for low-loss magnonics.
AI.motivation: Magnonics faces a persistent challenge: minimizing magnetic damping while understanding spin-lattice interactions. The paper aims to address this by investigating how site-specific cation substitution drives spin dynamics in spinel ferrites.
AI.method: Site-specific Al/Li ordering in spinel ferrites is demonstrated, and ab initio calculations are used to identify collective acoustic modes and sub-lattice-selective optical modes on tetrahedral and octahedral networks.
AI.result: The site-specific Al/Li ordering drives a ferrimagnetic insulating state that quenches the Fermi-level density of states. Ab initio calculations reveal collective acoustic modes and sub-lattice-selective optical modes. Low-frequency magnon and acoustic phonon modes intersect, enabling strong hybridization.
AI.conclusion: Substitution-driven spin dynamics in spinel ferrites are microscopically understood, and the magnon–phonon hybridization offers a pathway toward low-loss magnonic technologies.

title: First-principles theory of phonon renormalization from nonlinear electron-phonon interactions
summary: Electron-phonon interactions renormalize phonon frequencies and lifetimes and are central to the dynamical properties of solids. While these effects are usually described within linear electron-phonon coupling, the role of nonlinear electron-phonon interactions for phonon properties remains largely unexplored. In this work, we study phonon renormalization arising from the long-range linear one-electron-one-phonon and the nonlinear one-electron-two-phonon interactions within a diagrammatic framework. We derive the corresponding self-energy diagrams, which depend on the chemical potential and temperature, and evaluate them from first principles for the two polar semiconductors LiF and KTaO$_3$. In both materials, the two interaction channels renormalize the phonon spectrum in qualitatively distinct ways. The linear contribution is sharply localized near the Brillouin-zone center, whereas the nonlinear process couples an incoming phonon to other branches throughout the spectrum. As a result, it renormalizes phonons across the entire Brillouin-zone, with a pronounced temperature dependence governed by the thermal occupation of those branches. This behavior provides a clean experimental signature of the one-electron-two-phonon coupling. While the nonlinear phonon renormalization is small in LiF, it is somewhat larger in KTaO$_3$, which we attribute to its greater number of thermally populated phonon branches at room temperature. Our results establish a general framework to assess nonlinear electron-phonon effects on the phonon properties in materials with stronger lattice fluctuations, including soft semiconductors such as lead-halide perovskites.

AI.tldr: This work develops a diagrammatic first-principles framework to compute phonon renormalization from linear one-electron-one-phonon and nonlinear one-electron-two-phonon interactions, showing that the nonlinear channel renormalizes phonons across the entire Brillouin zone with distinct temperature dependence in LiF and KTaO3.
AI.motivation: Phonon frequencies and lifetimes are central to solid dynamics, but while linear electron-phonon coupling is well established, the role of nonlinear electron-phonon interactions in phonon renormalization remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors use a diagrammatic framework to derive self-energy diagrams for phonon renormalization arising from long-range linear one-electron-one-phonon and nonlinear one-electron-two-phonon interactions, with dependencies on chemical potential and temperature. title: A Gaussian process coarse-grained potential for Na-montmorillonite
summary: Hydraulic transport in compacted bentonite is diffusion-controlled and governed by the hydration and microstructure of sodium montmorillonite (Na-MMT). Experiments cannot resolve how platelet interactions govern pore structure, transport and stiffness, while existing coarse-grained models smooth hydration oscillations or require manual corrections. We develop a tabulated potential combining Morse interactions between platelet centre and edge sites with a Gaussian process regression correction trained on all-atom potentials of mean force. It captures the hydration-induced complexity of the potential-of-mean-force profiles, including the three-water (3-W) hydration minimum and transfers across geometries, layer-charge variants and unseen configurations. Applied to monodisperse and polydisperse Na-MMT assemblies at dry densities of 0.8-1.3 g cm^-3, the model captures the 3-W to 1-W transition, loss of non-interlayer porosity and evolution of pore structure, random-walk tortuosity, diffusion and stiffness. Predicted diffusion agrees with compacted Na-bentonite measurements.
